title: Gemini app limiting what models free & AI Plus users can access, AI Pro adding Deep Think
snippet: Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access. more…
fullText:
Following the compute-based usage change in May, Google will soon introduce limits on which Gemini models free users and AI Plus subscribers can access.

According to an updated support document this week, Gemini app users without a Google AI subscription will be limited to the (3.5) Flash-Lite model. Starting October 9, users who do not pay for Gemini will no longer be able to access (3.6) Flash or (3.1) Pro.

Meanwhile, AI Plus subscribers will be limited to Flash-Lite and Flash, with Pro no longer available. These $4.99 per month users will “receive an email that explains when these changes will take effect.”

There are no regressions for AI Pro and AI Ultra. Rather, $19.99/month customers will get access to the Deep Think option for “maximum parallel reasoning” that’s currently just on the $99.99 and $199.99/month plans.

	

Gemini 3.1 Pro with Deep Think on AI Ultra

In October, the Gemini app also looks to be adding new “low,” “medium,” and “high” effort levels “for each available model.”

This will increase the model’s ability to complete tasks and provide more thorough answers to queries, but will also use more of your limit.  

At the moment, you can just enable “Extended thinking: Complex problem solving.” The three new effort/thinking levels would match what’s available in Google AI Studio and Antigravity.

It’s not clear where Gemini 4 Argon will fit in. Google announced earlier this week that it’s first coming to AI Ultra subscribers. The company has yet to specify whether Argon will be classified as a Pro model or be part of a new tier above it.

title: Maximizing Privacy? New Apple Home Security Cameras Reportedly Won’t Record Video
snippet: Instead of a watchable video stream, you’ll get text descriptions or alerts about detected people, pets or activity.
fullText:
From Flock AI-powered security cameras to Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses, people are getting frustrated with their everyday movements being recorded and tracked. Apple likely smells a market opportunity to do something different.

According to Bloomberg News Managing Editor and Apple insider Mark Gurman, the company is developing a home security camera that can detect and notify about intruders — without capturing video footage. The device would be a companion to the new AI-powered home hub the company is slated to launch Oct. 13.

A representative for Apple did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

			

More from CNET

Speaking on his brand-new Power On podcast, Gurman said the cameras would be smallish cylinders — “like a metal ChapStick” — and could be placed anywhere and everywhere in the home. Acting more like sensors than video recorders, the cameras would reportedly use AI facial recognition to determine who and what is moving around inside and outside the house. The devices have a low frame rate, which means they’ll take far fewer still images than typical video cameras.

The upcoming Apple home hub will also use facial and voice recognition to identify homeowners and other users, so the security cameras may work with that data.

The camera would use text descriptions to inform homeowners about what is happening, such as “the dog is in the kitchen” or “someone is outside the back door,” for example. Visual input would interpret an event, but no video footage would be captured, Gurman said on the podcast. “It’s analyzing your environment and your home and around your home, simply using AI. It’s a very similar technology that they’re using for the AirPods with cameras.”

Without stored footage of a burglary or other crimes in the home, however, it’s unclear how police would retrieve much identifying information in an investigation, Gurman said. “You need the actual tape. So, it will be interesting to see how Apple markets this.”

Assuaging surveillance fears

Gurman said that avoiding video recording could be a selling point for Apple amid growing backlash over the surveillance environment of Flock cameras, smart devices and personal tech, like AI-powered glasses.

Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses have acquired the nickname “pervert glasses” because some people are using them to secretly record mostly women without their knowledge. Meta is now reportedly developing glasses that don’t have cameras and will instead rely solely on AI for speech and listening.

Having a smart home device that doesn’t rely on recorded, stored and analyzed data is a good privacy element, says CNET home security expert Tyler Lacoma. Presumably, Apple would rely on some type of on-device feature for capturing data, but we don’t have details. Short-lived machine analysis is quite different from a watchable video stream. 

Gurman didn’t say what kind of technology would be used in the cameras, but noted that the new home hub would not use Face ID, which is used to unlock iPhones and iPads. Whatever biometric template is used in the home hub might be the same as the one used by the cameras.

Nonetheless, if Apple does rely on true facial recognition technology, that could “open up a big can of worms,” Lacoma said, pointing to lawsuits against smart home security companies Nest and Ring over their use of identity tracking.

Gurman dismissed the notion that Apple would violate its customers’ privacy, though he said he thought the company will still be accused of turning over personal data to government agencies.

“Anyone who covers Apple close enough, or even remotely close enough, would know that would be hogwash for Apple,” Gurman said. “But I think we all know the reality is far different that Apple won’t be doing that with our data.”

Since Apple hasn’t publicly released the product yet, we’ll have to wait and see.

title: Reddit Is Choking Off RSS and Open Web Access to Keep AI Bots Out
snippet: Many are worried that killing RSS feeds will destroy one of the last open, user-controlled ways to read the web.
fullText:
People who post on Reddit often love to complain, especially if it’s about Reddit itself. Now they have a legit reason to do so.

The massive network of online discussion forums and social news aggregator has announced a timetable and details regarding its new antibot and data-scraping measures, which include discontinuing support for RSS feeds on Nov. 13.

The platform, which boasts over 500 million monthly active users, first hinted at these changes in early August and outlined measures it said were to protect the site from spam and to make moderation easier. But subsequent updates left users with lingering questions about when restrictions on public APIs — the rules that allow interaction between software programs — and changes to the site’s Old Reddit version would take effect.

			

More from CNET

Under the new policy, access to Old Reddit will be restricted to individuals who have used the legacy interface within the last six months. Many users still prefer this classic layout because it features fewer ads and loads faster due to its text-heavy design. As user shillyshally writes, “No geegaws, just straight up info and ads that are unobtrusive text only.”

As for slamming the door on RSS feeds, the company said those feeds have become a huge attack surface for “large-scale scraping and automated abuse,” though it will support moderators who need that option for subreddits through its developer platform. RSS is an open-web standard that lets users consume content on their own terms, without targeted ads, tracking cookies, sponsored posts or engagement-based algorithms that steer what you see.

And while it previously mentioned limiting its public API, Reddit now says it will move all public API access to its developer platform, Devvit, effectively closing the open web “front door.” That means any third-party developer accessing Reddit will need to be inside the site’s tightly controlled sandbox, barring any off-the-books workarounds or hacking.

The company said in a post on Wednesday that it’s easing the transition to its developer platform by working directly with creators to migrate over 14,000 registered apps, close technical capability gaps and help communities find new owners for abandoned bots.

A representative told CNET in an email that the company had no comment beyond the updates it had posted publicly.

Reddit frames the move as a necessary defense against abuse and theft by unauthorized AI scrapers, but some critics view it as a deliberate strategy to force users into its proprietary ecosystem. By killing open RSS feeds and shutting down public APIs, Reddit appears to be closing off ad-free, third-party alternatives that have allowed people to easily access and sort large volumes of news and messages. 

While Reddit points moderators toward internal tools like the Discord Relay app for alerts, the company says that general users relying on RSS feeds for reading Reddit content beyond moderation are out of luck: “If you use RSS for feeds outside of a community you moderate, there is no replacement. RSS has been a beloved part of the open web for a long time, and we’re grateful to everyone who used it to stay connected to Reddit.” 

Many have been quick to point out that eliminating open standards will break independent workflows and result in total platform enclosure. Users will be funneled directly into the official app and modern desktop site, where Reddit can capture ad impressions, collect usage data and ensure that its vast data — composed of many human conversations — is reserved exclusively for high-value corporate AI licensing deals with partners like Google and OpenAI.

Some users complained that Reddit’s current app and design are why they use a third-party app or still use Old Reddit. “old.reddit.com was first created in 2018,” said da_chicken, “and new reddit is still worse in every way except the lack of dark mode. You can’t compete with your own design from almost a decade ago.”

Not surprisingly, many on the RSS subreddit said they’re done with X (formerly Twitter) once RSS goes away. “I follow about 20 subs, and have nested posts/threads I subscribe to if I find something interesting and want to see replies. Without RSS, I don’t see how the site is even usable,” wrote way-too-lazy.

One user suggested reaching far back into internet history to replace Reddit. “Maybe we should go back to DIGG. Are they still around?” asked OneCalledWell.

title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS privacy controls amid the rise of AI agents
snippet: Amid the rapid rise in AI agents requesting “Full Disk Access” to your Mac, Apple says it is making changes to macOS to protect user privacy. While the company hasn’t shared specifics, Apple says users should understand what it means to give an app such “extraordinary” access to their Mac. more…
fullText:
Amid the rapid rise in AI agents requesting “Full Disk Access” to your Mac, Apple says it is making changes to macOS to protect user privacy.

While the company hasn’t shared specifics, Apple says users should understand what it means to give an app such “extraordinary” access to their Mac.

In a blog post on its Developer website, Apple explains that the Full Disk Access permission in macOS is meant to “allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac.” However, Apple says that “some developers” are using the Full Disk Access setting in macOS in “ways that could put users at risk.”

“We give developers powerful APIs to build incredible capabilities into their apps for Apple products, backed by a set of controls designed to protect users’ private data. Full Disk Access largely sidesteps these controls in order to allow backup apps to function properly on the Mac. Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems—including files, mail, messages, and even browsing history—without users’ full knowledge and understanding. For communication apps, this can also compromise the privacy of the people users are communicating with.”

In response, Apple says it will “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

The company hasn’t shared any additional details about these controls or the changes it plans. Nonetheless, it says that the rise of “increasingly capable and autonomous” AI agents necessitates a greater focus on privacy and security:

“Going forward, we will introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action. Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”

Apple’s announcement today comes amid the increasing popularity of tools like Meta Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. These are always-on AI agents that request substantial access to your personal data, and we’ve already seen some horror stories about Meta Muse in particular.

title: Apple says it’s tightening macOS ‘Full Disk Access’ controls due to new risks from AI agents
snippet: Apple says it will add new controls around macOS’s Full Disk Access permission, warning that increasingly capable AI agents make broad access to users’ files, messages, mail, and browsing history riskier.
fullText:
Days after a journalist claimed that Meta’s Muse app on Mac read their private messages — a claim that Meta disputed — Apple announced that it’s introducing additional controls around a setting called “Full Disk Access” on macOS. The feature was designed to allow backups to function properly, but AI agents have now increased “the risks associated with this level of access,” Apple said.

Apple’s statement comes shortly after Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Muse knew the content of his private messages — even though he claimed to have not given the AI agent permission. The report raised questions about the level of security and trust users have in desktop-based AI, which can control things on their systems and read their files and messages.

The decision also comes after a Wired report cited that a flaw in ChatGPT’s Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data.

AI agents that run on the desktop allow users to provide their respective apps with greater access to the files, messages, and other personal content on their computers by adjusting macOS settings.  

In Muse’s case, the AI optionally allows users to enable Full Disk Access. This setting, Apple explains, gives an app permission to access files, mail, messages, and even browsing history. 

“Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users’ full knowledge and understanding,” Apple said in a new blog post aimed at developers.

The company says that, going forward, it will introduce new controls aimed at ensuring that users who “genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access” can do so only with “very explicit user action.”

“Addressing this is critical. As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially. We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy,” Apple wrote. 

Apple did not respond to TechCrunch’s inquiry about the feature change.

Correction: Due to an editorial error, the change was described as Apple “limiting” permissions. After publication, the author of this article updated the wording to reflect their original intent: the change reflects informed consent, but is not a new limit.

title: Sanders introduces bill to ban the federal government from using Flock
snippet: The proposed legislation would extend to all automotica license plate readers.
fullText:
Flock Safety, whose cameras scan license plates across the country, continues to draw public anger, and now Senator Bernie Sanders wants the federal government out of the business altogether.

Sanders on Friday introduced the Ban Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) or tapping into data collected by readers run by local police and private companies. Despite its title, the bill doesn’t call out nine-year-old Flock in the text but rather covers any and all ALPR systems.

The bill allows exceptions only for toll collection and for uses that Congress approves in future legislation, which would have to limit data retention to 48 hours.

State and local governments would be dinged financially for not complying if the bill became law. (Like most bills, this one faces long odds.) Starting the first fiscal year after enactment, they would lose grants from five federal departments, including the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security, unless they ban the tech.

Americans could also sue the federal government over violations, and state attorneys general could enforce the law.

Flock is the largest ALPR vendor in the U.S., according to Sanders, with more than 120,000 cameras. In a blog post back in February, the company — currently valued by its venture backers at north of $8 billion — said its network processes more than 20 billion vehicle reads each month.

Under increasing pressure from communities that are protesting the product, suspending their use, and, at an escalating rate, canceling their contracts, Flock has tightened its rules. In August, CEO Garrett Langley, who’d previously said that how police use the cameras is up to local agencies, announced a new default data retention period of seven days, down from 30. 

Customers must also now use an audit tool that locks officers out pending review when it flags unusual searches. In one of the highest-profile cases of an officer abusing Flock’s platform, a former Milwaukee officer pleaded guilty to misconduct after searching for his then-partner and her ex 179 times, listing the reason as “investigation.” (During a recent podcast interview, investor Jason Calacanis suggested a “double-key” system in which two people must approve a search, and Langley said the idea is “on the whiteboard.”)

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) are co-sponsors.

We’ll be sitting down with Langley at our upcoming Disrupt event, October 13-15 in downtown San Francisco.

title: WhatsApp expands parental controls to teen accounts with group alerts, Meta AI restrictions
snippet: After introducing parent-managed accounts for pre-teens earlier this year, WhatsApp today expanded its parental controls to teen accounts, adding group activity alerts and additional restrictions for Meta AI. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After introducing parent-managed accounts for pre-teens earlier this year, WhatsApp today expanded its parental controls to teen accounts, adding group activity alerts and additional restrictions for Meta AI. Here are the details.

WhatsApp expands parental control options

Earlier this year, WhatsApp announced a series of new features aimed at giving parents more control over their pre-teens’ accounts.

That included letting parents decide who can contact the account and which groups it can join, review message requests from unknown contacts, and manage its privacy settings, with changes protected by a parent-set PIN.

Then, a few weeks ago, WhatsApp further expanded the feature on iOS by adding a dedicated “Parental controls” section to the Settings app, making it easier for parents to find and set up a managed account.

Today, WhatsApp expanded those controls yet again, this time bringing parental controls to teens rather than just pre-teens, while giving parents more visibility into group activity and more say over how their teens interact with Channels, Status updates, and, perhaps more importantly, Meta AI.

With the update, parents can now receive notifications when their teen joins or leaves a group, as well as when a group they are already in “grows meaningfully in size.” Parents can now also choose how their teen can use Channels, whose Status updates they can see, and who is allowed to see their own.

As for Meta AI, parents can now choose between the standard experience designed for users aged 13 and up, or a stricter “Limited Content” option, depending on what they consider appropriate for their teen.

According to WhatsApp, the Limited setting further restricts the topics a teen can discuss with Meta AI. Meta AI features that rely on Private Processing are also unavailable when the setting is enabled.

As before, WhatsApp notes that these parental controls do not give parents access to their teen’s actual messages or calls, which remain protected by end-to-end encryption.

title: Samsung reportedly confirms November launch for first Android XR glasses

Nearly a decade in, foldables have come a long way. Even Apple has noticed all of the fun Android users are having with their bendable smartphones, jumping into the crowd with next month’s iPhone Duo. Unfortunately, you usually need to break an arm and a leg to afford one, but with this one-day-only deal on the last-gen Galaxy Z Fold 7 at Amazon, your entry fee to the foldable club is down to the price of modern slab flagships. This model comes in just a single colorway and storage combination — mint, 256GB — but assuming you aren’t picky, it’s a great price for a foldable that really doesn’t feel all that last-gen in your daily life.

Sure, the upgrade from the Snapdragon 8 Elite to the 8 Elite Gen 5 is nice to see, and the brighter, anti-reflective main display is hard to argue with. But really, the only big difference between the two is the Fold 8 Ultra’s larger 5,000mAh silicon-carbon battery. You’ll have to settle for a smaller 4,400mAh cell — along with slower 25W charging speeds — though that should be enough to get you through all but your most taxing of days.

Even with a couple of minor sacrifices, considering the way smartphone prices are trending, scoring a foldable for just $50 more than Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra is hard to argue with. Amazon also supports trade-ins, meaning Pixel and Galaxy users can save up to a further $575 on the total price. It might not have that fancy anti-reflective display or a silicon-carbon battery — nor does it have the passport shape seen on the base Fold 8 — but for $1,350, it’s the best deal we’ve seen on a foldable in a while. You’ll have to hurry though, as this deal only goes until the end of today, or until sold out.

title: Sean Parker is rebuilding Stability AI around music
snippet: Sean Parker, who once taught the music industry what asking for forgiveness looks like, is now back with the labels' blessing and money.
fullText:
In Brief

Image Credits:Gilbert Carrasquillo / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Sean Parker, the Napster co-founder, has jumped back into the music industry, and he tells The Information that he’s playing by the rules this time. (Asking for forgiveness rather than permission didn’t work out so well last time around, he readily concedes.)

Two years ago, he joined an $80 million rescue of Stability AI, the image-generator startup that nearly collapsed after overspending and internal turmoil led to founder Emad Mostaque’s ouster. Now Parker and his longtime friend Prem Akkaraju, who became CEO, are taking the wraps off what they’ve been building.

The big idea, Parker says, is to turn Stability into the go-to AI toolmaker for music professionals. Toward that end, in late August, the company announced $76 million in funding from, among others, Sony, Warner, and Universal, which also licensed their catalogs for training as part of the deal. Stability has since released three new audio models and AI music-editing software. The AI can generate whole instrumental tracks or short snippets from text prompts. Parker says an upcoming update will let users hum a melody or beatbox a drum pattern to steer it.

title: Audible Will Soon Let You Use AI to Talk to a Book Character
snippet: Amazon’s audiobook service is rolling out new AI-powered features to make listening to stories more interactive.
fullText:
Audible is making audiobook listening more immersive. The Amazon-owned streaming service launched three new AI-powered features on Thursday to expand the book-listening experience. You’ll be able to explore character guides, interact with stories and access bonus content to learn more about cities and landmarks referenced in the book you’re listening to.

Yes, this means the ability to hold a conversation with a book’s character is on the horizon. Generative AI is the tool that’s powering the Interactive Story feature. Users will soon be able to engage, for instance, with Count Dracula’s rat-eating manservant, Renfield, through a new interactive story.

According to Audible, the interactive nature of this feature is guided by the creators and publishers of the titles it’ll be featured on, thus keeping the narrative grounded and believably connected to the events in the book. (Audible didn’t say who guides the feature on books by dead authors like Dracula’s Bram Stoker.)

			

More from CNET

“The character speaks first, assigning the listener a role, goal, and stakes; the listener responds in their own words, and the character reacts in real time,” Audible explains.

Audible’s new interactive AI features — Interactive Story, Character Guide and Visual Explorer — will expand your audiobook listening experience.Audible

The Interactive Story feature and Renfield on the Run will launch later this fall, an Audible spokesperson told CNET. The press release says these new AI features are in beta testing and will roll out in a limited capacity to customers in the US and UK.

What I did find in Dracula, though, was the newly launched Character Guide feature, which tracks the speaking character in real time and offers an information card with details about the performer playing the role. It’s all on the player page, minimizing distractions.

The Character Guide feature is now available for George Orwell’s 1984 and will be part of Audible’s upcoming original audiobook Exoplanet, written by Benjamin Percy and executive-produced by Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir. Audible plans to expand this feature to let listeners interact with the guide and ask questions as the story progresses.

Visual Explorer has yet to launch, but this feature will provide listeners with additional imagery and visual context for locations and important moments featured in a given narrative. 

“These new features invite listeners into a story in ways that simply weren’t possible before, marking the latest step in our nearly 30-year journey to push audio storytelling forward,” Audible’s Chief Content Officer Rachel Ghiazza said in a statement.

title: Welcome to Opt Out October: It’s Time to Ditch Unwanted Subscriptions and AI Spies
snippet: It’s a good month to reassess old accounts and retake control of your data and privacy.
fullText:
Tired of companies constantly updating their terms and conditions to train their AI with your data, recruit your personal info for their own ends, or charge ever-higher fees? On Thursday, the Electronic Frontier Foundation launched its 2026 Opt Out October guide, urging people to retake control of their data and devices.

If you’ve been wanting to change your privacy settings, stop social media from looking over your shoulder and avoid age verification requirements, this is the guide to start with. The EFF guide walks through all the toggles to flip and the platforms or services you should outright avoid, suggesting better alternatives where available.

The EFF notes on its blog that it will update the guide’s instructions and details if anything changes.

			

More from CNET

A representative from the EFF didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.  

What should I be opting out of?

Find privacy suggestions and alternatives to common choices.Screenshot by Stephen Shankland/CNET

EFF’s Opt Out October focuses on services that have been shown to treat your personal data poorly, and there are a lot of options. 

My personal favorite is the AI tools section, which teaches you how to stop chatbots and platforms like Twitch and Snapchat from training on your data.

If you’re frustrated with social media’s use of your personal data, its obnoxious ads or its face-analyzing age verification, the guide also includes a list of alternative social media. If you want to move away from Chrome’s activity tracking or find a free, user-friendly design tool beyond Adobe, this is the place to stop and plan your exit. And if you’ve finally had it with Windows cramming ads and AI into everything, the guide discusses how to get started with Linux instead.

More privacy guides

Ring offers a lot of AI options, including some you’re going to want to turn off.Tyler Lacoma/CNET

Your social media and AI tools are good places to start, but there’s much more you can do for your personal privacy.

First, check out our list of the best VPN services this year, which offers plenty of options to encrypt your internet data, hide what country you’re connecting from and more.

Physical privacy is important, too. My guides on checking your home privacy online and wiping your home address off the internet are great places to get started.

If you have smart devices or just want to improve your home’s privacy and safety, I’ve also got tips on the best privacy habits for your home and the tech you may be using inside it.

You may also appreciate guides for the best privacy settings for specific devices you use. Here are changes you may want to make to Alexa to improve the voice assistant’s privacy, and here are settings for Ring security devices you may want to turn off when using its video doorbells or security cameras.

title: All the AI agents that can live in your text messages
snippet: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
fullText:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. 

You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.

While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. 

Below are some of the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.

Caddy 

Image Credits:Caddy

Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.

For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. 

Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.

Fambot 

Image Credits:Fambot

Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.

The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.

Fambot currently connects to Gmail and Google Calendar, with support for Outlook and Apple Calendar planned for the future.

The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.

Folk

Image Credits:Folk

Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.

One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. 

Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.

Instinct 

Image Credits:Instinct

Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion, valuing it at $10 billion.

The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and cancelling subscriptions.

In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security.) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls. 

The company remains in private beta.

Iris

Image Credits:Iris

Powered by Hermes agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.

Martin 

Image Credits:Martin

Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app.

It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.

It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.

Miso

Image Credits:Miso

Miso takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel. 

It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details, flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.

Ohai 

Image Credits:Ohai

Ohai is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.

Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.

It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.

Ollie

ScreenshotImage Credits:Ollie

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie is that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aims to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It can keep track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then deliver relevant information to users through text. 

Its biggest differentiator from other agents is that Ollie is one of the first mainstream, family-focused AI assistants to achieve SOC 2 compliance, a widely used security standard. 

Launched in June 2026, Ollie offers a free tier, as well as paid plans starting at $25 per month for 150 messages. A $100-per-month plan includes up to 1,000 messages.

Orbits 

Image Credits:Orbits

Orbits also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.

It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.

Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.

Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.

Pally

Image Credits:Pally

Users can interact with Pally as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details. 

There’s a free plan available, which offers features like 15 minutes of calls per month, or there are paid plans, including $25 per month for 30 minutes of calls and $100 per month for 60 minutes.

Poke

Image Credits:Poke/The Interaction Company of California

Poke launched in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities. 

Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple approved Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.

Rene

Image Credits:Rene

Rene is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.

Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.

Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Skye 

Image Credits:Skye

Instead of waiting for users to open an app, Skye is an “agentic homescreen” for the iPhone that analyzes information from connected services and surfaces what it thinks is relevant through contextual cards, suggestions, and daily briefings. The assistant can generate audio briefings, prepare information ahead of meetings, surface reminders, and identify potentially useful information. 

The company, Signull Labs, raised about $3.6 million in seed funding in 2025. It entered private testing and beta in April 2026, and hasn’t yet announced a public release date.

Stanley

Image Credits:Stanley

Stanley is an AI content assistant aimed at content creators rather than general personal productivity. Available through iMessage, Telegram, and the web, it acts as a kind of AI head of content, helping users come up with ideas, turn them into posts, and maintain a consistent publishing schedule.

For instance, Stanley can connect to a user’s Instagram account, using that context to suggest content based on what the user has actually been doing. Users can also send voice notes, which Stanley turns into scripts, captions, and other social assets. It includes a content calendar and can schedule posts, with the broader goal of making content creation a more continuous, automated process rather than something users have to sit down and plan from scratch.

Tomo

The biggest differentiator with Tomo’s personal assistant for iMessage is that, instead of being a private assistant that only you interact with, Tomo can become part of group conversations. 

Also, like other agents, it’s designed to help with goals, accountability, scheduling, and everyday organization. It also has the ability to send reminders, search the web, work with calendars and email, watch videos, and edit photos.

The basic plan starts at $19.99 per month.

Town 

Image Credits:Town

Town is aimed more at professional life. It gives users a “Townie,” an AI assistant designed to learn how they work and handle recurring professional tasks. It can work with email, calendars, documents, Slack, and other platforms. 

In June 2026, the company raised a $55 million Series A led by Andreessen Horowitz and Forerunner.

Wajo 

Image Credits:Wajo

Wajo’s first consumer agent, Fo, can call businesses, send emails, join group chats, make bookings and purchases, and coordinate with people to complete everyday tasks.

A key part of Wajo’s approach is giving Fo its own identity. The agent has its own email address, phone number, and payment card, allowing it to interact with businesses without requiring users to hand over their own credentials. 

Notably, when Fo encounters something it cannot handle on its own, Wajo says it can bring in a human assistant to finish the task.

Fo launched publicly in September 2025 with a free tier, while heavier workloads and custom agents are available through a paid Pro offering.

title: GrayKey maker can reportedly bypass the iPhone’s ‘Inactivity Reboot’ security feature
snippet: As reported by 404 Media, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass the iPhone security feature that automatically reboots devices if they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As reported by 404 Media, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass the iPhone security feature that automatically reboots devices if they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Nearly two years ago, the iOS 18.1 update introduced Inactivity Reboot, a feature that forces iPhone reboots in case they haven’t been unlocked for 72 hours.

In essence, this feature makes it harder for law enforcement and forensic tools to access data on a locked iPhone, since a reboot causes the device to return to a Before First Unlock (BFU) state, rather than remaining in the less restrictive After First Unlock (AFU) state.

When an iPhone is in BFU, certain sensitive data remains protected by encryption keys that only become available after the user enters their passcode for the first time, thus putting the device in AFU.

From that point on, more of the device’s data remains accessible until the iPhone is rebooted again, which returns it to BFU.

Automatically rebooting an iPhone means that even if a device is seized by law enforcement, it can return to BFU before investigators can access it, since obtaining a warrant or transporting the device to a forensic lab can take time.

As 404 Media noted when iOS 18.1 was released, the feature can also make it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in AFU long enough to develop or use a way to break into it.

GrayKey reportedly gets around Inactivity Reboot

404 Media reported today that, based on an “educational and tutorial video, which was made exclusively for law enforcement agents and appears to be dated early 2025,” Magnet Forensics, the company behind the GrayKey phone unlocking tool, appears to have developed a way to bypass the iPhone’s Inactivity Reboot feature.

According to the report, Magnet developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve, as well as an Evidence Preservation Mode for its existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are reportedly designed to maintain an iPhone’s forensic state without immediately exposing the data stored on the device, allowing law enforcement to keep that state intact while waiting for authorization to search it.

The report notes that while the video doesn’t detail the technical mechanism behind the workaround, it explains that GrayKey can preserve an iPhone’s AFU state even if the device reboots.

From the report:

“That AFU state is captured,” by GrayKey Preserve and Evidence Preservation Mode, the employee says. “Even if that device does reboot for any number of reasons, memory maintenance or the power is lost or whatever, the AFU state is not lost. This is the true magic behind the GrayKey Preserve and the Evidence Preservation Mode function.”

404 Media reached out to Apple and Magnet Forensics, but neither responded to a request for comment. They also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to manipulate the iPhone’s clock, or to turn off the processes responsible for expiring certain data altogether.

While the video appears to date from early 2025, it is unclear how long the technology has been available to law enforcement, whether it has been used in actual investigations, or whether the workaround remains effective against the latest versions of iOS.

title: Most of Us Have Been Cyberattack Targets, Consumer Reports Finds. AI Isn’t Helping
snippet: From snooping smart glasses to AI bots going rogue, I’m not surprised US adults are more concerned about their privacy.
fullText:
Pretty much all of our personal data is online at this point. Whether it’s saved credit cards or photos in your social media profiles, your private life is easily accessible — including to hackers. 

That’s one reason why the vast majority of Americans have been targeted by scams or cyberattacks, according a new study by Consumer Reports, Aspen Digital and the Global Cyber Alliance. 

The report found 9 in 10 Americans have faced at least one digital scam or cyberattack. “That’s not a statistic, that’s almost everyone we serve,” Consumer Reports CEO Phil Radford said in a statement. “AI is making fraud faster, cheaper and more personal, and no one can outsmart that alone. Companies need to be held accountable. Governments need real guardrails. That’s the bar we’re setting – for ourselves and for them.”

			

More from CNET

What’s even worse is that US adults aren’t confident in personal data privacy — like having safeguards for their Social Security number or financial data. Over 1 in 4 (29%) aren’t confident at all. That figure has nearly doubled compared to the annual survey’s 2025 finding that only 16% weren’t confident at all. And the number of US adults confident in the privacy of their sensitive data has shrunk from 48% in 2025 down to 32% this year. 

That doesn’t mean we’ve given up. Many respondents reported looking closely at texts and emails before clicking (69%), using multifactor authentication (60%) and enabling automatic software updates (48%). But their efforts alone won’t do. 

AI won’t make personal data privacy any easier to manage 

What will it take to increase consumer confidence in personal data privacy in a world where AI is becoming more of a threat than a tool for evolution? 

Consider the latest news of the FBI employees’ data being stolen, your home router being a target of Russian military intelligence and the widespread and fast-growing cybersecurity incidents from AI model testing and training. 

Read more: Florida Asks Judge to Stop OpenAI From Training New Models After Latest Incidents

“AI will certainly make it easier for scammers to create personalized scams at scale and lower the amount of effort it takes to craft and send scams,” said Stacey Higginbotham, a policy fellow for Consumer Reports. 

Higginbotham said there are several measures that can reduce scams, but policymakers haven’t taken serious action. Congress could pass laws such as the federal SCAM Act or the SAFE Platforms Act that would penalize scammers who abuse online platforms with their malicious tactics. 

“So AI is a problem, but legislators could address some of the challenges associated with the looming glut of AI-enabled scams by shoring up the basics and making it more expensive for companies to profit off of scammers at the expense of consumers,” Higginbotham said.

For now, Higginbotham said the most important thing you can do is follow common password best practices like using different strong passwords and enabling multifactor authentication. Also, make sure you’re assessing all messages from strangers, whether it feels like a scam or not.

title: Can AI Fix Your Chaotic Inbox? I Unleashed It On 200,000 Unread Emails
snippet: I sifted through a boatload of emails with the help of Gemini.
fullText:
It happens almost without you realizing it. It’s insidious, the accumulation of unwanted, unread emails in overwhelming amounts. Like locusts, they descend daily en masse, flooding the compartmentalized chambers of Gmail, Apple Mail, Yahoo Mail and Outlook with promises of savings and harbingers of critical news.

Tragically, many go unread, and even more are tragically, utterly useless. As of this article, my Gmail was sporting a count of 52,299 emails in my main inbox and 93,717 in my Promotions inbox. In total, I had more than 192,000 emails mocking me from the inside.

This sounds like a job for someone (or something) who won’t become enraged by reading thousands of sob story subject lines from Nextdoor and hundreds of alerts informing them that they did not win the lottery. 

			

More from CNET

Here’s how I used Google’s Gemini AI to try to get a handle on my chaotic email inbox. 

Connect and crawl

In order to avoid scanning through the glut of subject lines for something of value, I gave Gemini access to look through my Gmail account. All I had to do was ask, and Gemini served up a direct toggle in our chat for me to connect it.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Alternatively, typing in “@Gmail” into the Gemini chat will pull up the option to connect your account as well. 

Ejecting repeat offenders

The way Gemini generally handled helping me clear and clean out unwanted email threads from my inbox was by crafting custom search queries that would root out the weeds. The first kind of email I tried to purge from my inbox was the daily alert I get via my neighborhood’s Nextdoor community about some sad thing happening with an animal. 

After a quick back and forth in the chat, it offered a prompt:

from:nextdoor.com (animal abuse OR animal cruelty OR coyote OR dead animal OR “lost dog” OR “lost cat”)

I plopped that sucker into Gmail’s search bar, and it quickly surfaced every icky Nextdoor post about a dead coyote or abandoned kitten so I could delete them all together.

Gemini/Screenshot by CNET

Reading so you don’t have to

Sorting out which e-commerce sites, government agencies and recurring services are abusing my inbox by stuffing it full of worthless sale announcements and thinly veiled threats around repaying my student loans? Ain’t nobody got time for that. 

In a quick chat session, Gemini was able to parse through the Gmail inbox and gave me a roundup of the senders who show up most often and which of their messages were the most frivolous so I could easily eliminate them.

Archiving the alerts

Some things you want to keep around just in case, like old invoices and email exchanges you might need for emotional blackmail. Google Gemini was able to help me craft a search query that sorted the threads I wanted to keep for later from the stuff that was useless. 

One of the tips Gemini outlined for me was around keeping promotions from sneaking into this lot by using quotations around keywords, an old-school Google search trick that applies to Gmail as well. 

Gemini was also able to scan through my inbox and look for promotional emails that contained words like “statement,” as in “statement armchairs” rather than “bank statement,” and provide me with a prompt crafted to target only the exact emails I actually wanted to archive.

Here’s an example of the search prompt Gemini gave that banished an email on buy one, get one deals from Benihana and a promo on statement armchairs from Wayfair: 

subject:(invoice OR receipt OR payment OR statement OR bill) -shop -sale -off -deal -furniture

How useful overall is AI at clearing your inbox?

Google’s Gemini AI tool was great at helping me sort through emails and isolate keywords and prompts, but the tool is not currently capable of deleting, archiving or creating custom folders in Gmail since it’s not an AI agent. You have to do that part yourself, but I honestly think that’s a good thing.

What it does well is cut down on the time and effort a person looking to organize their inbox might spend coming up with keywords and search-and-destroy methods. Gemini significantly cut down the mental load for me and saved me time, but the power to execute stayed safely in my hands.

Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

MacPaw spent nearly two decades building consumer software for Mac users. CleanMyMac is one of the Mac utilities on the market, and it’s my go-to when I need to free up hard drive space, uninstall apps, etc. The company is making a different kind of bet with Leebry, a Work AI platform aimed at helping IT teams.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The AI trust numbers

MacPaw’s 2026 AI at Work report is where you see the issue IT faces, as they found that 90% of companies deploy AI without thoroughly auditing their internal knowledge base first. That means that internal AI tools are answering employee questions based on whatever it can find, including old product docs, outdated policies, and random Reddit discussion forums.

In this survey, MacPaw found that 6 in 10 IT leaders see a real disconnect between what their C-Suite expects from AI tools (thanks to LinkedIn feeds) and what their teams can safely and accurately deliver. That gap is where most AI disappointment lives, and it’s the problem Leebry is attempting to solve for IT teams.

What Leebry actually does

Leebry began as an internal MacPaw hackathon project in 2025. The problem it was solving was employees repeatedly asking the same questions internally, even when the answers already existed somewhere in the company’s documentation, intranets, Slack threads, etc. MacPaw built a Slack bot to surface those answers and point employees to the exact source. Within a few months, it was resolving 30% of MacPaw’s own level 1 IT tickets, so that became the foundation for what they’re launching today with Leebry.

The platform automates level 1 support tickets, handles access provisioning and removal as employees join, move roles, or leave, and answers employee questions across the tools they already use. Every Leebry response links back to its source, so employees can verify the answer rather than just trust it (and prove it), and can flag stale or outdated information that could affect accuracy. That last part is the direct product response to the 90% knowledge audit problem from their own research.

One detail worth calling out for security-conscious IT folks: Leebry is permission-aware, meaning it authenticates each user and surfaces only the information they are permitted to see. That matters more than it sounds as a lot of AI tools draw on a shared knowledge pool and let users surface things they shouldn’t access. Leebry also ships with an MCP server that exposes the device management control plane to AI agents, with admin-set guardrails on every action, so teams can delegate repetitive work to agents without giving up control over what those agents can actually do.

For IT orgs that work extensively with Apple, the access provisioning aspect is interesting. Automating access changes as people move within the organization can be a huge pain point for SMBs without a dedicated IAM team. Most of the time, it’s manual, it’s slow, and departing employees end up with access that should have been revoked days earlier. I’ve run into this myself quite a bit.

“Businesses don’t need another tool to check, they need work taken off their plate, without sacrificing oversight or control,” said Dan Jaenicke, Director of B2B Product Development at MacPaw.

Wrap up

The fair question here is why an IT team should trust a consumer Mac software company to build enterprise tooling. I think the answer is actually in the product’s origin story. MacPaw built Leebry to solve their own internal IT problem first, which is a better foundation than most enterprise software gets. It wasn’t built to make money. It was built to solve a customer (even internal) problem, so it’ll work well for other teams. The reality is all orgs have docs spread out across team chat, file sharing, intranets, etc and we’re all guilty of asking for someone else to find it for us.

Leebry aims to make it easy for IT to solve the same questions folks ask over and over again.

title: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
snippet: Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599. more…
fullText:
Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599.

Effective as of today at the Google Store, Pixel 10a has jumped from $499 to $599. The reason is obvious, of course, with the current skyrocketing costs of components such as memory. Google has not officially commented on the price hike yet, though.

This follows Google issuing a price increase to each of its new Pixel 11 devices compared to the prior generation. 

When Google confirmed the Pixel 11 would be more expensive, the company said that this would eventually impact “in-market Pixel phones” which, at the time, we speculated could include Pixel 10a.

	

The 128GB base Pixel 10a is $599 as of today, with the 256GB model at $699. The updated prices have already kicked in at Amazon and Best Buy, and Google Store now shows Pixel 10a at $849 in Canada, £599 in the UK, and €649 in Europe.

	

In our review of Pixel 10a, we called the device a “well-rounded experience” for its $499 price, but a $100 jump certainly makes that a tougher conversation, especially considering Google’s mid-ranger is at this point using a two-generation-old chipset in its Tensor G4. But, of course, Google is far from alone here. Just this week, Samsung also issued price hikes across the Galaxy lineup including flagship and mid-range devices alike.

title: The Pixel 3a might be the most important Google smartphone to date
snippet: Google Pixel was designed to be a premium smartphone effort, but that all changed in 2019 with the debut of the Pixel 3a. The budget-conscious launch went on to be a turning point for the Pixel’s history and, looking back, it might just be the single most important Google smartphone ever. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel was designed to be a premium smartphone effort, but that all changed in 2019 with the debut of the Pixel 3a. The budget-conscious launch went on to be a turning point for the Pixel’s history and, looking back, it might just be the single most important Google smartphone ever.

Looking back over the past decade of Pixel smartphones, I’m not sure you can point at any one device and say it was more important than the Pixel 3a. The original Pixel set the foundation, of course, and Pixel 6 launched Google’s efforts into a new era, but Pixel 3a gave Google a taste of what it was always after – market success.

The Pixel 3a almost immediately shot up to the top of best-seller lists, massively propelled Google’s US smartphone sales, and was the driving force behind setting Google’s first big shipment records. That success ultimately led to several Pixel A-series successors that have similarly resonated in the market. These more affordable devices just nail the fundamentals at a price that’s hard to beat, especially considering the cost of a Pixel 10a is only $100 more (annnnnnd now it’s $200) than the Pixel 3a originally started at.

Google is finding at least some success in the flagship market nowadays. Pixel phones are very much hitting their stride in 2026 not only in terms of design and functionality, but also in the market as a whole. I’d very much argue, though, that the Pixel 3a was the lifejacket that kept this project going. The failure of the Pixel 4 left scars on Google’s smartphone efforts, but the Pixel 3a’s resounding success was surely a huge deciding factor on what would come next.

	
	

And, in 2026, I think this phone holds up remarkably well from a hardware perspective. There are modern budget phones that cost just as much as the Pixel 3a did when it came out that feel a lot worse than this one. The Pixel 3a is long dead at this point with software support having ended in 2022, but its legacy lives on.

Did you ever own a Pixel 3a?

title: OpenAI launches Dots, new ‘always-on agents’ you can assign tasks to
snippet: Right as Meta’s Muse avatar agent has taken the AI world by storm, OpenAI is today announcing Dots as “always-on agents” you can customize to your needs. more…
fullText:
Right as Meta’s Muse avatar agent has taken the AI world by storm, OpenAI is today announcing Dots as “always-on agents” you can customize to your needs.

Out of OpenAI DevDay 2026, Dots are OpenAI’s answer to giving users a way to assign tasks to an AI agent to run in the background. The company says that Dots, powered by GPT-6 Astra, has “their own cloud computer” and can use that to accomplish tasks that you have assigned. You can interact with Dots via ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams once they’ve been set up.

OpenAI explains:

Dots are frontier intelligence that have your back. Powered by GPT‑6 Astra, they have their own cloud computer, learn from feedback over time, and can work towards your goals 24/7. Through our ecosystem of plugins, they can readily connect to over 4,000 apps, giving them the tools to help wherever you need them.

Your dot is always within reach, whether it is through ChatGPT, Slack, or Teams. You can ask questions, explore ideas, and give feedback along the way; or you can simply hop on a voice call when you need to talk something out. The more you work together, the more your dot learns your preferences, how you think, and what good looks like to you.

Some examples of how OpenAI says it is using Dots internally include having Dots automatically investigate bugs when they are mentioned in Slack, creating working apps when a “new design” is ready, and more. Another example saw a Dot notice on its own that an invoice had not been sent, to which it created that invoice for the user’s approval. Dots do “proactive research” when not actively working on a task through read-only connections with tools you’ve connected.

	

As the user, you can see a Dot’s cloud computer at any time while it is working on a task, as well as giving it permission to use your computer. 

OpenAI further adds that Dots follow the same permissions and controls as ChatGPT, and they also support custom rules around when they can act on their own or require approval from you. 

Dots are available today to Pro and Business Premium users, with Enterprise users also able to try it out when workspace admins approve it. One Dot is included with these plans, with OpenAI saying you’ll be able to add more in the future. Dots must be created via the ChatGPT desktop app or browser, but can be interacted with via the mobile app after that.

GPT‑6 Astra Ultrafast is available today, Sol Ultrafast is “coming soon”

Private Intelligence for businesses “coming this Fall”

Codex can now run in the cloud

Agents API with Computer Use

Bedrock Managed Agents

ChatGPT Space where humans and Dots can co-work

title: Audible announces AI-powered character guides, interactive stories, more
snippet: Audible today announced three features coming to “deepen customers’ connections to their favorite stories.” Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Audible today announced three features coming to “deepen customers’ connections to their favorite stories.” Here are the details.

Audible announces Character Guides

Starting today, Audible users listening to the Audible Original Bram Stoker’s Dracula audiobook will be able to access Character Guide, right from the player page.

This is a new feature that shows who is speaking in real time, and provides spoiler-free cards with details about each character and the performer behind each voice, “complete with narrator headshots and bios.”

Audible adds that, coming soon, Character Guide will also allow listeners to ask questions about the production as the story unfolds.

Character Guide is also available with Audible’s adaptation of George Orwell’s 1984, and will be included with Benjamin Percy’s Exoplanet when it launches on November 5.

Two more features coming soon

In addition to Character Guide, Audible today announced two other AI-powered features: Interactive Story and Visual Explorer.

Audible describes Interactive Story as a “bonus experience beyond the original narrative,” explaining that it will allow users to have real-time conversations with characters from supported audiobooks.

Here’s Audible:

The first Interactive Story accompanies the Audible Original Bram Stoker’s Dracula and follows the character of Renfield, Dracula’s unpredictable, tormented servant. The character speaks first, assigning the listener a role, goal, and stakes; the listener responds in their own words, and the character reacts in real time.

The platform notes that creators have control over multiple aspects of the interaction, and adds that after Dracula, Benjamin Percy’s Audible Original Exoplanet will get the new experience.

As for Visual Explorer, Audible says it will “surface relevant imagery and visual context at key moments during listening,” whether it’s a map to help listeners better visualize where the story is unfolding, or an image “tied to a pivotal moment” in the narrative.

Visual Explorer is coming soon, with Audible highlighting The Cultural Tutor’s Grand Tour: The Story of Europe in Six Cities as one title featuring the experience, while Interactive Story is “rolling out this fall.”

To learn more about today’s announcements, which are rolling out as limited betas for Audible customers in the U.S. and UK, follow this link.

title: Nvidia Shield TV Pro is now $299 – a $100 price hike seven years after the Android TV box launched
snippet: The Nvidia Shield TV is an iconic piece of Android hardware but it also hasn’t seen a refresh in the better part of a decade. But, because of the increasingly depressing state of the entire tech industry, Nvidia Shield TV Pro is getting a $100 price hike to $299, seven years after it first launched. more…
fullText:
The Nvidia Shield TV is an iconic piece of Android hardware but it also hasn’t seen a refresh in the better part of a decade. But, because of the increasingly depressing state of the entire tech industry, Nvidia Shield TV Pro is getting a $100 price hike to $299, seven years after it first launched.

Nvidia Shield TV Pro made its debut in October 2019 and, to this day, remains one of the most capable Android TV streamers on the market. While certain aspects haven’t aged perfectly, such as a lack of AV1 support and others, it remains unmatched in other places.

That’s a big part of the reason that, even so many years after it launched, Nvidia continues to produce the Shield TV.

But the $199 price point is gone. Effective today, Nvidia Shield TV Pro now costs $299.99. Nvidia attributed the price hike to the fact that “the cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry.” Alongside the change in price, Nvidia has also ended production of the base Shield TV that was also introduced in 2019. The “tube” Shield has been out of stock for months at this point, but Shield TV Pro was just restocked at Best Buy.

	

Shield TV Pro at Best Buy

Early this year, Nvidia said that it would continue software support for the Shield TV for the forseeable future. 

Shield isn’t the only streamer going up in price as a result of RAMageddon. Google TV Streamer saw a price hike to $149 recently, while other devices including Apple TV 4K and various Roku streamers also saw price hikes earlier this year. 

AI is just great, right?

title: Gemini 4 Is Here: When You May Be Able to Use Google’s New AI Model
snippet: Gemini 4 Argon is only available to cyber defenders now, a sign Google is gearing up for a wider launch soon.
fullText:
After months of delays, Google is gearing up to get back in the AI game. The company on Wednesday announced its newest frontier model, called Gemini 4 Argon. But you won’t be able to use it yet. Here’s why.

A lot has changed in the 10 months since Google released Gemini 3 — and crushed its competition. One is the introduction of the White House’s voluntary review process for new AI models, with which Google said in a blog post it is “actively engaged.” Another is the increasingly potent cybersecurity risk that new AI models pose for online companies, governments and consumers. Just take a look at all the AI agent hacks we’ve seen this summer.

Right now, Gemini 4 Argon is only available to specific cybersecurity defenders in Google’s Fairwind program. This has become the new way that AI companies roll out new frontier models: first to cybersecurity experts, who use it to shore up their own defenses and report any weaknesses, then to subscribers, and then eventually free users. OpenAI did this with GPT-6 Astra, same as Anthropic with Fable 5.

			

More from CNET

The slow-roll release is meant to give experts the time to find and patch issues before the AI is let loose on the internet. Past releases gave defenders a few weeks before the model was given a general release. Given that this is Google’s first model to go through this process, it could be a little bit longer. Google did not immediately respond to questions about the time frame of Gemini 4’s release.

Gemini 4: What we know so far

Gemini 4 Argon is the latest AI model from Google, capable of coding, multimodalities (like understanding images and charts) and reasoning. If it follows past releases, we can expect Gemini 4, or a version of it, to become the new model powering Google’s many, many AI features in Search, Docs and more. Google said that Gemini 4 Argon is particularly adept at business-related tasks, like software engineering, cybersecurity and knowledge work in legal and finance fields. Benchmarking data released by Google, comparing Gemini 4 to OpenAI’s Astra and Anthropic’s Fable 5.1, seems to back up those claims.

Google says it has been using Gemini 4 internally to help make the company more efficient, including in its quantum computing research and memory operations. It has a 1-million-token output limit. More tokens mean the AI can do more work and handle more complex tasks.

Google was rumored to release Gemini 3.5 Pro earlier this year, but reports say it held off to keep working on it. Even this week, there were concerns within the company that Gemini 4 wasn’t up to par on key tasks, such as coding, Bloomberg reports. We’ll have to wait until the model is released and put it to the test to see if those concerns were addressed before then.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Google Home update rolling out with better ‘Find My Phone’ voice commands, smart home improvements
snippet: A new Google Home update has arrived with various improvements including better support for the “Find My Phone” voice command on Gemini speakers. more…
fullText:
A new Google Home update has arrived with various improvements including better support for the “Find My Phone” voice command on Gemini speakers.

In the Gemini for Home early access branch, Google says that users can expect “quality and reliability improvements” for the “Hey Google, find my phone” command that’s been around for years. It’s unclear exactly what’s changing, but this is a very useful voice command, so any upgrades will be welcome.

Improved Find My Phone reliability: Rolled out quality and reliability improvements to this fan-favorite feature when you ask Gemini to help locate your phone.

Other Gemini voice improvements in this latest update include filtering out background noise and voices, further speed/latency improvements, better support for multilingual households, and improved reliability to custom commands within Routines/automations.

In the Google Home app itself, there are quite a few updates to smart home functionality. This includes turning off lights when the brightness slider is dragged down to zero, improving camera and doorbell tiles, reducing Matter switches being incorrectly shown as offline, and improving setup for Nest devices.

	

Device Controller Enhancements

Accurate smart light shutoff: We’ve resolved an issue where sliding brightness down to 0% on single lights or group dimmers left bulbs powered on at minimum illumination instead of turning them off completely. Lowering your brightness to 0% now sends a definitive power-off command, preventing wasted energy and unexpected ambient glow.

Clearer online camera and doorbell tiles: Online cameras and doorbells now show as filled icons and accented tile colors at a glance, helping you instantly distinguish active cameras from idle ones.

Accurate offline switch status: We’ve resolved an issue where Matter switches failed to show their offline status or respond to taps on the All Devices tab, ensuring tiles properly render greyed out when disconnected.

Reliable Favorites tile gestures: We’ve resolved issues where long-pressing tiles in the Favorites tab failed to open device controllers or routine editors.

title: Reddit is making two changes some long-time users won’t like
snippet: Reddit has announced two upcoming changes which are likely to prove unpopular with some long-time users. The company has already placed one restriction on Old Reddit, and it has now announced a second one. Additionally, RSS support is being discontinued … more…
fullText:
Reddit has announced two upcoming changes which are likely to prove unpopular with some long-time users.

The company has already placed one restriction on Old Reddit, and it has now announced a second one. Additionally, RSS support is being discontinued … 

Old Reddit

Reddit significantly changed its user interface way back in 2018, sparking significant objections from those who preferred the original version. To address this, the platform said that it would continue to provide access to what has become known as Old Reddit for as long as people kept using it.

The first change to this policy came in August of this year when the company required Old Reddit users to be logged in. It has now announced that the original UI will be limited to those who have used it within the last six months, denying access to new users.

In the next few months, we’ll further limit access for logged-in users to only those who have used Old Reddit in the last six months (which covers the vast majority of all Old Reddit users).

Reddit says that both moves were made to reduce AI scraping by companies (though this is apparently fine if they pay for the privilege).

The same rationale has been cited for discontinuing RSS feeds.

Because RSS is now a common surface for large-scale scraping and automated abuse, we’ll stop supporting RSS feeds on November 13, 2026.

This could be particularly problematic for subreddits who rely on these for moderation workflows. Reddit says it is aware of this and is recommending moderators use Devvit apps like Discord Relay.

Users unimpressed

Reading the comments in the thread, it’s clear that a lot of long-time users are very unhappy about the latest developments.

They said Old Reddit wasn’t going away, but Reddit lies all the time […] They’ll keep messing with stuff until they turn the site into a Twitter/Facebook hybrid and everyone except the Facebook/Twitter crowd abandons them.

What’s your take on the latest changes? Please share in the comments.

snippet: Good morning and happy October.
