fullText:
Good morning and happy October. Today, I’m cringing at this gaggle of billionaires pretending to be human, vibing to the new Tinashe album, Popstar, and heartily dining on all the brutal ‘Digger’ reviews.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

What year is it?

	

After months of waiting, Gemini 4 ‘Argon’ is finally out — sort of. Google unveiled the new state-of-the-art model late yesterday but has only made it available to “a set of trusted cyber defenders” while it undergoes testing. The company says it will get a wider release “as soon as possible.”

This is a big moment for Google. Many users and critics alike wrote it off completely, with one analysis firm saying “for all intents and purposes, we believe DeepMind is no longer a frontier lab.” While the company has released several useful, fast and affordable Flash-branded models in 2026, its latest salvo into state-of-the-art AI was back in November 2025 with Gemini 3 Pro. In fact, it was so good that for a brief time Google was considered to be well ahead of OpenAI and Anthropic, and presaged a “code red” inside the frontier labs.

It’s hard to overstate how important it is for Gemini 4 to succeed. After a massive executive shuffle in August saw Demis Hassabis and Jeff Dean removed from the core management team, most of DeepMind’s operations were shifted from London to Mountain View, where new head Koray Kavukcuoglu reports directly to Google CEO Sundar Pichai.

While there has been speculation that Google, with its entrenched customer base, would walk away from the frontier in favor of cheaper, more product-focused pursuits, Kavukcuoglu has refuted those rumors. Earlier this month, he said, “To put it very bluntly, there’s nothing other than being at the frontier that is important for us. We have the whole full stack… and we are able to optimize to be able to achieve our goals.”

According to benchmarks, Gemini 4 is competitive with GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 in most tests, and is trained to be much better at agentic tasks than any previous Gemini model. It’s also better aligned, with a focus on cybersecurity, and has a massive 1M token output limit, which makes it far more capable of producing large bodies of work in one prompt with less compaction.

The big question, though, is whether Argon will be competitive in the real world. A Bloomberg report published shortly before the embargo lifted on the Gemini 4 news quoted anonymous Google employees skeptical of its coding abilities. From Bloomberg: “While Gemini 4 has performed well on benchmarks widely used to gauge model efficacy, it does less well when employees actually put it to work, according to people with direct access to the effort. The model struggles to handle certain coding tasks, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss an internal matter.”

Argon is also curiously priced. Its introductory rate of $2/$10 per million input/output tokens matches OpenAI’s Sol 6.1 cost right now, but will eventually double to hit the $4/$20 price of Claude Opus 5.5. While still significantly cheaper than Astra or Fable, it has to prove its mettle with users before Google is welcomed back into the arms of the fickle AI masses.

Unfortunately, I have some real-world bad news to share in this section. Android Central, the blog I worked at from 2016 through 2021, was shut down yesterday by Future, the company that bought it in 2020 alongside iMore and Windows Central. iMore was already shut down and turned into…something AI slop-related, and I guess it was AC’s turn to be culled.

title: Google Play adding Usage-Based Billing subscriptions aimed at AI apps
snippet: Google Play today is giving Android developers more payment options around subscriptions, including Usage-Based Billing. more…
fullText:
Google Play today is giving Android developers more payment options around subscriptions, including Usage-Based Billing.

Google says the “subscription landscape is evolving rapidly” due to generative AI and “increasingly sophisticated app experiences.” 

End users should be on the lookout for Usage-Based Billing to support generative AI apps and other usage-based services. This “prepaid metered billing” works by letting users “automatically top up their balance whenever it falls below a set threshold.” 

For large groups like businesses and schools, there’s Multi-Quantity Subscription Purchase. Organizations can “make multiple subscription purchases in a single transaction and easily assign those as seats or subscriptions to team members or students.”

	

Mixed Carts allow developers to sell auto-renewing subscriptions and one-time products at the same time. For example:

This unified experience also opens up powerful upsell opportunities for your business—such as offering targeted discounts if an end user purchases a complete bundle of a subscription and complementary in-app items together.

Cross-Developer Bundling lets developers “create and sell a hard bundle of two or more complementary subscriptions in your own catalog.” The example Google gives is bundling a language-learning app with a travel guide service for a “combined subscription at a discounted rate.”

This capability allows you to team up with other developers—or combine offerings across your own portfolio of apps—to deliver massive value through a single purchase.

These Play Store features are “currently available or rolling out through [Google’s] Early Access Program.”

title: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery to become Skydance
snippet: The roughly $110 billion deal is expected to close October 6.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

8:53 AM PDT · October 2, 2026

Image Credits:Skydance (opens in a new window)

		

							

											
									

					

	

Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will operate as Skydance once their merger closes, Paramount CEO David Ellison announced Friday. Skydance is the name of Ellison’s original film production company.

The roughly $110 billion deal is expected to close October 6. It will combine two major Hollywood studios, Paramount+ and HBO Max, and networks including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network. Skydance will also control franchises such as “The Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” the DC Universe, and “Yellowstone.”

The merger followed a drawn-out corporate battle. Netflix had agreed to acquire Warner Bros.’ streaming and studio businesses before the broader Paramount deal moved forward. Twelve states challenged the deal, arguing it could reduce competition and harm consumers and workers, but a judge approved a settlement with the state attorneys general this week.

Ellison said the Paramount and Warner Bros. brands will remain central. “We never wanted a new corporate identity to diminish, alter or overshadow either one,” he wrote on X. The new name, he said, gives the company “an identity of its own” while letting both studios “remain in the spotlight.”

What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.

title: Texas school district ditches Chromebooks, approves $11M iPad and MacBook Neo deal
snippet: A Texas school district is going all-in on the iPad and MacBook Neo as part of a new $11 million deal. The Beaumont Independent School District is ditching its Chromebook fleet and opting for Apple gear going forward, citing better reliability, lower costs, and performance. fullText:
A Texas school district is going all-in on the iPad and MacBook Neo as part of a new $11 million deal. The Beaumont Independent School District is ditching its Chromebook fleet and opting for Apple gear going forward, citing better reliability, lower costs, and performance.

As reported by the Beaumont Enterprise this week, the Beaumont Independent School District’s board has approved an $11.19 million four-year lease to upgrade its technology ecosystem.

As part of the deal, the school district will provide 14,585 Apple devices to teachers and students from pre-K through 12th grade. The new Apple gear will replace an aging collection of Chromebooks, many purchased more than five years ago. The district was spending nearly half a million dollars on repairs and support for that Chromebook fleet.

The new initiative includes more than 4,000 iPads for students pre-K through second grade and 9,500 MacBook Neo units for third through 12th grade students. The district also allocated 1,000 MacBook Neo devices for teachers.

The district compared the MacBook Neo to products from Lenovo and Asus and ultimately concluded the MacBook Neo had the “strongest performance and reliability among the devices evaluated.” Apple’s financing terms were also more favorable. Access to AppleCare also influenced the decision.

From the report:

According to the district’s comparison, the Lenovo model had a minimum financing rate of 4%, a higher four-year cost and a guaranteed buyback value of $10 per device. The Asus model had competitive upfront pricing and met instructional needs but also cost more over four years. The district said the Asus model’s plastic parts would require more repairs.

title: Here’s everything we know so far about Apple’s next entry-level iPad: A19 chip, more
snippet: Apple’s current iPad, the A16 model, has gone untouched for well over a year. It remains the only device in Apple’s core product lineup without support for Apple Intelligence. Rumors had swirled for quite some time about an A18 model coming this year. Now, it’s sounding like Apple has an even bigger plan. more…
fullText:
Apple’s current iPad, the A16 model, has gone untouched for well over a year. It remains the only device in Apple’s core product lineup without support for Apple Intelligence. Rumors had swirled for quite some time about an A18 model coming this year. Now, it’s sounding like Apple has an even bigger plan.

It’s likely safe to assume that the delays with this product launch have much to do with the ongoing memory crisis affecting the electronics industry. It wouldn’t surprise me if Apple had the A18 refresh roadmapped for earlier this year alongside the debut of the M4 iPad Air, then had to push it.

As a reminder, Apple raised the price of the base iPad from $349 to $449 this summer alongside the rest of its memory-related price hikes. This brings it back to the price it initially launched at in 2022.

New iPad details

However, a new leak from MacRumors contributor Aaron Perris paints a more promising picture. Instead of utilizing the A18 chip, it sounds like the next entry-level iPad will equip the A19 chip. Alongside that, you’ll get the N1 networking chip, as well as the C1X modem on the cellular version. This’ll bring support for Wi-Fi 7 to Apple’s cheapest iPad.

The A19 iPad will also be equipped with 8GB of memory, allowing users to run Siri AI, though you’ll still miss out on the most capable local models and the more advanced dictation models, as those features require 12GB of memory. It’s not a major loss, but worth pointing out.

Another possibility is that the A19 iPad might offer a new name. With the debut of the MacBook Neo, Apple marketing exec Greg Joswiak pointed out that calling the MacBook Neo just “MacBook” would leave it without an identity. Hopefully, with the next entry-level iPad, we also get some sort of proper name like “SE” or “Neo” so we have something to call it.

Beyond that, don’t expect any sort of redesign or display improvements. There may be new colors, but probably nothing else. I personally wish Apple would bring USB 3 to the product, so users don’t have to suffer with such slow transfer speeds. It’d certainly help justify the new higher starting price.

Release date

	

Apple’s next budget iPad should be releasing next Spring, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. That’ll accompany other products like the M6 MacBook Air, A19 Pro MacBook Neo, M7 14-inch MacBook Pro, and more.

Are you someone in the market for the entry-level iPad? What are you most looking forward to? Let us know in the comments.

title: Circuit Breaker Labs hopes to make AI safer for your kids (and you)
snippet: With all the talk about how AI might one day kill us all, it's easy to forget that AI has already harmed some people psychologically. Circuit Breaker Labs has created "crash-test dummies" to solve that.
fullText:
With all the talk about how AI might one day kill us all, it’s easy to forget that AI has already been life-threatening to some, not through bioweapons, but psychologically.

For example, Character.AI settled several wrongful death lawsuits earlier this year brought by families of underage users who died by suicide after interactions with its bots. Multiple families have also sued OpenAI over ChatGPT’s alleged role in their loved ones’ suicides and delusions.

Making AI safer across languages and cultures is the mission of Circuit Breaker Labs, one of TechCrunch’s 2026 Startup Battlefield 200 finalists. (Circuit Breaker will be pitching at TechCrunch Disrupt, which takes place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco from October 13-15.)

Founders Shirali and Arul Nigam, who are siblings, were motivated by Sewell Setzer, the 14-year-old who developed an emotional attachment to a Character.AI chatbot and confessed thoughts to it of harming himself before dying by suicide. The chatbot, the parents alleged in a 2024 lawsuit, encouraged him. The bot may not have understood what words like “I want to be with you” really implied, said Arul, who is Circuit Breaker Labs’ CTO.

“A lot of people, especially young people, turn to these systems for support, and usually they aren’t actually getting the help they need. But in many cases, they’re actively being harmed, and people unfortunately have taken their lives already,” Arul said. “Those sorts of safety vulnerabilities, where people aren’t necessarily actively trying to break the system — they’re engaging in a natural way — and the system has context pollution or it doesn’t understand the nuance, and then takes really dangerous action, we’re trying to prevent that.”

Circuit Breaker Labs has created AI agents that it likens to an army of crash-test dummies. These agents mimic folks from all ages, backgrounds, languages, and cultures, and are used to test models on their ability to detect dangerous, psychologically harmful interactions.

“The way a six-year-old girl versus a 45-year-old man, or someone who speaks English as a first language versus a second language, or … gamer slang versus someone else who uses a different kind of slang, all of those can really trip up a model,” said Shirali, who is Circuit Breaker Labs’ CEO. “Models are really good at handling standard speech patterns, but nobody actually talks like that and so if the model misunderstands nuance or slang, it can go really badly.”

The startup works with human domain experts to build its hyper-realistic user simulations in order to run “red-team” tests against models, which are adversarial tests meant to uncover weaknesses. The tests are built to reflect real human speech patterns, slang, coded language, and typos. Circuit Breaker Labs then runs tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of simulated interactions per day.

The idea is to ensure that a model can appropriately respond to risky interactions that may emerge over time and over many conversations. Circuit Breaker Labs then uses a proprietary scoring method to create auditable, explainable scores.

Circuit Breaker Labs is currently operating as an AI safety testing lab for high-risk AI applications such as AI coaching, journaling, or other mental health support apps, though Arul declined to name its marquee customers. Although the startup has a working product, it is in the very early stages, with only five employees, including the Nigam siblings.

Eventually, though, the testing platform could be applied to any app where someone may fall down an “AI psychosis” hole, where the human is at risk of developing a parasocial relationship with a chatbot. Examples include AI “co-worker” agents, whose responses can vary from one interaction to the next.

“People are becoming more skeptical of AI or more resistant to adopt it across the board,” Arul said, adding that while skepticism is healthy, banning a potentially valuable tool over safety concerns would be “regressive.”

Circuit Breakers Labs believes the answer to those fears is making AI safer. “We want to help build that trust for people.”

Come learn much more about Circuit Breaker Labs and many other innovative startups that have been vetted by TechCrunch at our Startup Battlefield competition, happening in downtown San Francisco on October 13-15.

fullText:
Kakul Srivastava is the CEO of Splice, the sample platform countless producers rely on for one-shots and melodic loops. Samples pulled from the service have found their way into massive hits like Lisa’s “Money” and “Espresso” by Sabrina Carpenter. (The original samples are here and here, for the curious.)

Before that, Kakul held executive roles at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub, and Adobe. Throughout her career, Kakul has found herself at the intersection of Silicon Valley and creatives. That’s been especially true at Splice, where she’s not just expanded the platform’s footprint by acquiring Spitfire Audio, but also overseen its forays into the world of generative AI.

Last year, she was very outspoken on an episode of Decoder about avoiding the sort of “push-button, get-song” AI that has made companies like Suno so controversial. And based on her answers to our questionnaire, it doesn’t seem like her skepticism has waned. When it comes to Splice, the company has made a point of trying to offer AI products that still keep the human at the center of the creative process. And when it comes to communicating with colleagues, Kakul sees the same need to keep AI at bay.

What is your most indispensable tool?

A well-written document and a real conversation about it.

Splice is remote-first, so we don’t have a hallway. What we have instead is somebody sitting down and actually thinking something through, and then a bunch of people arguing with it. Almost everything good that’s happened here started that way.

Which is why I’m careful about AI-written documents. Once you can’t tell whether there’s a person behind the words, the conversation you have about it becomes a different conversation, and a worse one. And you can’t really go back from that. I think the same thing is true of music.

What is your happy place online?

Instagram, which I know is not the fashionable answer. My feed has turned into almost entirely people making music in ways I would never have thought of. There’s gothic western, which I did not know was a thing. There’s a woman in Russia who organizes street dancing. There’s a guy playing modern hits on a hammered dulcimer. The Indian chai-wala rapping. I could watch it all, all day.

What game do you have the fondest memories of?

Antakshari. It’s an Indian game — you sing a bit of a song, and whatever letter the line ends on is the letter the next person has to start their song with. You play it on long car rides, at weddings, any time a group of people is stuck somewhere together.

I love that the whole game is made out of music and none of the players are musicians. You just have to remember, and you have to be willing to sing in front of your family, which for most people is the harder part. And then when you watch people’s faces get soft when the song really hits — even when it’s sung badly. That’s the power of music.

What’s the most disappointing gadget you’ve owned?

A cup warmer. It warms the cup. It does not warm the coffee. I want to be clear that it works exactly as designed.

What creation are you most proud of?

I can’t not say my kids. Watching a person go from nothing to a fully formed human with opinions you did not give them is the most amazing thing I have been anywhere near. And the strange part is that it isn’t rare. It’s happening in every house on the street. We all just watch it happen and then go about our day.

Which are you least proud of?

I was on the early team at Tiny Speck, the company that later became Slack. Before Slack, we made a game called Glitch — a massively multiplayer open world — and it was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever worked on. The art, the sound, the writing, the way the world actually worked. Some of the most talented people I’ve ever been around.

It failed, and it failed for reasons that were sitting right there in front of us. It was built on Flash, and Adobe had already stopped investing in Flash. It was a PC experience at the exact moment the whole world was moving to playing games on a phone. Two enormous tectonic trends, and we didn’t account for either one in time to do anything about them. I feel like I let down the creativity of the people who built something beautiful.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

Say the thing, then explain it. Don’t lay all your proof out first, hoping it earns you the right to make your point. Nobody is listening to the proof yet. They’re listening for whether you sound like you believe it. The confidence you say it with is what makes room for the explanation.

What is your current obsession?

Cooking my mother’s food. She died before I learned most of it from her, so I’ve been reconstructing her recipes off YouTube — strangers in their own kitchens, making the thing the way their mothers made it. It takes a lot of tries. I got one of them right last year, and the taste put me straight back to being eight years old with my mom by my side.

This is what I think about when people ask me what technology is for. Some guy uploaded a video of his family’s recipe and gave me my mother’s cooking back. He will never know that.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Live jazz. There is nothing else like being in a room where people are making decisions in real time and can’t take them back. I travel a lot for work, and if there’s any way to get to a show in whatever city I’m in, I’ll do it, even when it means I’m useless the next morning.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

A heist movie where nothing gets stolen and everybody gets paid.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

title: iOS 27’s Siri gets one thing very right that other AI assistants get wrong
snippet: Siri AI is a major upgrade to Apple’s assistant that’s now available in iOS 27. And there’s one standout area I’ve noticed where it differs greatly from other AI assistants—for the better. more…
fullText:
Siri AI is a major upgrade to Apple’s assistant that’s now available in iOS 27. And there’s one standout area I’ve noticed where it differs greatly from other AI assistants—for the better.

iOS 27’s new Siri doesn’t pretend to be human, unlike every other AI chatbot

I’ve been using Siri AI for nearly four months, since the first iOS 27 beta launched. Overall, it’s checked all the boxes I was hoping for.

The new Siri is far more capable than its predecessor, delivering on the original promise of being a truly capable assistant on Apple devices.

I’ll admit though: if you need the most powerful, cutting-edge AI tool, you might be better served by competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Google Gemini.

However, after using Siri AI and comparing it to those third-party tools, I’ve noticed a key difference where I greatly favor Siri.

Unlike other AI chatbots, Siri doesn’t pretend to be human.

It’s not overly verbose, mimicking a human-like personality that might lull you into forming a personal relationship with it.

Siri is helpful, intelligent, and does what you ask it to do. But the way it responds makes clear that it’s a tool, not a person. It reminds you regularly that it’s an AI, so it can make mistakes. And it won’t faux date you.

Whereas ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini are all bursting with personality, opinions, and demonstrate more human-like tendencies in a way that, for me, feels disingenuous.

I imagine some users enjoy that more “personal” approach. But I much prefer that AI assistants stay in their lane and don’t pretend to be something they’re not.

AI is changing the world. But AI chatbots are tools, not people. And I love that Apple gets that, and built the new Siri accordingly.

What’s your view of how “human-like” an AI assistant should be? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google stands by Gemini 4 performance as some claim it ‘struggles’ in real-world use
snippet: Google yesterday unveiled its new flagship Gemini 4 model with some impressive scores, but a report suggests that it might “struggle” in some cases. more…
fullText:
Google yesterday unveiled its new flagship Gemini 4 model with some impressive scores, but a report suggests that it might “struggle” in some cases.

Google announces Gemini 4 Argon as its new frontier model

Bloomberg reports that, internally, Google employees have found that Gemini 4’s real-world performance doesn’t always line up with its benchmark scores. During the unveiling of Gemini 4 Argon, Google showed that its new model outpaced competitors including OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in many key areas.

The report cites Googlers who found that the model “does less well when employees actually put it to work,” and that it “struggles to handle certain coding tasks.” Google, speaking to Bloomberg on the claims, said that it “would be inaccurate to say that Gemini 4 is underperforming in areas such as coding,” also referencing comments from Koray Kavukcuoglu, the head of Google DeepMind, from late September, when he said that “it’s a certainty that we are always gonna be at the frontier.” The report cites one Googler who said that there’s a “large consensus” that Gemini 4 is at the frontier amongst employees, while others are concerned that Gemini “will still lag behind” competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Clearly, there’s a split in how employees view the model’s performance.

Gemini 4 Argon brings welcome upgrades to the model, including an expanded output limit of up to 1 million tokens, while Google also explained that the model is “highly capable at cybersecurity defense” and shows “leading performance” in other use cases. Gemini 4 Argon comes at a cost of “$4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens” but will see introductory pricing which is half of that.

title: iFixit teardown of the new AirPods 5 reveals first real repairability improvement
snippet: iFixit’s teardown of the new AirPods 5 is now up, revealing an important, albeit tiny, repairability improvement. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit’s teardown of the new AirPods 5 is now up, revealing an important, albeit tiny, repairability improvement. Watch it below.

Record repairability score at 2/10

Since Apple launched the original AirPods in 2016, iFixit has consistently given them a 0 out of 10 for repairability. From heavily glued-in batteries and soldered connections to housings that are nearly impossible to open and reassemble without damage, AirPods have always been notoriously difficult to repair.

With the new AirPods 5, however, iFixit says Apple has taken a tiny step in the right direction, provided the repair is being done by a skilled professional or particularly adventurous DIY enthusiast.

In their new teardown video, iFixit shows that the batteries inside each earbud can be removed and replaced without necessarily destroying the AirPods in the process, which has led them to give AirPods a repairability score above zero for the first time.

Granted, the new AirPods 5 only scored 2 out of 10, but that’s still two points more than every previous generation combined.

iFixit notes that the left and right batteries are not interchangeable, as they use reversed polarity and slightly different contact placement.

That said, this is basically the long and short of AirPods 5 repairability. As iFixit shows in the video, going any further into the earbuds is still impossible without destroying them, and the same is true of their charging case.

iFixit’s teardown also includes its always-fascinating CT scans, which offer a detailed look at just how densely Apple has packed the batteries, MEMS microphones, H2 chip, and other tiny components inside each earbud.

title: HBO Max and Paramount+ set to merge under ‘Skydance’ brand
snippet: Paramount Skydance will complete its acquisition of Warner Bros. next week, and CEO David Ellison just revealed ‘Skydance’ as the new company name ahead of a planned merging of HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services. more…
fullText:
Paramount Skydance will complete its acquisition of Warner Bros. next week, and CEO David Ellison just revealed ‘Skydance’ as the new company name ahead of a planned merging of HBO Max and Paramount+ streaming services.

‘Skydance’ is name of merged Paramount-Warner Bros. company, and likely name of merged streaming service too

Warner Bros. Discovery is officially set to be merged with Paramount Skydance next Tuesday, October 6.

Following a lengthy approval process and recent settlement, and after beating out Netflix’s initial deal for WBD, the owner of Paramount+ will merge with the owner of HBO Max. 

And the new name for this merged company? Skydance.

CEO David Ellison just joined X and made the name announcement in his first post.

What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.

Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren't rewriting history — we're equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for… pic.twitter.com/uInLRY3IrE

— David Ellison (@ellisonskydance) October 2, 2026

	

Earlier this year, when asked about plans for HBO Max and Paramount+ if the merger went through, Ellison said the streamers would be combined into a single service. Per CNBC:

Paramount+ and HBO Max will be combined into one streaming service if regulators approve Paramount Skydance’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, Paramount CEO David Ellison said on a conference call Monday. A combined service would have about 200 million subscribers given existing totals, Ellison said during his company’s investor call about the WBD transaction. […]

Paramount executives didn’t offer any details Monday on how the company may price a combined service or what it would be called. Still, Ellison said he wouldn’t disrupt the HBO brand. “HBO should stay HBO,” he said, citing its long history of quality programming. HBO is likely to be a sub-brand within the larger service, according to a person familiar with Paramount’s plans.

Now that Skydance is the official name for the merged company, there’s a very good chance it will become the name of the new, combined streaming service too.

There’s been no timeline communicated yet for HBO Max and Paramount+ to merge, but we may get those details next week after the merger closes.

What do you think of the Skydance name? Will you be glad to see the streaming services merge, or do you think they should be kept separate? Let us know in the comments.

title: It’s not just you, Claude is down in confirmed partial outage [U]
snippet: Anthropic has confirmed an outage affecting multiple Claude services this morning. more…
fullText:
Anthropic has confirmed an outage affecting multiple Claude services this morning.

Confirmed on the Claude Status dashboard, a “partial outage” is affecting Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, as well as the Claude API and Console. Anthropic confirmed it was aware of the outage just prior to 10:30am ET (7:30am PT). 

Update: Anthropic says that the outage is already resolving, with services back up and running for many users, though sign-in issues remain.

The errors that began at 14:00 UTC were mitigated at 14:36 UTC, and existing conversations are mostly working again. A second issue is preventing many users from signing in (single sign-on and Sign in with Apple are unavailable), starting new chats, voice conversations and Claude Code or Cowork sessions, making purchases, and uploading files. If you’re signed in, please don’t sign out. We’re working on a fix…

User reports on DownDetector spiked starting at the top of the hour, with limited reports of ChatGPT and Gemini also being down – these do not appear to be accurate, though, with neither OpenAI nor Google confirming any issues.

	

Previously, there were partial Claude outages on September 22, September 15, and September 11, as well as a major outage on September 3 that happened at the same time as outages with other AI models including ChatGPT and Grok.

We’ll update this post as more details become available.

title: Your Next Mobile Games Will Get AI Graphics Boosts That PCs and Consoles Have Had for Years
snippet: AI upscaling and frame generation are coming in upcoming premium Android phones running the new highest-tier Snapdragon chips.
fullText:
Gaming on phones has gotten good enough that graphics and gameplay are beginning to approach what players expect on PC and console. Those more established platforms maintain the edge, with massive GPUs and energy budgets that power AI enhancements that render smoother experiences. While there will never be enough room on a smartphone to fit a full-size graphics card, next year’s top handsets will finally get those AI boosts — and mobile gaming will never be the same.

It’s all because of technology making its debut on the latest phone chips. At its Snapdragon Summit 2026 recently, Qualcomm debuted the new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, which comes with GPU upgrades, including new Adreno Neural Fusion tech that uses AI to upscale resolution, generate frames to increase frame rate and extend battery life while gaming. 

On stage at the Snapdragon Summit, Chris Patrick, Qualcomm’s SVP and general manager of handsets, shows off the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6’s graphics gains with Adreno Neural Fusion.David Lumb/CNET

How AI gameplay improvements can come to mobile

Not every Android phone uses Snapdragon chips, but AI graphics boosts could come to them as well — the first time this tech will reach mainstream phones. In early September, chip designer Arm debuted its Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, which has similar technology that upscales resolution and inserts frames, as well as a denoiser to improve image quality when rendering complex effects like ray-tracing reflections and lighting. Arm GPUs are used in top-end chips from companies like MediaTek.

			

More from CNET

This tech has been used in high-end PC and console hardware for years in the form of Nvidia’s DLSS and AMD’s FSR, which uses AI to bolster graphics in more affordable GPUs and boost frame rates for smoother gameplay. In beefy PC rigs and consoles that plug into wall outlets, or even laptops or handhelds like the Asus ROG Ally, this tech mostly eases complex workloads and makes good graphics better. 

But the challenge in adapting this modern graphics tech to phones lies in one word: thermals. PCs have a constant flow of power, laptops have giant batteries, and gaming-specific computers are cooled with massive fans. But phones are so small that their batteries are measured in milliamp-hours, often running on a handful of watts of power per day, and increasingly rely on thermal paste and cooling chambers to vent heat. 

The big challenge was getting even better graphics out of the latest generation of Snapdragon chips and even boosting battery life, said Qualcomm Director of Product Management Amandeep Dhaliwal, who leads Snapdragon’s GPU strategy.

“That was the main thing when we were building this Adreno Neural Fusion model,”  Dhaliwal said. “How do I factor in thermals as I’m building this upscaling model so that eventually, if in my game, let’s say the power I was consuming was 1 watt, how do I then save 20% on that and come out ahead?”

On phones, AI boosts can eke out more battery life while gaming. With the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6’s tech, rather than render graphics in full resolution, they’re dialed down to 540p and then AI upscales it to 1080p — it’s much more efficient for AI to make up that difference. Likewise, they can run at 30 frames per second and AI can insert more frames to boost the count up to 60 or even 90fps. This could result in noticeably better energy efficiency while gaming on phones using Snapdragon’s top chip, Dhaliwal said. 

“Improving your battery life in a gaming session — people will [cheer] if you do it for 1 to 2%, and here we are talking about 20 to 30%, right?” Dhaliwal said. “Which is huge.”

Both of the new Snapdragon chips have improvements to their Hexagon GPUs, with the 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 getting 44% improved GPU performance over the Hexagon in last year’s chip, while the 8 Elite Gen 6 has 37%. General battery efficiency for GPU tasks has improved 40% across both chips, too. But the Elite Extreme’s graphics processor has extra hardware that puts it above its Gen 6 sibling, like matrix GPU cores that enable Neural Fusion, AI enhancements that plug directly into the graphics pipeline rather than needing to tap traditional memory and other top-of-the-top-end boosts.

Lekha Motiwala, director of product management at Qualcomm, debuted the benchmark gains in the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6’s Adreno GPU.David Lumb/CNET

Tech coming to today’s phones, but only the best of the best

In Snapdragon’s case, this new technology is only coming to the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6, the most top-of-the-line chip in the company’s newly revised lineup. 

Neural Fusion isn’t available on the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, which is still a premium chip at the same level as last year’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 — that is, it’s silicon that is already slated to power the Xiaomi 18 Pro and will almost certainly come in many of next year’s upper-tier phones. The Extreme version is a cut above even that, and will only be used in the highest-end Android devices, like the Motorola Signature 27 and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max revealed at this year’s Snapdragon Summit alongside the new chips.

Neural Fusion could, in theory, be used in the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, but it wouldn’t be efficient and the gains wouldn’t be as substantial, Dhaliwal said. “Technically, it’s possible to have [Adreno Neural Fusion] on a nonmatrix core GPU, but it’s not advised because you are not going to see a good experience,” he said.

It comes down to the cores: Since the 8 Elite Gen 6 lacks its more premium sibling’s matrix cores, it’s heavily using all its existing cores to render scenes already, and Neural Fusion would tax them even further, requiring a compromise somewhere that would worsen the player experience. Decreasing frame rate to compensate could lead to players noticing dropped frames and choppy visuals, degrading quality for limited benefit. 

Dhaliwal compared the two chips’ graphics capabilities to those on the higher and lower ends of the same PC GPU line.

“When it comes to gaming, we are approaching the Dual 8 Elite launch similar to other hardware competitors in the PC market,” Dhaliwal said in an email after the event. “While there are differences between Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, they are built on the same architectural principle while offering more performance options for our customers, similar to how you would see performance vary within a specific series for consumer graphics cards.”

Qualcomm’s Chris Patrick introduced a list of game titles that will support improvements from the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6’s Adreno Neural Fusion tech.David Lumb/CNET

What’s coming in tomorrow’s mobile gaming

Rendering graphics at lower resolutions and frame rates to upscale them to rates that gamers expect (1080p at 60fps) is an impressive way to extend battery life and offset some of the computational load from the CPU to neural processing. But there are even greater heights for the technology to reach.

For this generation of phone chip tech, Neural Fusion generates a frame for every one traditionally rendered — so going from 30 frames per second to 60, or 60 to 120. But the big trend in China is for even higher frame rate gaming, Dhaliwal said, with games natively rendered to 120, 144 or even 165fps. Since rendering those rates is power-taxing, which leads to swift battery drain on mobile gaming, Qualcomm’s next frontier is looking to generate more frames for each one rendered — boosting a native 30 frames up to 120, for instance. 

But with Snapdragon and Arm introducing these PC gaming AI boosts and Apple adding neural accelerators to GPUs on its A-series chips, the mobile industry is heading toward harnessing this tech in phone gaming on a greater scale. That affects game developers, too, who have been working miracles to get their games running on pocket-sized devices with very limited power budgets — but now have more power savings to boost the graphics in their games.

“Now the developers are basically thinking, look, I was doing something in a given 1-watt budget,” Dhaliwal said. “Now with upscaling, I suddenly have these 200 milliwatts or 300 milliwatts available, which means I can enhance my game to do more things, right?”

These GPU improvements aren’t limited to gaming, either. They can run AI models. Even if they’re not going to be as power- or performance-optimized as on a laptop or desktop, they can run on a GPU, Dhaliwal pointed out. It’s another tool alongside the neural processing unit that developers programming mobile AI models can tap. 

“It’s all those things which are going to be really, really exciting,” Dhaliwal said.

title: The MacBook Air M5 is $200 off for the first time in months
snippet: Pictured: The 15-inch Apple MacBook Air. | Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge Amazon’s October Prime Day has effectively chopped off Apple’s June price increases. Usually $1,299, the 13-inch MacBook Air with the M5 chip and 512GB of storage is on sale for $1,099 at Amazon. That’s a more palatable price for a machine that’s significantly faster than Apple’s $699 MacBook Neo. The 15-inch version, also with 512GB of storage, is $1,299 at Amazon (was $1,499). In addition to the larger screen, it has two additional speakers, for a total of six, and two additional GPU cores for better overall graphical performance. Apple MacBook Air (M5) Apple’s 2026 MacBook Air has an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage that’s significantly faster than previous generations. It’s still as excellent as ever despite a higher base price. Read our review. Where to Buy: $1299 $1099 at Amazon (13-inch, 512GB) $1499 $1299 at Amazon (15-inch, 512GB) The latest update to Apple’s midrange laptop includes a noticeable improvement to the speed of both the processor and storage. Even without flashy new features compared to the last-gen model, it’s still one of our favorite laptops, thanks to its long battery life, bright screen, and excellent speakers. Read our Apple MacBook Air (2026, M5) review.
fullText:
Brad Bourque

fullText:
Samsung is now rolling out its Android 17-based update, One UI 9, to its collection of supported Galaxy smartphones and tablets. Here’s the full list of devices that have been updated so far, and what you should know about the update.

What’s new in Android 17 on Samsung Galaxy?

One UI 9, Samsung’s Android 17 update, continues the trend of evolution more than overhaul. The update introduces some slight design tweaks, more AI-powered features, and other changes built on the redesign that debuted in One UI 7 and was iterated in last year’s Android 16-based One UI 8. 

Some key changes in One UI 9 include:

Warranty & Samsung Care status in the Settings menu

Broader support for Now Nudge

My FanCam automatic video cropping based on a select subject

More Quick Panel (quick settings) customization

AI privacy alerts

Upgrades to Samsung DeX

New lock screen clocks that can adapt to your wallpaper

Samsung Galaxy devices with Android 17 – The full list

While Samsung hasn’t confirmed an exact schedule for its One UI 9 and Android 17 rollout for Galaxy devices, there are updates now rolling out in parts of the globe. Below you’ll find a regularly-updated list of every Samsung Galaxy device that has received a stable Android 17 update so far.

Galaxy S26

Galaxy S26+

Galaxy S26 Ultra

Galaxy S25 (limited availability)

One UI 9 changelog

Here’s the full changelog from Samsung for One UI 9, as listed for the Galaxy S26 series. Some features may vary by device.

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

title: Lenovo’s first Googlebook actually costs $200 less than announced, and it’s not the only one
snippet: Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099. more…
fullText:
Lenovo today put a spotlight on its Googlebook release, also confirming that initial pricing was incorrect and that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 will, in fact, start at $1,099.

The Lenovo Googlebook 15 is one of the first five machines running the new Googlebook OS which replaces ChromeOS. This is designed for “professionals, creators, and business owners,” Lenovo said in a press release:

Powered by Intel Core Ultra 5 processors with built-in Gemini Intelligence, up to 32GB of memory and up to 512GB of storage, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 helps users stay productive and connected – no matter where the day takes them.

Designed for professionals, creators and business owners, the Lenovo Googlebook 15 delivers up to 47 TOPS of performance while weighing under 3 lbs., making it the lightest 15-inch device in Lenovo’s portfolio.

It’s certainly a workhorse, with core specs including a 15-inch OLED 120Hz refresh rate, Intel Core Ultra 5 processors, up to 32GB of RAM, and up to 512GB of storage. Lenovo also touts a haptic trackpad, 12.5-hour battery life, top-facing Dolby Atmos speakers, a metal chassis, and Lenovo even built a wireless mouse with a matching “Glowbar” for the Googlebook platform.

And it’s cheaper than we first thought.

	

Google initially announced that the Lenovo Googlebook 15 would start at $1,299, but Lenovo has now confirmed it actually starts at $1,099. That’s for the model with 16GB of RAM, 512GB of storage, and a Core Ultra 5 chip. Google Store, for some reason, still lists the machine at $1,149, but Best Buy has the correct pricing. 

	

Lenovo says its Googlebook, like others, will be available starting on October 4.

This isn’t the only model where Google messed up the intial pricing announcement. The Dell XPS Googlebook was initially announced at a starting price of $1,199, but is actually $999.

These probably aren’t a result of feedback on the high overall pricing – Best Buy was always showing the correct prices, so this was only on Google’s end – but Google hasn’t publicly acknowledged exactly what’s going on. For those actually looking to buy a Googlebook, though, lower prices are great news. Asus and HP’s Googlebooks still start at $1,299, while the Acer Googlebook is the most affordable of the lot at $899.

title: Here’s how many iPhone Duo units Apple is reportedly making
snippet: A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more. more…
fullText:
A recent report from Chinese outlet Jiemian News offers an update on iPhone Duo production, including how many units are being made, assembly troubles, and more.

Latest iPhone Duo report covers production struggles, target inventory, and more

iPhone Duo goes up for pre-order on October 16, just a little more than two weeks from now. And a recent report from Jiemian News provides the latest update on Apple’s production status.

We’ve seen reporting before that Apple’s foldable is having a slow ramp-up due to a complex assembly process. 

Right now, iPhone Duo assembly yield is reportedly just over 60%. And per Jiemian, suppliers believe it could take another six months or more for production yields to reach a “mature” level.

That’s far below what would be expected for other models, but perhaps not surprising considering the Duo is packed with all-new product designs and components.

Per the report, Apple is targeting having 6-8 million iPhone Duo units ready to go for 2026. This compares to 20-30 million typical units for a flagship new Pro or Pro Max model.

	

With a starting price of $1,999 and unique form factor, iPhone Duo isn’t targeting as broad a set of users as models like iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. The overall foldable market is still fairly niche, too. 

If Apple sells anywhere near 8 million units before the end of 2026, that will no doubt be seen as a major win. But the iPhone Duo’s success will ultimately come down more to popularity over time. Will it be an early adopter model only, or prove a mass-market hit too?

A source told Jiemian that Apple so far has been unwilling to relax its strict quality standards for the iPhone Duo, thus leading to lower than expected yields. While that potentially will lead to shortages when the new model launches, I suspect anyone spending $2,000+ on an iPhone will want the highest quality product, so it’s not exactly bad news.

title: Bank of America says Meta’s Muse highlights a new risk for Apple’s services revenue
snippet: In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new investor note issued today, Bank of America says Meta’s new Muse AI agent highlights how third-party AI agents could increasingly bypass Apple’s ecosystem and threaten its services revenue. Here are the details.

BofA maintains “Buy” rating

Apple’s shares dropped more than 2.5% today, after Bank of America’s Wamsi Mohan issued an investor note warning that AI agents such as Meta’s Muse could increasingly capture product discovery, referrals, and transactions that currently take place through Apple’s ecosystem.

From his note, via SeekingAlpha:

“The risk for Apple is that it can keep every handset sale and still lose discovery, referral, and transaction initiation.”

Mohan’s note comes as Meta’s Muse nears two weeks at No. 1 on the US App Store’s free apps chart. According to Sensor Tower estimates cited by TechCrunch, Muse has amassed more than 3.4 million downloads as of last week.

Meta’s OpenClaw-like AI agent can browse the web, fill out forms, book trips, send emails, and make purchases on a user’s behalf, and it seems to have caught on with the general public, as it took just 10 days to overtake ChatGPT at the top of the US App Store.

Back to Mohan’s note, he maintained a “Buy” rating and $370 price target on Apple, arguing that despite the new risks posed by AI agents, he still sees the company as an “eventual winner of AI at the edge.”

From his note, via Yahoo! Finance:

“Whomever the agent chooses becomes the merchant, and whoever owns the agent collects the routing economics that previously accrued to operating systems, search, and app stores.”

Mohan also points to Muse’s growing list of commerce integrations, including Shopify and Shop Pay, Expedia, and PayPal, as examples of how AI agents can increasingly handle transactions from discovery through checkout.

Additionally, Mohan notes that modern iPhones already have more than enough computing power to run AI agents, making software execution and integration the bigger challenge for Apple.

In his note, Mohan argues that Apple needs its Services, silicon, payments, privacy, and Siri AI teams to move together more quickly if the company wants to compete for what he calls the “economics of user intent.”

	

Specifically on Siri AI, he also noted that it lacks some of Muse’s capabilities, including persistent background tasks, broad third-party action support, and a dedicated agent payment rail.

He also pointed out the difference in development pace, with Apple typically shipping major software updates once a year, while AI agents can “improve daily.”

That said, Mohan sees Apple’s massive installed base and reputation for privacy as important advantages, particularly when it comes to convincing users to trust AI agents with sensitive tasks.

title: Some Pixel models reportedly experiencing an NFC bug that breaks contactless payments
snippet: Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11. more…
fullText:
Following several Pixel 11-specific bugs after the phone’s launch, another one reportedly breaks NFC tap-to-pay, used for contactless payments. But this one is affecting more than just the Pixel 11.

A slew of reports on Reddit have been posted within the last two weeks regarding a new Google Pixel bug that affects NFC payments (via Android Authority). Users have been reporting that their Pixel devices can no longer use tap-to-pay, whether directly in the Google Wallet app or at automatic transit terminals that don’t require the app to be open.

The issue isn’t affecting just the Pixel 11, so this can’t be piled onto the list of device-specific issues users are coming across – of which there are a good few. The Reddit posts and comments within list Google Pixel models ranging from the Pixel 8 to the new Pixel 11 Pro XL. The bug is agnostic to model or series, given it’s still supported.

	

The obvious response, noted by more than a few commenters, suggests using the Pixel 11 correctly. The NFC antenna is placed slightly higher than on other models, so the first suggestion appears to be “move your phone” to solve the Google Pixel’s NFC bug.

	

Of course, this would only apply if the Pixel 11’s NFC antenna were alone in experiencing this bug. Because it isn’t, it’s easier to point at a software update that made NFC unusable with Google Wallet. Some users note NFC still works in other functions, but not with payments.

Google has yet to respond, it seems. That doesn’t mean the company isn’t aware of the Pixel bug, but it might suggest users will need to wait a little longer for a fix. That being said, loss of tap-to-pay is a pretty big deal for a phone in 2026.

title: Hollywood’s Newest Media Colossus: Paramount and Warner Bros. Merge Under Skydance
snippet: Skydance will now be one of the largest media companies in history, consolidating film studios, broadcast and cable networks, news and streaming.
fullText:
With Paramount CEO David Ellison overcoming the final hurdle blocking his expansion of the Paramount media empire, the billionaire media executive announced on X (formerly Twitter) that the newly merged entity combining Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery will be named Skydance.

The announcement comes after the company entered into a consent decree to settle antitrust claims brought by a group of 12 state attorneys general, who had sued in July over concerns that the merger would concentrate too much control over news networks, cable TV and the film industry. With the last legal opposition cleared, the path was open to finalize the massive the $111 billion merger on Sept. 21.

“Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for bold, quality storytelling,” Ellison posted on Friday. “We wanted a name that would give the combined company an identity of its own while allowing Paramount and Warner Bros. — and all our extraordinary brands — to remain in the spotlight.”

There was a year-long bidding battle for Warner Bros. Discovery, leaving Ellison as the top bidder after Netflix dropped out. The name Skydance comes from Ellison’s love of aviation and aerobatic “skydancing.” David’s father is Larry Ellison, who is co-founder and chief technology officer of Oracle and one of the richest people in the world.

What once was the peak, is now just the beginning.

Paramount and Warner Bros. shaped over a century of culture. By combining them, we aren't rewriting history — we're equipping these iconic studios with a more powerful engine. Together, we are Skydance: a creative-first home for… pic.twitter.com/uInLRY3IrE

— David Ellison (@davidellison) October 2, 2026

A Hollywood empire of studios, news, networks and streamers

As viewers, it’s unclear how streaming content from Warner Bros., HBO and Paramount via apps like HBO Max and Paramount Plus will change. But the merger will undeniably affect employees at the mega media company, now one of the largest in history. Much of the legal opposition concerned their fate, and the consent decree attempted to safeguard employment, film production and distribution and consumer pricing. 

In practice, employees usually lose out in corporate consolidation, regardless of protections. Harvard Business Review estimated that up to 30% of workers get laid off in mergers like these, where there’s a significant overlap in the business, though that oft-cited figure is from 2017. 

		

			

The bigger worry, though, is media monopoly. Critics worry that adding CNN to the company’s portfolio could lead to widespread restructuring and corporate upheaval, similar to recent struggles at the CBS News division. Corporate convergence also risks homogenizing news content by potentially suppressing divergent viewpoints — all for minimal reward, given that CBS’s own ratings are reportedly way down.

“If this trend of consolidation continues, we will be left searching dominant media outlets in vain for news and information that challenges the powerful and stands up for people who are struggling to pay monthly bills, put food on the table and engage in local civic life,” nonprofit watchdog Free Press co-CEO Jessica J. González said in a prepared statement earlier this week.

The Block the Merger coalition also posted a follow-up statement: “Allowing the Paramount Skydance-Warner Bros. Discovery merger to move forward with no meaningful structural remedies will cost jobs, mute creativity, weaken independent journalism, and damage our First Amendment rights. The ripples of this merger will be far-reaching, long-lasting, and impossible to contain.”

The Writers Guild of America East and Writers Guild of America West had filed a separate lawsuit to halt the merger, alleging that it was illegal and would harm writers. Once the state attorneys general backed out of the battle, WGA cited an inability to sustain legal costs on its own and dropped its companion lawsuit.

As part of the consent decree, Paramount agreed to establish an oversight board of journalists to protect the editorial independence of CNN and CBS News. Critics have called the oversight board “toothless,” noting that its members are appointed and paid by the company, that its authority is unclear and unbinding, and that final control rests with Ellison. 

We reached out to Skydance for comment and didn’t immediately hear back.

Disclosure: Lori Grunin has stock in Paramount from when CNET was owned by CBS.

title: Federal judge calls Flock ‘indiscriminate mass surveillance’
snippet: A federal judge ruled that a sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock to search for her license plate without a warrant.
fullText:
A federal judge ruled this week that a Tulsa, Oklahoma sheriff’s deputy violated a woman’s Fourth Amendment rights when using Flock Safety to search for her license plate without a warrant. 

As reported by 404 Media, this ruling does not create a binding precedent, but it is one of the first times that a federal judge has ruled that a Flock search is unconstitutional.

In this case, Judge Sara Hill said the deputy should have obtained a warrant before searching the Flock database for the woman’s license plate, as he had “no apparent reason” for the search “other than the fact that [the woman’s vehicle] had a California license plate.”

The deputy then used the woman’s travel history in Flock as part of the justification for searching her car, where he allegedly discovered 91 pounds of meth. But Judge Hill wrote that all evidence obtained after the Flock search “must be suppressed as the fruit of a poisonous tree.”

Judge Hill also took broader aim at warrantless searches of the Flock database, writing that tracking people’s location — even when they’re in public places — becomes “constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient.”

“This is a type of indiscriminate mass surveillance,” Hill wrote. “It is not targeted on a single individual, as in [Carpenter v. United States, a Supreme Court case focused on how government agencies access location data from cell phones]. It is a tool that collects information about all vehicles that pass by any network-connected camera at all times, and it serves up the information to law enforcement on demand.”

Hill joins a growing chorus of Flock critics from across the political spectrum. Numerous local and state governments, including Florida and Texas, have said they will stop using the technology. And on Friday, Senator Bernie Sanders — a Democrat from Vermont — introduced the Block Flock Act, which would bar federal agencies from using automated license plate readers such as Flock.

Flock CEO Garretty Langley — who we’ll be interviewing on-stage at TechCrunch Disrupt — has called for a “compromise” between privacy and safety and offered an apology to women who have been stalked by law enforcement officers using the Flock system. And with all those cancellations, Flock has also reportedly offered voluntary employee buyouts as a way to shrink its workforce.

Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor. Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm. He lives in New York City.

title: Pope Leo XIV is not a fan of AI-generated art
snippet: "There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others," the pope wrote. "Algorithms lack the spark of humanity."
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

8:39 AM PDT · October 2, 2026

Image Credits:ALBERTO PIZZOLI/AFP / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Critics of AI-generated art have a powerful new ally: His Holiness the Bishop of Rome (Episcopus Romanus), Primate of Italy (Primatus Italiae), and Supreme Pontiff of the Universal Church (Summus Pontifex Ecclesiae Universalis).

In a post on X Friday morning, Pope Leo XIV detailed the spiritual difference between human-generated art and art that is generated by machines, as part of a call to preserve human art from the encroachment of AI.

“In this era of artificial intelligence, it is becoming urgent to distinguish human art from what machines produce,” the Servus Servorum Dei wrote. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others. Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”

Pope Leo XIV gave a more detailed statement on AI in an encyclical letter in May, which emphasized the importance of human dignity in a world of increasing automation.

But that hasn’t stopped AI companies from lobbying the supreme pontiff. According to a recent New York Times report, Anthropic has actively lobbied the Vatican to reconsider its position on non-human consciousness — apparently finding little success.

fullText:
Update, 10:13 p.m. ET: Apple has now confirmed the launch for “customers with Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards.” The original story follows below.

Nearly twelve years to the day after Apple first announced Apple Pay, the feature is now rolling out in India, one of the few major markets where it had yet to become available. Here are the details.

Apple Pay finally expanding to India

Earlier today, TechCrunch reported that Apple Pay would launch in India “later Tuesday with Axis Bank as its initial banking partner.”

Now, as spotted by Aaron Perris on X, Apple has begun enabling Apple Pay support in India on its servers, suggesting the rollout is officially underway.

According to an Apple support article, there are now 101 countries and regions that support Apple Pay, including India.

India has quickly become one of the most strategically important countries for Apple, both in terms of manufacturing and consumer growth.

In addition to expanding its retail presence and repeatedly highlighting strong growth in the country during quarterly earnings calls, Apple and its suppliers have been shifting more iPhone production to India as part of a broader effort to diversify manufacturing beyond China.

That expansion has not been without its controversies. Apple is currently fighting an antitrust case brought by the Competition Commission of India over its App Store practices, and the company has also refused to comply with a government order requiring smartphone makers to preinstall a state-run app on new devices.

Apple manufacturing partner Tata Electronics has also recently come under fire after an Indian pollution regulator alleged that wastewater from one of its iPhone component factories contaminated groundwater and nearby farmland.

Tata was also recently targeted by a cyberattack that allegedly exposed confidential files from several companies, including Apple.

All of that said, Apple’s launch of Apple Pay in India signals another step in the company’s broader expansion in the country and comes at a potentially useful time for its Services business.

During the last fiscal quarter, Apple saw its first sequential drop in Services revenue since fiscal Q4 2022. Of course, India is unlikely to move that needle on its own, but with iPhone sales reaching record levels in the country, Apple Pay gives the company another way to keep building on that momentum.

title: The Pixel 4 is still my favorite Google smartphone hardware, and it holds up
snippet: Google Pixel has evolved tremendously over the years, with some radically different designs showing up between generations. As the lineup turns 10, the Pixel 4 remains the one that stands out as my favorite smartphone hardware Google has made yet, and it’s not just about the looks. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel has evolved tremendously over the years, with some radically different designs showing up between generations. As the lineup turns 10, the Pixel 4 remains the one that stands out as my favorite smartphone hardware Google has made yet, and it’s not just about the looks.

Elephant in the room: The Pixel 4 series is objectively the worst pair of smartphones Google ever released. Funny, given that the beloved Pixel 4a came out of it, but it’s impossible to argue that Google nailed it here. Following up on its Pixel 3 series which, at the time, was the first launch that really started gainig traction, the Pixel 4 took a big swing in practically every way and it did not work.

But for all of its failings, the Pixel 4 remains my favorite piece of hardware overall.

Why?

	

I think this is the most unique smartphone Google made, and also the one most meant for actual people to use it. The looks themselves aren’t exactly groundbreaking. The mostly blank back with a single square camera module is relatively generic by today’s standards. I’ll still vouch for “Oh So Orange” any day – and still actively regret not keeping mine – but I’d also argue there’s beauty in the simplicity here. It’s timeless.

Of course, less timeless is that big forehead over the display. Used to house the Soli sensor and face unlock hardware, this was another place where Google made a big swing that didn’t work out. Fundamentally, I don’t think Google made a mistake here. The face unlock sensor still works, and even recognized me with a beard that I didn’t have 7 years ago when I was actively using this phone. Impressive! I still think I prefer Google’s forehead design to Apple’s iPhone notch of the time, but the cleverness of Apple’s Dynamic Island is way better than Google’s solution here. But with newer Pixels splitting the difference between security and hardware on face unlock, I think we’re in a pretty good spot nowadays. 

But what really lets the Pixel 4’s hardware live rent-free in my head is how it feels.

Again, for all of this phone’s failings, the physical hardware is truly just so nice. The soft-touch matte of the back panel hasn’t been replicated, and the visually contrasting side rails not only look great, but feel incredible in the hand. These really feel like they were born out of Google’s cozy, human take to product design of the time and I wish the company had continued down that path. 

Don’t get me wrong, the modern Pixel design is gorgeous. I’m a big fan of the camera bar and Google’s approach to color, but the aesthetic of the Pixel 4 is something that I wish we’d seen more of. It was such a great foundation that felt not just unique, but better at the time.

	

Of course, that was largely ruined by the shortcomings. Pixel 4’s legacy is largely around being too expensive, ditching a fingerprint sensor at exactly the wrong time, and truly atrocious battery life. 

Still, if I had any influence whatsoever over the next 10 years of Pixel design, stop number one would be revisiting some of the core design ideas behind the Pixel 4.

What do you think?
