title: McDonald’s and Walmart Are Part of the Widening Fray Over Surveillance Pricing
snippet: The Federal Trade Commission has urged companies to be transparent about their pricing, but that may not be enough.
fullText:
The debate over whether companies can set prices based on information they have about individual customers continues to grow. So-called surveillance pricing is in the news again on reports that Walmart patented technology for dynamic AI pricing about six months after filing for patents related to digital shelf labels.

Walmart, faced with a backlash, has been trying to assure the public that different customers will see the same digital shelf label prices and that its backend AI systems won’t engage in discriminatory pricing. “Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won’t change the price,” Walmart CEO John Furner wrote in a Sept. 25 letter to customers. “And whether you’re buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it’s never a reason to charge you more.”

Reached for comment, a representative for Walmart pointed CNET to the web page and letter to customers regarding pricing.

			

More from CNET

“Walmart does not set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won’t,” the representative said in an email. “A patent does not define Walmart’s pricing practices or intent.”

But the backlash may continue if customers aren’t convinced. One consumer advocate, Jeff Rossen, went as far as to suggest in a recent video that Walmart customers should leave their phones in the car when they shop in order to avoid being datamined. 

Separately, but in a similar vein, McDonald’s has been the target of media coverage over its shift to AI systems that could mean different prices for different burgers at different restaurants for different customers. The company has bristled at some of that coverage, calling it “speculative and misinformed,” but it hasn’t stopped reporters from asking why burger prices can vary from neighborhood to neighborhood as part of the company’s technology makeover.

A representative for McDonald’s didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Two of the largest American brands are now caught in the publicity crossfire over a topic that is drawing attention from lawmakers, the Federal Trade Commission and consumer advocacy groups: how companies are using AI to set prices and whether those practices may harm certain shoppers or even break the law.

Surveillance pricing, which is often conflated with the terms “dynamic pricing” or “algorithmic pricing,” is a broad term that includes something that’s been happening for decades: prices set automatically based on supply and demand (say, gasoline prices). For years, shoppers also heard about “surge pricing,” such as the cost of an Uber ride increasingly dramatically during spikes in activity or around big events.

But as AI has gone mainstream and more companies have access to an array of information collected about their customers — whether it’s through apps, loyalty programs or just website tracking — it’s increasingly likely that those companies can set different prices for different shoppers based on that information.

It may not always be personal: In June, a lawsuit was filed in California claiming gas stations were inflating the price of fuel illegally due to AI software used by thousands of gas stations. But lawmakers in states are concerned about more personalized dynamic pricing. This summer, New Jersey passed a law set to go into effect in 2027 banning the use of personal data to set prices; the law primarily targets grocery stores.

Walmart’s new digital shelf labels, like these seen in Albany, New York, can update prices automatically. Consumers are worried that means prices can change unexpectedly based on who’s shopping.Larry Rulison/Albany Times Union/Getty Images

Last year, shoppers in New York began seeing warnings on product pages due to new laws mandating that customers let people know when shopping prices were set using personal data in an algorithm. 

According to the Electronic Privacy Information Center, for instance, personal data and market data are being used by retailers to determine the highest price a customer is willing to pay, leading to higher prices.

In a report released in August, the Consumer Federation of America called out retailers, hotel booking sites and airlines for engaging in practices like raising prices based on things like how much AI determined they’d be willing to pay, their income or their proximity to a store.

What the FTC is doing

The Federal Trade Commission said in August that it’s looking for public comment on policy around surveillance pricing, but it has implied that it may not be able to do much to stop companies by enforcing rules; its approach appears to be geared toward helping consumers be more aware of potential surveillance pricing and requesting that those engaging in this kind of pricing be transparent about it.

That’s not enough, according to consumer advocates like the CFA, which responded to the FTC’s proposal with a letter demanding it do more than promote transparency.

“Not even the most detailed disclosure of what information they’re using to hike your prices will change the fact that those prices are still going up,” said Emily Peterson-Cassin, director of competition and market fairness at the CFA, told CNET in an email. The CFA argues in its letter that surveillance prices can be based on proxies for protected characteristics like race or age and are likely to disproportionately hurt low-income and working families who can’t easily comparison shop.

“To put it bluntly, the more vulnerable you are, the harder you stand to get hit,” Peterson-Cassin said. “If companies know you must have, for example, baby formula, they are more likely to charge you a higher price for it. “

title: Samsung Suddenly Raises Prices by $100 on Most Galaxy S26 Phones
snippet: An S26 Ultra with 1TB of storage now lists for $2,000.
fullText:
Call it what you want: RAMageddon, chipflation, the AI tax. Amid a global memory shortage that’s compelling companies to hike prices on phones, PCs, laptops and gaming consoles, our devices keep getting more expensive. 

On Thursday, Samsung quietly raised prices on the Galaxy S26, S26 Plus and S26 Ultra by $100, without issuing an official company statement. The Galaxy S26 FE didn’t go up in price, and Samsung’s newest foldables — Galaxy Z Fold 8, Z Fold 8 Ultra and Z Flip 8 — were also spared the carnage.

For the larger 512GB models, the Galaxy S26 now lists at $1,200, the S26 Plus at $1,400, and the S26 Ultra at $1,600. The S26 Ultra with 1TB storage went up $200 and is now $2,000. All the company’s smartphone prices are listed here.

		

			

A Samsung representative did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The RAM shortage is a result of the massive buildout of AI data center infrastructure, which requires huge amounts of memory, especially high-bandwidth memory, or HBM. Apple and Google also raised prices by about $100 on their most recent phones.

Read more: Why RAMageddon Might Force Apps and Operating Systems’ Performance to Suck Less

Is there relief in sight?

In its Q2 earnings call in July, Samsung said it expects the memory shortage to be worse next year and persist through 2028.

At Amazon, the S26 Ultra is still available at lower prices. It’s not yet known whether any of the Galaxy S26 phones will be available during October Prime Day, Oct. 6 and 7, but check out CNET’s constantly updated coverage of all the deals.

Cellphone carriers such as Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T could mitigate some sticker shock with installment plans, trade-in credits and refurbished devices. But that won’t reverse higher prices nor solve the memory shortage problem, GlobalData senior analyst Amanda Mitchell said in a new analysis.

“Lasting relief depends on additional production capacity, but manufacturers’ expansion plans will take years to reach the market, and much of the new investment is intended to serve AI demand rather than consumer devices,” Mitchell said. “With meaningful new capacity years away, price pressure is likely to persist.”

title: Here’s how much Google is testing paying web publishers for AI Overview usage
snippet: A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies. more…
fullText:
A new report details how Google is testing paying web publishers for content used in its AI Overviews, including how much they’re making and how much that varies.

Google’s AI Overviews have drastically reshaped the web, and it’s hard to argue that it hasn’t harmed publishers across the web. Traffic is down almost universally, though Google insists AI isn’t to blame. Still, Google’s AI Overviews and other AI responses rely on publishers around the web to continue operating, something that’s increasingly difficult to do.

Following a report earlier this month, The Information is now offering a few more details on Google’s test to directly pay web publishers when their content is used in AI Overviews. 

The company is apparently paying around 100 digital publishers including “small to midsize blogs and websites.” Revenue seems to vary wildly, though. For some, it amounts to “less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue.” Some “smaller sites” have apparently earned less than $1,000 over several months, where another publisher that “joined a few months ago” has already made around $50,000-60,000 so far, “which doesn’t represent that much of its business.” Yet, another publisher said that a “bigger slice” was covered with Google’s payments earning “more than $1 million a year.”

	

The test, as previously reported, gives publishers insights into how often AI Overviews leverage their content. What’s not yet clear is how Google determines how much a publisher is paid, with some finding that “less widely covered” topics that “draw strong user interest” currently earn more, with examples including anime and gaming. 

It’s still unclear if Google plans to expand this program, but The Information reiterates that Google “needs these web publishers to stay active” for its models and answers to stay current and accurate.

title: Google announces Gemini 4 Argon as its new frontier model
snippet: Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash. more…
fullText:
Gemini 4 Argon is Google’s “next era of frontier intelligence” and built for “deep reasoning across complex, long-horizon workflows.” It follows the cancellation of Gemini 3.5 Pro and focus on 3.8 Flash.

With this new model (which has a new naming scheme), Google wants to offer “frontier-level capabilities” across coding, knowledge work, cybersecurity defense, and creative writing.

Gemini 4 Argon’s output token limit is 1M tokens (up from 64K) to allow for longer and more complex use cases. This is paired with expanded coding, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities.

When the model has the headroom to think deeply and generate hundreds of thousands of tokens in a single trajectory, it adds a new level of depth in reasoning to solve tough problems in one go.

In terms of benchmarks, Google touts a DeepSWE v1.1 score of 77.9%. Claude Opus 5.5 comes in at 74.2% followed by GPT-6 Astra’s 74.1%.

	

Google trained Gemini 4 Argon to be “highly capable at cybersecurity defense” with leaps over 3.8 Flash Cyber. The model will be made available “without cyber guardrails” to trusted defenders and internal Google teams so that they can “leverage its full frontier-level cybersecurity defense capabilities.”

“On CWE-bench v1, which evaluates the model’s ability to remediate security vulnerabilities, Argon ties for first place with a top score of 68%”

Outside of coding, Gemini 4 Argon also has “leading performance across other domain specific evaluations,” such as Vals Finance Agent v2 (multi-step financial research) and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark (legal research and drafting).

“On AutomationBench, Zapier’s benchmark measuring end-to-end execution across core business functions, Argon ranks #1 with a score of 51.3%.”

“…on LVBench, which measures long video understanding, Argon is state of the art with a score of 91.7%.”

Gemini 4 Argon is “rolling out soon,” starting with Google AI Ultra subscribers and paid API customers. 

“Argon will launch at an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.”

“After the introductory period expires, the price of $4 per 1M input tokens and $20 per 1M output tokens will apply.”

So far, it has been made available to trusted testers and cyber defenders (via Fairwind Program). Before the broader release, Google is focusing on:

Defending against misuse from cyber or chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) attacks: Google has improved “techniques to monitor the model’s internal activations to spot misuse.”

Defending against prompt injection attacks: Google’s “most resilient model yet against indirect prompt injections” with “leading in prompt injection robustness on the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark.”

Hardening systems: “we are hardening our sandboxed environments by isolating and sealing them before high-risk training or evaluations begin.”

Monitoring for misalignment: Google is “deploying misalignment mitigations that monitor Argon’s chain-of-thought and actions and stop execution when necessary.”

“We used a similar system to monitor our training runs and send alerts to a dedicated incident response team, taking careful precautions against feeding the findings back into training so as to not risk shaping Argon’s reasoning to evade our monitoring.”

Inside Google, Gemini 4 Argon is already powering internal workflows with “thousands of Googlers highlighting the model’s strengths in specialized coding tasks, conducting deeper research, and writing quality.” The company shared some examples today:

Memory efficiency: A team of Argon agents analyzed fleet-wide profiling telemetry to autonomously identify and apply memory optimizations across Google’s data centers, freeing up over 300 TiB of memory once rolled out, with an estimated 500 TiB to 1 PiB in total savings.

Large Scale Codebase Migrations and Optimizations: Argon agents are working on migrating C/C++ codebases to Rust across Google—scaling from tens of thousands of lines in core libraries like re2, libgav1 up to 800K+ lines for the Fuchsia OS Zircon kernel. Given the criticality of many of these systems, such large-scale rewrites are undergoing rigorous automated and manual auditing, emulation testing, and review before rolling out to production.

For libgav1, Google’s open source software for decoding video, Argon agents took an existing Rust port and replaced 32K lines of SIMD code by running many rounds of profile-guided experiments, studying the compiler’s output, producing safe Rust so the compiler would vectorize it automatically. The end result is a memory-safe video decoder that runs 2.7x faster than the Rust port, with identical video output, bringing it closer to the optimized C++.

Capcom’s Pragmata might be all about the horrors of AI, but in practice the studio doesn’t seem so down on the tech. During the Capcom Open Conference RE: 2026 programmer Satoshi Ishida gave a presentation with the mouthful of a title: “The Outlook and Future of the REX Project, Further Evolving the RE Engine for the Next Generation.” During the talk he laid out the challenges facing studios producing games at the scale of Resident Evil, which can make even simple tasks extremely time consuming. The solution Ishida said is “successfully integrating AI technology into development workflows.”

Capcom has said previously that it will not use AI-generated assets in its games, and instead would focus on using the tech to make development more efficient. Ishida’s comments seem to lineup, though definitely seem to leave the door open to more extensive use. He laid out a plan to turn RE Engine slowly, and incrementally, into an “AI-generation game engine” building towards a “a future where we create games together with AI,” according to IGN’s translation.

title: This $100 Power Washer Whupped My More Expensive Model. I Was as Shocked as Anyone
snippet: Electric power washers range in price from $100 to $400. I tested one at each end of the price spectrum to see how they compare.
fullText:
Electric pressure washers promise a way to clean patios, driveways, cars and siding without the noise, fuel or maintenance associated with gas-powered machines. Because of their convenience, it’s no surprise that these battery and corded electric models dominate our testing. But with prices ranging from entry-level to premium, it’s fair to ask how much performance you get for your money, especially at the higher end of that spectrum.

To find out, I compared the LawnMaster LT506-2000A pressure washer, which retails for $100 to $120 depending on PSI, with my AR Blue Clean 383SS. This specific 383SS model doesn’t appear to be available for sale anymore. I bought it for about $250 a few years ago, and while the specific 383SS model doesn’t appear to be available, similar models go for $300 to $400.

The LawnMaster is positioned as a budget-friendly machine, while the AR Blue Clean has a longer track record and a more established feature set. I tested both washers on the same surfaces, using the same water source and comparable spray settings.

			

More from CNET

The LawnMaster performed extremely well, even when considering the AR washer’s age, and especially given the price difference. For a budget model, the LawnMaster is an impressive machine and will more than suffice for most homeowners. 

How does the hardware compare? 

The LawnMaster LT506-2000A is rated for up to 2,300 pounds per square inch and 1.4 gallons per minute. Its owner’s manual lists a rated pressure of 1,650 PSI and a 13-amp, 120-volt motor. The machine weighs approximately 22.6 pounds.

The AR Blue Clean 383SS produces up to 1,900 PSI and 1.3 GPM and also uses a 13-amp motor. It weighs approximately 32 pounds and includes a 30-foot high-pressure hose, a 35-foot power cord, a hose reel and an integrated 28-ounce detergent tank.

Those numbers give the LawnMaster an advantage in maximum pressure, although maximum PSI is only one element of a pressure washer’s performance. Nozzle design, pump consistency, water flow and how easily the machine can be positioned all affect how well it removes dirt.

Both models are intended for cold-water use and suit typical household cleaning tasks rather than heavy-duty commercial work. Neither should be treated like a professional gas-powered pressure washer, particularly for removing deeply embedded grime across large areas. While gas-powered pressure washers could be expected to handle power-intensive tasks like stripping paint, or could supply pressure across a wide enough zone to clean large driveways or even small parking lots, smaller models like the ones I tested here are more suitable to household tasks like washing cars, patio furniture, grills and small decks.  

Design, assembly and accessories

The LawnMaster LT506-2000A power washer comes with several handy accessories.Alan Bradley/CNET

The LawnMaster arrives with an adjustable spray gun, high-pressure hose, turbo lance, foam bottle, cleaning brush and wheel-hub brush. Its 20-foot hose and 35-foot power cord provide reasonable reach for cleaning a vehicle or small patio, although the hose is shorter than the one supplied with the AR Blue Clean.

The included brushes could make the LawnMaster especially appealing to people who plan to clean cars, wheels and garden equipment. They also reduce the need to buy extra accessories right away. The foam bottle is useful for applying detergent, though you shouldn’t expect the same thick foam produced by a dedicated foam cannon.

The AR Blue Clean takes a more conventional approach. It includes a pro-style spray gun, quick-connect nozzle tips, a rotary or turbo nozzle, a detergent tank and onboard storage. Its hose reel makes setup and storage less awkward and is one of its most useful design features. The trade-off is weight: At roughly 32 pounds, the 383SS is noticeably heavier than the LawnMaster at just over 22 pounds.

In practice, the LawnMaster is easier to lift and carry, while the AR Blue Clean feels more substantial when being pulled across a driveway. Both models include a Total Stop-style system that shuts off the motor when you release the trigger, reducing unnecessary pump operation.

In terms of assembly, it’s been a while, but I remember the Blue Clean being fairly fiddly, and every time I reconnect the hoses and nozzle, I inevitably spend more time than I’d like tightening and troubleshooting leaks (though, again, this is a pressure washer that’s a little over 3 years old). 

The LawnMaster, on the other hand, was a breeze to assemble. Aside from a handful of screws, most components snap together easily, and the instructions were simple and clear. I had the unit unboxed, assembled and connected in less than 15 minutes. 

The fully assembled LawnMaster LT506-2000A ready for testing.Alan Bradley/CNET

Three washing tests

For all the tests I conducted, I used the default 25-degree nozzle tip on the AR Blue Clean. The LawnMaster comes with an adjustable nozzle, so you can easily change the spray width (and pressure) on the fly. 

I measured the Blue Clean’s width by spraying a section of dirty pavement, then adjusted the LawnMaster nozzle to match it at the same distance, mimicking a 25-degree nozzle. I did single passes at medium speed with both to give a fair impression; naturally, a secondary pass or a longer, lingering sweep would yield better results from both models.

Test 1: Vehicle cleaning

For the first test, I used both machines to wash the side of my black 2017 Chevy Bolt. I first applied a mud slurry to the side panels and wheels, then cleaned the front panel and wheel with the AR Blue Clean and the rear with the LawnMaster.

For testing, my Chevy Bolt had to get a little dirty.Alan Bradley/CNET

AR Blue Clean result: The AR did a decent job on an initial pass, but left significant dirt and streaking in its wake. Dirt was still visible on the sidewalls of the tires and on several areas of the door panel.

This the result of a single spray-down with the AR Blue Clean 383SS on my car.Alan Bradley/CNET

LawnMaster result: The LawnMaster yielded better results, particularly on the rear tire, though it did also leave a fair amount of smudging and streaking after a single pass.

The LawnMaster left a few spots of mud, but it generally did a better job of washing my car.Alan Bradley/CNET

The main difference was that the LawnMaster didn’t leave full patches of dirt in its wake, while the AR did. The LawnMaster appeared more comprehensive and provided slightly better control and coverage.

Test 2: Concrete patio

Next, I tested both machines on a similarly dirty section of my back patio, which is finished, sealed concrete. This surface was heavily stained and had large patches of algae. I first sketched out two rectangles on the surface, then used the AR Blue Clean on the left and the LawnMaster on the right.

To compare the two power washers, I marked off two big areas of my patio.Alan Bradley/CNET

AR Blue Clean result: The AR did a decent job cleaning up the general patina and staining, but it did little to remove the stubborn algae, much of which remained after a single pass.

This is how my concrete patio looked after I washed it with the AR Blue Clean 383SS power washer.Alan Bradley/CNET

LawnMaster result: The LawnMaster did a much better job, removing not only the staining and patina but also blasting away the vast majority of visible algae in one pass.

This is how my concrete patio looked after I washed it with the LawnMaster LT506-2000A power washer.Alan Bradley/CNET

This test clearly showed how the LawnMaster’s higher maximum pressure translated into faster cleaning. It did a much better job cleaning the concrete in a single pass; while I removed most of the remaining algae with the AR Blue Clean in subsequent passes, the LawnMaster handled it in one quick run.

A side-by-side view of the two sections of concrete patio post-wash, with the AR Blue Clean section on the left and the LawnMaster section on the right.Alan Bradley/CNET

Test 3: House siding

Finally, I sloshed more of the mud slurry onto the gray siding of my house and, following the pattern from the first two tests, ran the AR Blue Clean on the left and the LawnMaster on the right.

The two sections of muddy siding, prewash.Alan Bradley/CNET

LawnMaster result: The LawnMaster easily blasted away the mud from both the siding and the concrete pad beneath it, leaving them cleaner than the surrounding surfaces.

The LawnMaster power washer made quick work of muddy house siding.Alan Bradley/CNET

AR Blue Clean result: The Blue Clean also did an excellent job on the siding, easily and fully cleaning both the siding and the concrete below it in one pass.

The AR Blue Clean also did an excellent job of cleaning up muddy house siding.Alan Bradley/CNET

This is the test where the two were closest in performance, likely because the slurry was more diluted or didn’t cling to the side of the house as much. For an application like this, the AR Blue Clean was perfectly suitable, though the LawnMaster looks significantly more impressive given their relative prices.

Which one should you buy?

The LawnMaster LT506-2000A is an attractive combination of low weight, high pressure and varied accessories. Given the LawnMaster’s portability and maximum cleaning power, and the fact that it comes in at $150 less than I paid for the AR Blue Clean, it’s easily the better value.

One consideration for any piece of equipment from an upstart budget brand is longevity, which is more difficult to test. For $100, though, it might be worth the risk, especially if you plan to use it only sparingly.

Based solely on my testing, the LawnMaster matched or significantly exceeded the AR Blue Clean in overall cleaning performance. Given its price and the excellent job it did in all three tests, it not only easily surpassed my (admittedly aging) Blue Clean, but it’s an easy recommendation overall for a value-priced, electric pressure washer.

snippet: Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad, is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg. fullText:
Apple’s long-awaited smart home hub, which we’ve been referring to as the HomePad, is set to launch on October 13, according to Bloomberg.

The device is said to feature a 6-inch display and a design inspired by the iMac G4, and will launch alongside a HomePod mini update with new colors and a new Apple TV 4K with Siri AI support …

A previous report from the same source had said only that it was expected to launch “as soon as October,” but the latest report specifies October 13th.

Apple Inc. plans to make its long-delayed push into the smart-home market on Oct. 13, marking a critical product expansion for the company under new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus.

The iMac G4 was one of the company’s most iconic designs, with a hemispherical base and a free-floating screen that could be rotated, raised, lowered, and tilted to position it anywhere you wanted. I said a year ago that I very much hoped Apple would bring back this beautiful design for the upcoming product.

It’s previously been reported that the device will come in two versions: the tabletop one referenced here, and a second version intended to be mounted on a wall.

	

The upcoming device is expected to include a speaker to enable it to act as a HomePod as well as a smart home control panel. It’s expected to have a new operating system combining elements of iOS, tvOS, and watchOS – and to center around Siri AI.

Daring Fireball separately suggested that iPhone Duo review models would be handed over to tech writers on October 13 or 14, and that as Apple likes to do this in-person for high-profile products it would make sense to combine this with an event for the new products.

Today’s report says that the device is codenamed J490. Do you expect to buy one? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Pages, Keynote, Numbers, and Pixelmator Pro just got new features
snippet: Today alongside a big update to Final Cut Camera, Apple announced that it’s rolling out updated versions of Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, and Freeform. Here’s what’s new. more…
fullText:
Today alongside a big update to Final Cut Camera, Apple announced that it’s rolling out updated versions of Pages, Keynote, Numbers, Pixelmator Pro, and Freeform. Here’s what’s new.

Apple rolling out updates to ‘Creator Studio’ apps, but non-subscribers get new features too

Apple has announced new features coming to its popular iWork suite today—Pages, Keynote, and Numbers—alongside improvements for Pixelmator Pro and Freeform.

Some additions are exclusive to Apple Creator Studio, but select features will be available for all users. Here’s everything new, per Apple Newsroom:

Pages, Keynote, Numbers

Apple says that today’s updates bring support for asking Siri questions about Pages, Keynote, or Numbers and get answers. It’s unclear if Siri AI is required or not, but that’s likely. The updates also enable “the ability to request access to a shared presentation, document, or spreadsheet.” This makes collaboration easier, as the file owner no longer needs to initiate file sharing.

Pages for Mac has a new Screen View, which “optimizes content for reading and focused writing.” And Numbers gets “new trigonometry, statistics, and logic functions for solving complex problems in a spreadsheet.”

Additionally, for Apple Creator Studio subscribers there are new templates and themes available across all three iWork apps. And in Keynote, intelligent slide generation will automatically make images that are tailored to a given presentation.

Pixelmator Pro

Pixelmator Pro on iPad adds Select and Mask tools that were previously Mac-exclusive. And both Mac and iPad apps gain two template collections for sports and action-centric projects, plus new templates for “launching a new creative idea, business, or product.”

	

Additionally, there’s a new Podcasts category for creating cover artwork that’s sized to fit well on major podcast platforms.

Freeform

Freeform gains several highly requested features. Boards now automatically adapt to Dark Mode, and folders let users organize boards into collections and invite others to collaborate. Writing Tools with Apple Intelligence can rewrite, proofread, and summarize handwritten notes; users can also request access to collaborate on shared files, or automate adding content using Shortcuts. Freeform becomes even more powerful in visionOS 27, letting users pull multiple items from a board — including images, videos, sticky notes, shapes, and 3D models — into their space, and view 3D models together as a group.

What new features in today’s app updates stand out most to you? Let us know in the comments.

title: Laytr’s new app lets you save anything you find online, not just articles to read
snippet: Laytr lets you save articles, recipes, screenshots, videos, PDFs, and more for later, while keeping your archive private and synced across your Apple devices.
fullText:
After Mozilla’s read-it-later app Pocket shut down in August, a number of alternatives popped up to take its place. But one newcomer, Laytr, is taking things further than offering a way to save things to read. The app lets you save anything on the web for later consumption, whether that’s an article, recipe, screenshot, video, PDF, bookmark, or tab.

The app also automatically sorts those different file types and lets you organize them into collections it calls “cases.” It can also remind you about a saved item on a date you choose, which could help you remember local events or places you want to visit on certain days, for instance. (Or perhaps as a way to force you to get through your reading list!)

Image Credits:Laytr

What’s interesting about how the app works is that everything you save becomes a private archive that’s only accessible on your own device. That means you don’t have to create an account to use Laytr, and the developer can’t see anything you’ve saved either. Still, you can access your content across multiple Apple devices, including iPhone, iPad, and Mac, because the content syncs over iCloud.

The idea for Laytr comes from Ontario-area indie developer Mostafa Talaat, and is published under his company’s name, Waitery Inc. Talaat told TechCrunch he was inspired to build his own read-it-later app after hearing about Pocket’s shutdown. Creating an app without a server was a privacy choice on his part.

“What you save says a lot about you, and I didn’t want to be holding it. Everything stays on your device and in your own iCloud,” Talaat explained. “When you save something, Laytr asks when you want it back and reminds you on that day. It also imports your old Pocket export, so nobody has to start over,” he added.

Because the app is privacy-focused, there are things it won’t do, including personalizing a feed or using AI to summarize or automatically tag items. 

Image Credits:Laytr

The app is free to try, but limits you to 30 saved items. For full access, the app’s Premium tier costs either $1.99 a month, $14.99 a year, or a one-time $39.99 for a lifetime plan. (The lifetime offering is on sale for $24.99 until the end of December.) Talaat said the app will focus on adding more languages over time.

If your subscription lapses, you also won’t lose your saves — you just won’t be able to add more until you rejoin a plan or get your archive back under the 30-item limit for free plans. You can also leave Laytr at any time, as the entire archive can be exported as a ZIP file, with readable Markdown and HTML for every item, note, tag, date, and collection (aka “case”).

title: OpenAI safety employee resigns, claiming the company’s ‘culture is broken’
snippet: By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.
fullText:
By his own admission, David Robinson is “something of a cliché”: an employee at a leading AI company who issues a dire warning while resigning from their job.

In an essay published in The Atlantic, Robinson said he led the writing of safety reports that accompanied OpenAI’s major product launches. He also said that with three-and-a-half years at OpenAI, he is “among the longest-tenured employees at the company.” Now he’s quitting, because in his view, the company’s “culture is broken.”

In some ways, Robinson’s comments echo those of Jacob Coxon, who worked as a researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic before quitting and declaring that these companies are “gambling with our lives.” Coxon’s comments led to a broader debate about AI safety, with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei unveiling a plan for more cautious AI development; AI executives met with President Donald Trump this week and signed what appeared to be hastily written, non-binding  pledge to implement more safety controls.

But in Robinson’s view, the debate needs to go beyond “specific rules or new laws,” addressing the overall culture at these companies. And while much of the reporting around OpenAI has focused on how the company’s CEO Sam Altman lost the trust of former colleagues, Robinson’s essay suggests that OpenAI’s culture issues are the same as those of Silicon Valley at large.

“OpenAI has thrived by trial and error (which it calls ‘iterative deployment’), looking for problems and improving its guardrails in response,” he wrote. “But this approach, by its very nature, guarantees periodic failures — and the scale of those failures is growing as systems get more capable.”

Pointing to the recent breach of Hugging Face systems by OpenAI agents, as well as continuing revelations of OpenAI discovering more rogue agents, Robinson argued, “An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to.”

Given the increased risk, Robinson argued that frontier AI companies need to start operating “like nuclear-power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.” 

But Robinson said that in his time at OpenAI, he “never encountered a colleague who had experience making airplanes fly safely or nuclear reactors run without melting down, or helping the financial system grow without collapsing.”

In response to Robinson’s essay, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company continues to improve its safety measures.

“We’re making sure our models don’t become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down,” Pusateri said in a statement. “We’re making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process.”

Beyond calling for changes in OpenAI’s culture, Robinson also said it’s time to ask bigger questions about alignment — something that he admitted could sound “touchy-feely,” but he said it’s critical as companies’ current “measures of how well” AI systems “match human values are coarse.”

“The smarter the industry lets models grow while these problems remain unsolved, the more dangerous our situation becomes,” he said.

Robinson’s departure was first reported by Business Insider. In his essay, he also acknowledged that he’s following an apparently a common step in the AI whistleblower playbook: He’s hired a PR firm. But he insisted, “The decision to speak out is mine alone.” 

“Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them,” Robinson said. “That’s why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right.”

title: Pixel Watch 4 & 5’s handy USB-C travel charger is currently on sale
snippet: Launched earlier this year, that useful little USB-C charger dongle for Google’s Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches is currently discounted. more…
fullText:
Launched earlier this year, that useful little USB-C charger dongle for Google’s Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches is currently discounted.

Google’s latest take on smartwatch charging debuted on last year’s Pixel Watch 4 series, with two pins popping out of the smartwatch to connect with a magnetic dock. Google’s official charging cable works well enough, but it’s just another thing to plug in when you’re traveling. 

Wasserstein, a long-time Made for Google accessory partner, launched a handy alternative earlier this year. A simple charger that attaches to the end of any USB-C cable give you the option to cut down on some bulk while still being able to easily top off your smartwatch on the go. Its price was in flux for quite a while, but eventually settled at $30.

Right now, though, it’s discounted to $25. Not a huge discount, but it certainly makes the handy charger an easier buy if you have any travel coming up through the end of the year.

	

Wasserstein USB-C charger for Pixel Watch 4 & 5 at Amazon

As a reminder, this works with all Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 smartwatches, regardless of if you’re using the 41mm or 45mm sizes. You’ll want to plug into at least 7.5W of power, but you’re likely getting that from whatever charger you’re using with your smartphone anyway. Just keep in mind that Pixel Watch 3 and prior cannot use this charger.

title: YouTube says Shorts recommendations won’t surface unoriginal content
snippet: YouTube says it wants to ‘focus on originality’ in a push to surface better Shorts recommendations for users. more…
fullText:
YouTube says it wants to ‘focus on originality’ in a push to surface better Shorts recommendations for users.

Shorts is built on quick and attention-grabbing content, which makes cutting portions of long-form videos one of the easiest ways to put out quick videos with high view potential. Of course, that also means channels can just as easily take content from other established creators and stamp out short-form videos from it.

YouTube says it’s adjusted its Shorts recommendations so users will see less unoriginal content. Users who upload content that blatantly steals video from another channel will not get the same reach as they did before the change, according to what YouTube laid out in its release.

To improve the Shorts experience for everyone, we’re updating our recommendation systems to further prioritize original content and reduce the reach of content re-uploaded from other creators without adding anything of your own.

There’s a small amount of room for interpretation. YouTube’s language seems to imply that Shorts that contain no changes form another’s work would be affected, but no clear line in the sand has been drawn out.

	

Remember, YouTube announced it was testing a new feature that would let users reimagine other channels’ videos using AI, which was released in March. Whether those videos will still be surfaced in the recommendations system is unclear.

The change should mean users will see a focus on original content, and creators that upload original Shorts will likely be rewarded. YouTube hasn’t detailed a rollout date for this change, but it sounds like it may be live already.

title: Slovenia’s .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump’s ‘super intelligence’ order
snippet: The .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump's super intelligence executive order.
fullText:
In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name — associated with the country Anguilla — spiked and brought in millions for the island territory. 

Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump.

Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30, the day after President Trump signed the executive order, and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours. 

We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said. 

But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30 and about 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India. 

Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later. 

Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.”

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”  

There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.” 

Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.” 

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. For Slovenia, .si is a nice bonus.”

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Clay’s Kareem Amin on the rise of the GTM engineer
snippet: Clay Co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin joins the AI Stage to discuss the rise of GTM engineer at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. Register for your ticket and get a second pass at 50% off.
fullText:
Two years ago, most companies didn’t have a GTM engineer. Now the role is showing up across tech, with practitioners using AI and automation to build revenue systems that once required multiple people, tools, and manual processes.

What changed — and what does it mean for the way companies find customers and grow?

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Clay co-founder and CEO Kareem Amin will take the AI Stage for “The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category.” He’ll trace how AI has changed the traditional go-to-market stack and helped create a new discipline in its place, giving attendees a look at what AI-native GTM looks like in practice and how it’s changing company growth.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

AI is giving go-to-market teams new ways to research prospects, work with data, personalize outreach, and automate workflows that once moved between separate tools and teams. As those capabilities converge, companies are rethinking not only their GTM technology, but also who builds and manages the systems behind growth.

If you’re building a company or rethinking how your team approaches sales, marketing, and growth, this is a new role worth understanding. Secure your Disrupt pass and see where GTM engineering fits into the next generation of go-to-market. Get a second pass at a 50% discount, and more savings for groups of four or more.

What does a GTM engineer actually do?

Traditional go-to-market work can involve hours of researching accounts, cleaning data, qualifying leads, preparing outreach, and moving information between systems. GTM engineering uses AI, data, and automation to turn more of that work into repeatable systems.

Clay coined the role in 2023. Its own GTM engineering guide describes GTM engineers as practitioners who build automated revenue workflows rather than executing individual GTM tasks by hand. The company says roughly 100 GTM engineering job listings are now appearing each month, including roles at companies such as Cursor, Lovable, and Webflow.

For founders and GTM leaders deciding where to put their next dollar or whether to make their next hire, this session offers another way to think about growth. Do you add more people to execute the existing process, or build systems that let the people you already have execute differently?

At Disrupt, Amin will put the shift into context and explore what AI-native GTM looks like in practice. Get your ticket to Disrupt to understand a role that barely existed a few years ago but could change how your next sales, marketing, or growth team operates.

Clay puts AI to work across the GTM stack

Clay started in Brooklyn in 2017 with one goal: Give more people access to the power of programming. Its original spreadsheet let users connect information and automate work without writing code. When salespeople, growth teams, and agencies began using it to find and reach customers, Clay followed them into go-to-market.

Today, the company provides infrastructure for GTM teams to access data, run agentic workflows, and launch campaigns. Its OpenAI-powered agent, Claygent, automates research and outreach for sales, marketing, and recruiting teams.

That evolution has been accompanied by rapid growth. TechCrunch reported in February that the company had tripled annual recurring revenue to $100 million in a year and announced an employee tender offer at a $5 billion valuation. Clay has continued growing since then, announcing a $115 million Series D in September at a $7.1 billion valuation.

Clay is also investing directly in the job category at the center of Amin’s Disrupt session, announcing a $1 million scholarship fund in September to train GTM engineers.

For companies trying to determine where AI can make a meaningful difference in revenue operations, add Amin’s session to your Disrupt agenda and see how one company is putting that model into practice.

From product leader to a new GTM approach

Kareem Amin co-founded Clay in 2017 and serves as its co-founder and CEO. Before Clay, he was VP of product at The Wall Street Journal and co-founded collaboration startup Frame, which Sailthru acquired in 2012.

Amin started Clay around the idea of putting programming capabilities into more people’s hands. AI eventually gave that idea a new application: enabling GTM teams to build systems that automate research, data enrichment, and outreach without relying on traditional engineering resources for every workflow.

Want to understand what a GTM engineer could mean for your own growth strategy? Secure your Disrupt pass and hear directly from one of the founders helping define the category.

See what AI-native GTM looks like in practice at Disrupt

GTM engineering may be a new job category, but the problem it addresses isn’t: How do you find and reach the right customers without simply adding more people and more tools? At Disrupt, you can see how AI is changing that equation — and meet the people building what comes next.

“The GTM Engineer: How AI Created Tech’s Next Big Job Category” is one of 200+ sessions across six industry stages, roundtables, and breakouts at Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers and 300+ exhibiting startups.

In addition, matchmaking, dealmaking, and networking give attendees opportunities to meet potential customers, investors, partners, and other founders confronting many of the same growth challenges.

title: iOS 27 breaks 15 years of muscle memory on iPhone and iPad
snippet: Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order. Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad. iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it. more…
fullText:
Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how users open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Siri AI takes over the swipe gesture for a lot of the iPhone and iPad top edge

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

Apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the new Siri experience.

The last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Notifications now live in the top left corner

Now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

	

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri. 

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s new Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the new behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

What do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

title: This fake Mac Zoom installer has a sneaky way to bypass Gatekeeper
snippet: Cybersecurity company Jamf has discovered a fake Mac installer for the videoconferencing app Zoom that uses a sneaky way to bypass Apple’s Gatekeeper protection against malware. The malware does actually install Zoom, but also an infostealer that captures data and sends it to the attacker’s server … more…
fullText:
Cybersecurity company Jamf has discovered a fake Mac installer for the videoconferencing app Zoom that uses a sneaky way to bypass Apple’s Gatekeeper protection against malware.

The malware does actually install Zoom, but also an infostealer that captures data and sends it to the attacker’s server …

Normally, when you try to install a Mac app that Apple hasn’t notarized, macOS will refuse to open it. There is a workaround to allow you to do so, but it’s somewhat fiddly, and attackers have to find some way to persuade users to do it.

The criminals behind the malware Jamf has dubbed CloudSyncD have found a clever way to make this seem more normal to users. The app installer dropper includes a background image with instructions, as shown above.

CloudSyncD arrives as a disk image that mounts as a volume named Zoom, laid out to look like any ordinary Mac installer: an application icon on the left, an alias to Applications on the right. The difference is the background image, which carries a numbered Setup list telling the victim to open System Settings, go to Privacy & Security, scroll to the Security section, click Open Anyway, and enter their administrator password. Those are instructions to bypass Gatekeeper.

You kind of have to admire the creativity of this.

Once the malware is installed, it can record user-entered data and send it to the attackers as frequently as every eight seconds.

As always, you should only ever install Mac apps from the official Mac App Store or the websites of developers you trust.

title: Samsung rolling out Android 17, One UI 9 for more Galaxy S26 users – here’s everything new
snippet: After a lengthy delay, Samsung is finally rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update for Galaxy S26 users in the US more broadly. more…
fullText:
After a lengthy delay, Samsung is finally rolling out its Android 17-based One UI 9 update for Galaxy S26 users in the US more broadly.

Samsung announced its One UI 9 rollout early this month, but updates didn’t start flowing. Last week the update finally started to trickle out in the US, but only for users on T-Mobile. 

Now, the floodgates are starting to crack. 

Galaxy S26 users on unlocked devices in the US are now seeing One UI 9 land, Android 17 in tow, at least for those who were enrolled in the beta program. It’s still not a full rollout, but it’s another step towards the full debut. SammyGuru and others spotted the rollout which, for those in the beta, measures around 650MB, while Android Authority also cites some Samsung changelogs that detail everything new.

	

Samsung’s official changelog follows (edited for formatting):

One UI 9

Galaxy AI

Enhanced Now nudge

Now nudge provides helpful suggestions in more places throughout your Galaxy experience. In addition to the keyboard, suggestions will now appear in conversation notifications and in a floating button in the bottom right corner of the screen. There are also several new types of suggestions, like entering reservation details or addresses and saving places in Google Maps.

Focus on someone important

My FanCam lets you select a person in a video and follow them automatically while cropping out the rest of the video.

Interpreter keeps your conversation in front of you

In conversation mode, you can scroll through the whole conversation while you’re still talking.

See useful information during calls

See relevant events and other information related to your current call on the call screen.

Productivity and multitasking

More customizable quick panel

You can now rearrange and customize the controls in your quick panel even more than before. You can change the size of the brightness and volume sliders as well as the media player. You can also separate the sound mode button from the volume slider.

Privacy, security, and device protection

Warranty and care

The new Warranty and care menu in settings lets you check your warranty information and access diagnostic checks and useful information for keeping your Galaxy in top condition.

Lock down your phone quickly

It’s now easier to securely lock your phone in a hurry. Just press and hold the Volume down and Side buttons at the same time or tap the Power button in the quick panel. This prevents biometrics from being used the next time you unlock your phone.

Location access transparency

Stay on top of your location privacy. A blue indicator will appear at the top of the screen when an app accesses your location. Tap the indicator in the quick panel to see which app it is.

Stronger security and privacy protection

Alerts will appear in your Now brief to let you know about risks from malware, apps from unknown sources, unnecessary permissions, and other issues that may put your security and privacy at risk. Apps that have been identified as malicious or vulnerable will be blocked from opening until you make a decision about whether to remove them.

AI privacy alerts

Get help protecting your personal data. AI will monitor how apps use permissions and notify you about unnecessary access to your personal data.

Samsung Health

New look for Samsung Health

Samsung Health has been redesigned to make your health data easier to understand. Enjoy clearer visuals, improved charts, and a more engaging experience to help you reach your health goals.

Customize your Health home screen

Resize cards and organize them by category, like Activity, Sleep, Mindfulness, and Nutrition, so your top priorities are easy to access.

Log health data quickly

It’s now easier to add your health information right from the Samsung Health home screen. You can log your mood, meals, and more. You can even use the camera for faster input.

Advanced trend analysis

Track your progress with improved trend charts in Samsung Health. View data in hourly, daily, or weekly intervals, pinch to zoom in for a closer look, and overlay multiple charts to compare your performance across different periods.

Monitor changes in your sleep vitals

Samsung Health helps you notice meaningful changes in your sleep health data. Use Galaxy Watch or Ring measurements to better understand your daily health patterns.

Manage your heart health

Track key health metrics and lifestyle factors that affect your heart. A daily score based on your sleep, exercise, BMI, and blood pressure helps you better understand your current heart health trends.

Track your cardio load

See how your workouts and activity impact your heart so you’ll know when to push harder and when to rest. Your target cardio load range adjusts daily based on your recent activity and training focus.

Check your fitness index

Your Fitness Index is an overall score calculated using five key fitness metrics: body composition, cardio, strength, flexibility, and endurance. Set a goal and unlock personalized insights tailored to your results.

Keep your ears safe

The new Hearing tracker monitors sound levels detected by your Galaxy Watch and headphone audio levels to help you manage your exposure to loud sounds.

View your cycle and body rhythm

Get a more personalized view of your cycle and body rhythm with new cycle tracking options. You can view your cycle information in your calendar and better understand your health patterns.

Bixby

Activate Bixby with a gesture

Talk to Bixby just by raising your phone close to your mouth and speaking. No wake-up word needed.

Manage your conversations

Keep your chats organized. Search them, rename them, or pin your favorites. You can also delete all of your past conversations at once.

Bixby on the Home screen

Add a Bixby widget to type or talk to Bixby or jump directly to your conversation history.

Accessibility

Discover new Accessibility features

Check the What’s new menu in Accessibility settings to learn about and try the latest Accessibility features for your Galaxy.

Text spotlight for easier reading

Need a closer look? Tap any text on the screen to show it enlarged and highlighted in its own window. You can also customize the font size, colors, and other settings to match your preferences.

Physical keyboard shortcuts

Use shortcuts on your physical keyboard to access the Accessibility settings you need without touching the screen.

Mouse keys enhancements

New options are available when using your keyboard for mouse interactions including speed and acceleration control. You can also use the keyboard’s number pad to point and click.

Replace swipe with single tap

The Replace swipe with single tap option is now located in the Dexterity and interaction menu instead of the Assistant menu for easier access.

Select to speak

Get quick audio readouts without turning on full TalkBack. With the new Select to speak feature, you can select an item on your screen, like text or an image, and hear it read or described out loud.

Improved TalkBack updates

TalkBack updates can now be applied with a simple app update from the Play Store, helping you get the latest accessibility features and enhancements.

Even more improvements

New Lock screen clock

The default clock on your Lock screen has been redesigned with a cleaner and more modern look that adapts to match your wallpaper.

Samsung DeX enhancements

It’s easier to move an app window from one desktop to another using the menu at the top of the window. Desktop previews are now available at the top of the Recents screen, making it easier to switch with a single tap.

Notably, SamMobile also spotted that One UI 9 is now rolling out to the Galaxy Z Flip 7 FE.

snippet: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. This week, I'm wishing I could do Walmart potato drone delivery in Portland, watching Mike Tomlin explain his incredible Minecraft city, pondering if the Gears of War pizza cutter is awesome or terrible, exploring Craig Mod's walks, nodding along with MKBHD's video about YouTube's A/B video testing feature, hoping that more concerts ban phones, and celebrating soup season. fullText:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, it’s October already?, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)

Programming note: David is back next week! It’s been a blast writing Installer again, and thanks to everyone for reading and for your recommendations. For now, I also have for you Amazon’s new Kindles, OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, and more.

(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / zoned out to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)

The Drop

Amazon’s new Kindles. Amazon might have crushed it with the Kindle updates this year. The new base e-readers look like they’ll be a nice upgrade from previous generations, with flush front screens, an option for an aluminum back, and some nice new colors. The new Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions are compatible with a case with page turn buttons. And now there’s a “Kindle Click” remote to let you turn pages and adjust brightness. My years-old Paperwhite is still trucking along just fine, but if it suddenly broke, these would be really tempting options.

OpenAI’s Dots. OpenAI’s Muse-like AI agent is here, though the company is pitching it more as something to help you with work than an all-encompassing assistant for your personal life. (That’s probably coming later.) The Dots are also adorable, though I think I’d give the Muse mascots the edge in cuteness.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Eleven years after its initial launch, The Witcher 3 is getting yet another big update. This free update for existing owners adds a lot of features and tweaks, including visual improvements, changes to skills, a new accessibility section in settings, cross-platform mod support, and more. The game is also now on Switch 2. Might be time for me to finally dive in.

Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds. These $99 USB-C wired earbuds have noise cancellation and an in-line remote for adjusting volume with a built-in microphone for calls, and they come in three colors. As a huge fan of Apple’s wired EarPods, these could be a great option that’s a step above those in quality.

Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. Bandai Namco’s latest entry in its fighter-pilot franchise sounds like a thrilling experience with a campaign filled with optimism, and it’s become one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Seems like a soaring success.

Keurig’s Alta. The new Keurig coffee machine can make you a cup of joe with compostable pucks instead of the recyclable pods. Plus, it can also make espresso and looks super fancy. It’s not cheap at $499.99. But it’s tough to beat the convenience of a Keurig — I learned firsthand when my toddler was a newborn — so this could be a good option if you want to lead a Keurig life with more Earth-friendly pods.

HP’s OmniBook 5 14. This HP laptop is thin and light, has 8GB of RAM, comes in good colors, and starts at $699.99, making it extremely MacBook Neo-adjacent. If you want the Neo ethos paired with Windows, this might be a solid option.

Ikea’s Förlig lamp. This LED Ikea lamp lets you swap between 10 different colors, can be used from the floor or on a wall, and looks kind of like a lightsaber. Super fun.

Today I’m featuring Scott Stein, CNET’s editor at large. I’ve been a huge admirer of Stein’s work, especially his excellent coverage of wearables and VR, for years, and I had the great fortune of finally meeting him in person at Snap and Meta’s events last month.

I asked Scott to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:

Screenshots by Scott Stein

The phone: I use an iPhone 16 Pro Max right now.

The apps: So I randomize my Home Screen apps. Madness? Maybe. I started doing it for fun by adding suggested Siri app widgets a few years ago. I add two of the widgets, 8 apps each, and then the bottom 8 are fixed ones plus the four on my dock.

My fixed ones are: Google Calendar, Photos, Notes, Camera, Music, Gmail, GMaps, Bluesky, Phone, Messages, Mail, Safari. My core go-tos.

But the others are a contextual-slash-frequency-based mix of things I might be using (or not). The locations shift. In some ways it’s like Home Screen gaslighting… but it’s also a living Black Mirror life, and often it’s actually helpful. Today there’s the United app since I’m flying, Uber, Siri, Voice Memos, Signal, GChat, YouTube, Asana, Yahoo Sports… mostly pretty useful.

The wallpaper: My background’s also randomized. I pull from family and trip photos so I can see my kids (and other odd moments) when I’m out and about. It comforts me.

I also asked Scott to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:

The apps:

I have had an ongoing magic hobby since I was a kid. I’m reading The Intuitive Magician: Mastering Magic Through Improvisation, by Justin Higham. Kind of technical but it’s an exploration of where practice and fluid improvising meet, which feels holistic for other things. 

Also reading Stephen King and Peter Straub’s Black House, after reading The Talisman. I loved the Dark Tower books and the new Talisman trilogy end is coming soon which apparently blends them all together. 

I’ve also been semi obsessed with runes lately, part of my interest in portable trinkets and talismans, and how readings can feel like a form of meditation.

Still playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and carving out time ahead for Panic Playdate’s third season. I love that little handheld.

Crowdsourced

Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge.

“Arc Raiders (Expedition done and 2.0 coming in a week!) and Control Resonant. East of Eden.” — ProtoPhil

“I just started Widow’s Bay last night. Currently reading The Velvet Rage. Listening to the new Orville Peck album, Madonna, Adele, Amy Winehouse. Playing Stardew Valley. — antwhat

“Started watching American Horror Story: 13 and the first three episodes were pretty interesting! Love seeing the old characters’ reunion.” — alee

“I’m watching Star Trek: Voyager again! Light, serious, funny and introspective, a great watch in a time where the AI news has been a serious of scary headlines.” — BlubberBacon

“I’ve got a stack of spooky season reading that I can’t wait to dig into: The Nudge by Joseph Fink, Breakable Things and The Salt Grows Heavy by Cassandra Khaw, and The King in Yellow by Robert Chambers (Cthulhu’s grandpappy).” — Barbarian Librarian

“I’m playing Antivirus Survivors 2003 Professional because I’m apparently an ‘unc’ gamer.” — bubble_boy

“Two separate reading recommendations: Andrew Sacher’s Emo Revival and Tress of the Emerald Sea by Brandon Sanderson. Loved them both.” — securingsincity

“The latest episode of South Park America was brilliant!” — verge_user_BlorpBlorp

Signing off

Remember my minimal homescreen I showed off in my first issue I wrote back in August? I have to confess: It became a mess of apps during my travels this month. Multiple airline apps, an expense reporting app, Notes, Voice Memos, Uber, and more — it gave me hives.
