title: I Tested the Galaxy S26 Ultra Cameras Against the Pixel 11 Pro: One Captures Vibes Better
snippet: I brought two of the best Android camera phones with me to Cape May, and one was noticeably better.
fullText:
September just ended, but I’m still reminiscing over my end-of-summer trip to Cape May. It was the perfect weekend getaway to the southernmost town of New Jersey, where the sun beamed through voluminous clouds and the streets were bustling — I even remembered to fold the bed sheets that first morning. 

This was also the perfect opportunity to test and compare the camera quality of the $1,299 Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and the now-$1,400 Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, two of the best Android phones we’ve tested at CNET. 

This year’s flagship models feature iterative hardware updates, with the most notable changes being modifications to camera sensor architectures that allow for more light and, therefore, detail to be captured. This was mostly expected, as my colleague Jeff Carlson found last year’s Samsung and Google models already quite adequate.

			

More from CNET

Instead, both companies leaned more into image processing and how their respective AI models could detect and modify subjects to get you an “ideal” shot. Below, I’ll walk you through a gallery of photos I captured throughout my trip that I took under various lighting conditions and with moving subjects to help you determine which phone camera is best for you.

Note that all of these photos were captured using each phone’s native camera settings and were not modified after the fact, except for straightening in Adobe Lightroom. 

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Ultrawide

Let’s begin with ultrawide shots I took before driving through the Garden State Parkway. The first difference I noticed between the Pixel’s 48-megapixel sensor and the Samsung’s 50-megapixel sensor was how they process colors. The Pixel portrays trees, roads and the sky in more neutral, realistic tones, whereas the Samsung leans toward more vibrant, saturated tones. 

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

The better camera ultimately comes down to the flavor of green and blue you prefer, but if I had to pick a phone based on its color science alone, I would choose the Pixel, as it appears less modified.

One camera is decisively better when you look at the details of the clouds. Samsung wins here with a more balanced exposure and highlights, depicting the ever-random, cotton-ball shapes of clouds. You can clearly distinguish how each cloud merges with another. On the Pixel, however, the clouds are blown out, appearing as a single white blob.

Generally speaking, the Pixel captures photos with a warmer color temperature, as you can see the difference in my wife’s sleeves and the surrounding tree leaves as we walked through the Cape May Zoo. 

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

If you prefer something cooler, like on the Samsung, you can always tweak things in post or through the new Camera Looks introduced with the Pixel 11 lineup. They’re effectively real-time filters that apply to the phone’s imaging pipeline, giving you creative control before the phone even processes the image. 

In the same photos above, notice how the edges of the ultrawide angle are blurrier on the Samsung. This can be chalked up to a slower shutter speed or less effective stabilization, though it can also be interpreted as giving the photo a more dynamic feel. I would still pick the Pixel in this case.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Telephoto

The far-distance, telephoto comparison may be the biggest toss-up between the two phones. On paper, Samsung should have the advantage, with an extra 10-MP telephoto (for 3x optical zoom) to accommodate the 50-MP telephoto (for 5x optical zoom). Google, on the other hand, uses a main sensor crop for close-up shots, then switches to its single 48-MP 5x telephoto for longer distances.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

In practice, the quality of both phone cameras is quite good, with natural-looking bokeh (background blur) and separation between the subject and what’s behind it. When we walked by a crocodile lounging by the fence, it was a great opportunity to see how well the sensors captured the textures of its rough skin while gradually smoothing out the grass behind the animal. I took these crocodile photos using the 5x optical zoom option on each phone.

My ideal shot is somewhere in the middle. I like how natural the colors and background blur on the Pixel, but I prefer the contrast levels on the Samsung, which give the crocodile more depth and detail. For some, Samsung’s output may almost be too sharp. But if what you’re after is as much detail as possible from far away, it’s the superior camera system.

In the middle of the walk, we stopped by a gift shop for souvenirs and snacks. (I also stopped by for the abundance of colors in the room, but that’s between you and me.) I picked up a name tag, swiped over to portrait mode on both phones, then snapped a picture.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

The result is the Pixel producing an ever-warmer photo with a generous amount of bokeh and smoother edges around the name tag, while the Samsung produces one with sharper edges and subject isolation, but worse blurring. You can see the artificial processing overworking in Samsung’s photo, with the two B’s in “ABBY” slightly blurred. 

The portrait mode effect can be toned down in both the viewfinder and the gallery afterward, but as I mentioned earlier, I am only comparing photos straight out of the camera’s default settings here.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Main camera

For lunch, we settled on a Cape May classic: the Lobster House. The half-century-old institution, which is docked by the harbor, is best known for its fresh seafood, including lobster, oyster and fish. And the dim-lit ambiance, an old-school maritime theme with fishing ropes and wooden planks made for a good test of the phones’ dynamic range.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

In this first shot at the table, I’m very impressed with the sharpness and contrast from the Samsung. The highlights are managed well, too, with noticeable detail in the ships parked outside. The Pixel’s image is flatter, with just about everything appearing too smooth, and shadows that would otherwise make things more dramatic are lifted.

After the meal, we wandered through Cape May to view the iconic Victorian houses, with their high-gabled roofs and distinctive color schemes that would fit any Roald Dahl movie. In this scenario, both phones produced great-looking photos, juggling the various lines and textures of the houses with the bright sky and commendably well-maintained lawns. 

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

If there’s one comparison where the difference truly comes down to color fidelity, this is the one. Take your pick.

Pixel 11 Pro XL vs. Galaxy S26 Ultra: Moonshot

A few years ago, a big controversy surrounded the Samsung Galaxy S21 Ultra and its seemingly unimaginable ability to capture clear, detailed photos of the moon. The company reportedly used AI to detect when a moon was in the camera frame, then enhanced the image to fill in details such as craters. Apparently, that’s still a thing, and Google is in on the artificial magic, too.

Google Pixel 11 Pro XL (left) and Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (right).

Compared with Samsung’s 100x Space Zoom, the Pixel’s 120x Pro Zoom produces a brighter image, though not as detailed. There’s simply more surface clarity of the Moon in the Samsung image, likely due to the underexposure. By reducing the overly bright planet at night, the Samsung camera renders its textures more accurately. By the way, I took both of the shots with the devices held in hand, so the electronic stabilization on both devices helped a lot.

There’s no easy way to validate the results of both images, but if I had to choose one for a moonshot, I would pick Samsung.

Which is the better camera?

In most cases, the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra is the better, more capable camera phone for me. I also prefer a camera that produces social-ready imagery, so the touch of saturation and sharpness makes Samsung’s output more ideal. 

While I based the comparison on camera samples shot with default settings, know that both devices offer creative tools to tweak how images are captured. The Pixel 11 Pro’s Camera Looks, for example, lets you modify colors, tones, and sharpness in ways that can dramatically transform the expression of shots. CNET’s Andrew Lanxon put it to the test during a stay in Paris.

And as you saw above, the better camera phone ultimately comes down to your own preferences for color fidelity, detail, depth and bonus features. The undeniable truth is that you can’t go wrong with either phone.

title: Apple’s new ‘homeOS’ will launch this month, here’s what’s coming
snippet: Apple reportedly plans to launch new Home products on October 13 alongside an all-new operating system rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’ Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple reportedly plans to launch new Home products on October 13 alongside an all-new operating system rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’ Here are the details.

homeOS will run on new ‘HomePad’ product, featuring mix of other Apple OS designs

Apple’s highly anticipated ‘HomePad’ smart home hub is reportedly being unveiled on October 13. And per Mark Gurman, it will run on a brand new operating system that’s rumored to be called ‘homeOS.’

A recent Bloomberg report offers a lot of details on what to expect from homeOS. It reportedly features a blend of other Apple OS designs, including:

iPhone-style widgets

iPad-like app designs

Apple Watch-style icons for its Home Screen 

The default UI, per Gurman, “is built heavily around photo slideshows and clock displays, similar to the new StandBy Mode on the upcoming iPhone Duo” and users can “swipe up from the clock screen or photos to open the app launcher.”

We’ve seen multiple leaks this past week around this Photo Face in homeOS, as seen below.

Siri AI is the central input method, but Apple apps and a Home Screen will also be available via touch

Siri AI will be central to homeOS interactions. Per Gurman on his new podcast:

The new operating system is basically, what would an OS look like if Siri AI had an OS? If Siri AI was not just an app on the phone, if it wasn’t just an interface on the phone. What if it was an operating system?…It’s all about this concept of personal search and personal context, being able to ask for songs, podcasts, notes, calendar items, photos that are bespoke to you.

Voice won’t be the only interaction method though. Apple apps and a Home Screen will be part of homeOS too. Siri AI can be used to control these apps, but touch input will be supported too.

Built-in homeOS apps will include Music, Podcasts, Photos, Weather, FaceTime, Notes, Calendar, Messages, Reminders, and more. No App Store is expected to be available, but third-party widgets can be brought over from your iPhone.

Like on the current HomePod though, the idea is that most of the time, your interactions with homeOS happen via Siri.

title: iPadOS 27.2: Two new features coming soon to your iPad
snippet: iPadOS 27.2 is coming later this month as a new iPad software update, here are two new features it will bring. more…
fullText:
iPadOS 27.2 is coming later this month as a new iPad software update, here are two new features it will bring.

Siri AI is a major improvement over the old Siri, and I’m using it all the time on my iPad—often with a CMD + Space keyboard shortcut since Siri and Spotlight are now integrated.

In iPadOS 27.2, Apple is introducing another convenient way to interact with Siri that first debuted on the Mac in macOS Golden Gate.

When you select text in iPadOS 27.2 via a trackpad or mouse, there’s a new Siri contextual popup that appears to the left of your selection. If you hover over the Siri icon with your cursor, it instantly expands to offer an ‘Ask Siri’ text field.

This makes it quick and easy to ask Siri about whatever you’ve highlighted. And if you’re in the writing process, the Siri popup even has suggestions like ‘Proofread,’ ‘Rewrite,’ and ‘How does this sound?’ so you can get help with just a click.

#2: Profiles in Apple TV app

iPads make great video devices whether you’re an adult or a kid. And if you share an iPad with a partner or child, the Apple TV app has a welcome addition coming soon: user profiles.

iPadOS 27.2 brings over the same profiles feature that tvOS already offers on Apple TV 4K.

When you open the Apple TV app on iPad, you’ll see a new profile selection screen at startup. From here, you can choose who’s watching and the TV app will automatically update its queue, playback history, and content recommendations based on your selection.

If you’re a parent, profiles will take content restrictions into account. So when your child’s profile is active, they’ll only see films and TV shows that match the age settings you’ve previously set.

title: Vessev built an electric ferry that almost flies
snippet: Vessev hopes its electric hydrofoil ferry will change the way people and cities think about boats.
fullText:
“When will we start flying?” I asked  Vessev co-founder and CEO Eric Laakmann, as we pulled away from the Brooklyn marina in the startup’s VS-9 electric ferry.  “We already are.” 

I’ll admit I was a bit disappointed. I thought the moment when it transitioned from sailing like a regular boat to almost-flying as a surface-skimming hydrofoil would be more … momentous. 

I’ve been on my share of boats, including large ferries, small sailboats, and plenty of others in between, but never been on a hydrofoil and I was curious what flying along the water might feel like during the brief ride from the Brooklyn Marina out toward Governors Island on the East River in New York. 

It didn’t feel like flying, but it was a bit like a riding in a sports car. 

The wake when foiling in the VS-9 is minimal.Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Traditional boats of this size — about 30 feet — start to bounce and slap the water as they gain speed. But on a hydrofoil, that’s when the foils start to do their work.

On the surface, the VS-9 looks like plenty of other catamarans. But under the hull are two wing-like structures that lift the boat as they slice through the water. Computer-controlled underwater flaps keep the ride smooth and stable. In the VS-9, most of the lifting is done by the front foil, with about 20% handled by the rear.

The VS-9 can raise its foils to access docks in shallower waters.Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

The rear foil also hosts the electric motor, which Vessev makes in-house. Why not outsource it? Laakmann said that it’s important to keep costs in line — eventually, you’ll have to bring production in house, so why not do it earlier in development? The only thing Vessev doesn’t build are the batteries. “Those have been commoditized,” Laakmann said.

By lifting the hull clear of the water, hydrofoils can operate more efficiently than other boats. That’s especially important for electric boats, where every kilowatt-hour counts.

Shipbuilders have been experimenting with hydrofoils for well over a century. The design offers several advantages, including lower drag and a smoother ride. The subtle transition I experienced on the VS-9, from sailing to almost-flying, underlined just how smooth a hydrofoil can be.

The Vessev VS-9 can charge using a typical EV charger.Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Despite hydrofoils’ advantages, they’re not a panacea. The design works best in waters the boat can clear when sailing on its foils. For the VS-9, that’s about two and a half feet, or 0.75 meters. If the waves go higher than that, they start hitting the hull, ruining the smooth ride and sapping some efficiency. While they’re not ideal for the open ocean, hydrofoils make sense for other waterways, including lakes, rivers, and bays. 

Vessev, which raised a $19 million Series A in August, is targeting transit operations to start. Laakmann thinks the combination of electric propulsion and hydrofoils can bring down the cost of operating smaller vessels and make them comfortable enough that they could augment urban mass transit systems. 

Somewhere like New York City could use them to zip people to Brooklyn or Queens without needing to build much new infrastructure.

The VS-9 can carry a full passenger load up to 40 nautical miles (46 miles or 74 kilometers).Image Credits:Tim De Chant/TechCrunch

Hotels and tour operators are also an early target market, and public demonstrations like the one I attended have attracted wealthy individuals looking for another toy, Laakmann said.

For now, the VS-9 I rode is one of a kind, but Laakmann said Vessev plans to build more. Eventually, the company might shift to producing electric hydrofoil kits, allowing other boatbuilders to design their own vessels around the technology, Laakmann said.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate reporter at TechCrunch. He has written for a wide range of publications, including Wired magazine, the Chicago Tribune, Ars Technica, The Wire China, and NOVA Next, where he was founding editor. 

De Chant is also a lecturer in MIT’s Graduate Program in Science Writing, and he was awarded a Knight Science Journalism Fellowship at MIT in 2018, during which time he studied climate technologies and explored new business models for journalism. He received his PhD in environmental science, policy, and management from the University of California, Berkeley, and his BA degree in environmental studies, English, and biology from St. Olaf College.

title: Apple Watch Series 12, Ultra 4 adding two new features soon
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have arrived, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 have arrived, and later this year they’ll get even more powerful with two new features: Siri Recap and Live Rewind. Here are the details.

#1: Siri Recap

Siri AI is a major tentpole of watchOS 27, and later this year there’s a powerful Siri addition coming to Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. It’s called Siri Recap.

Here’s what it does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

Siri Recap seems like the kind of feature that no one was necessarily asking for, but it could add valuable utility if the privacy protections are done right. You can read the finer details around privacy in Apple’s white paper here.

#2: Live Rewind

Live Rewind is another ‘Audio Intelligence’ feature coming to the new Apple Watch models later this year. It provides a more direct way to revisit something that was just said.

Here’s how it works per Apple:

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Like Siri Recap, Apple has in-depth details on Live Rewind’s privacy protections outlined here. For me personally, the utility of Live Rewind seems less obvious beyond accessibility needs. But I’m interested to see how it works in its finished form.

title: Galaxy S27 series pricing may not only increase, but cost more to upgrade storage
snippet: Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker. more…
fullText:
Samsung’s new Galaxy S27 series is rumored to come at a higher price than previous versions, but that’s no surprise. What’s a little harder to swallow is the larger rumored gap between storage variants, according to one leaker.

In succession to the Galaxy S26 lineup, the Galaxy S27 series is expected to take on plenty of physical changes. Namely, in design. Previous leaks have provided CAD renders of the new camera island and overall look, but those have also been caveated with a promised price increase.

Following rumors that the Galaxy S27 Ultra could start at $1,400, a new bit of information has surfaced from a leaker on Naver. According to Lanzuk, the Galaxy S27 series, as a whole, is expected to come at a higher price. The estimated jump is reportedly in the “high 130,000 won range” (~$100). But the post also suggests Samsung is setting a “steeper rate of increase” to the prices of each capacity, likely referring to storage variants.

That could suggest that, instead of a $200 gap between some storage variants, the disparity could expand. Then again, the post isn’t clear on whether this is a linear price increase or one that also increases upgrade costs over previous generations.

	

The posted leak is courtesy of domestic Korean sources, indicating this price increase is specific to Samsung’s home soil. That doesn’t mean it won’t translate to other regions, like the US or Europe.

We’re a bit wary of a report like this. Not because a price increase is unlikely for the Galaxy S27 series – statistically, it very much is – but because of clashing numbers. The previously noted leak also suggested the Galaxy S27 series would remain unchanged as a whole, apart from the most premium flagship model. This leak contradicts that, noting every device will see a jump.

It’s very possible that Samsung is flipping between the two until it ultimately decides on exactly how much it needs to increase the cost of each device and variant to make a profit off of devices stuffed with NAND and LPDDR6 RAM, which the post also notes will be included on “some models.”

Until the Galaxy S27 series launches early next year, there will likely be little confirmation on Samsung’s finalized price increases.

title: California Legalized Plug-In Balcony Solar Panels, but Don’t Buy Any Just Yet
snippet: Units that comply with the new law are expected by spring.
fullText:
Energy prices are high, no matter what state you live in, but they’re especially high in sunny California. Homeowners in the Golden State have been able to get some relief by installing solar panels to defray their electric bill, and now renters and apartment dwellers can, too, as California officially legalized plug-in balcony solar panels this week. But don’t go buy a kit just yet. 

The so-called Plug and Play Solar Act (Senate Bill No. 868), signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom and sponsored by state Sen. Scott Wiener, permits the use of plug-in solar for apartments, condos and single-family homes, as long as it meets the regulations in the bill.

“This new law will deliver cleaner power, greater energy independence and real savings for consumers,” Bernadette Del Chiaro, senior vice president for California at the nonprofit Environmental Working Group, said in a statement.

Plug-in solar units don’t have to go on balconies.

Zoltux

Until the passage of bills like this, installing solar panels required you to have an interconnection agreement for anything with the potential to put power back into the grid. In the case of California, the process of completing an interconnection agreement required an upfront cost of $100 to $800 and would take an hour, with approval typically taking three days, according to PG&E.

			

More from CNET

While the process has been simplified, the new law still has some requirements. The solar system can’t generate more than 1,200 watts per home, which is about enough to power a window AC unit. You also need to register the balcony solar kit, like it’s a rooftop panel system, and it needs to be certified by an outside safety organization. It also needs to be configured not to feed power back into the grid during a power outage, potentially through the use of a separate smart power management meter, such as the Smart Gateway Lite from Mango Power.

Jackery’s SolarVault system works for balcony solar.Ajay Kumar/CNET

Plug-in solar panels can be installed almost anywhere there’s open space and a standard AC outlet. The big advantage of them is that you can deploy them in a backyard, on a balcony or on a roof without having to do the expensive wiring and installation of rooftop solar panels. This technology has been popular in Europe, especially in Germany, where 4 million systems have been installed, but it’s also making steady inroads in the US.

Dozens of US states are considering or have already passed legislation to legalize balcony solar. According to the Environmental Working Group, California is the 10th state to legalize balcony solar, effectively doubling the size of the US market. The first to pass the law was Utah, which did so in March 2025. A more recent one was New Jersey, where Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a bill that would prevent landlords and local governments from blocking residents and tenants from installing solar panels with a maximum power output of 1,200 watts.

Bluetti showed off its balcony solar system at IFA Berlin 2026.Ajay Kumar/CNET

The passage of this law may be a tipping point for balcony solar. When I was at IFA Berlin 2026 in September, I saw several balcony solar systems from Jackery, EcoFlow, Bluetti and others, with a Bluetti representative specifically informing me that they were waiting for some uncertainty around US regulations to be resolved before releasing in the US market.

A representative from Mango Power, which makes solar kits and home backups, told me last year that it was difficult to advise US customers on what solutions are available for their specific states because, ultimately, consumers need to be clear about the regulations before buying.

None of the units currently on the market meet California’s requirements, so you can’t just go out and buy one right now if you’re a California resident. The systems will still need to be registered as rooftop solar systems. Noncompliant systems will also become illegal in the state in 2030, though the groups sponsoring the bill expect that models that are compliant with California’s requirements will come to market in the spring. 

Various balcony solar manufacturers did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the availability of California-compliant units.

title: What has been the best Google Pixel to date? [Poll]
snippet: On 4 October 2016, Google introduced the original Pixel and Pixel XL, marking a major pivot away from the developer-focused Nexus line and ushering in what is now a decade of “Made by Google” hardware – but which is best and why? more…
fullText:
On 4 October 2016, Google introduced the original Pixel and Pixel XL, marking a major pivot away from the developer-focused Nexus line and ushering in what is now a decade of “Made by Google” hardware – but which is best and why?

Over the past 10 years, the lineup has expanded from a pair of traditional slab smartphones to a product portfolio that includes foldable devices, watches, earbuds, a single tablet, and budget-focused A-series models, culminating in the Pixel 11 series.

I’m biased, I think that the 4a is the best of the bunch, but determining which device holds the title of the best Pixel to date is going to be a fun, healthy debate for those of us who have used more than a few of the lineup over the years, especially as not all have been covered in glory.

The initial breakthrough

The original Pixel and Pixel XL established Google’s focus on camera processing and clean software integration. While the launch models lacked water resistance and stereophonic audio, their computational photography capabilities set a new baseline for mobile imaging.

	

A year later, the Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL introduced the iconic “Panda” design and front-facing stereo speakers. Although the LG-manufactured Pixel 2 XL faced criticism regarding display viewing angles, the series remains highly regarded for solidifying Google’s image processing dominance.

The Pixel 3 and 3 XL introduced Night Sight and a dedicated Pixel Visual Core chip, alongside dual front-facing cameras with an ultra-wide sensor. Despite memory management limits tied to its 4GB of RAM and the prominent display notch on the XL model, the third-generation devices brought significant refinements to software performance. Shortly after, the Pixel 3a series created the mid-range budget category for Google, pairing flagship camera capabilities with lower price points.

Pivots, Experiments, and Design Changes

Google shifted its approach with the Pixel 4 and 4 XL, introducing Soli radar gesture controls, 90Hz Motion Sense displays, and the only instance of 3D Face Unlock. The removal of the rear fingerprint scanner and poor battery life on the smaller model limited its appeal, though the 4 XL maintains a loyal following for its build, slim profile, and biometric features.

The 4a and 4a 5G focused back on value during a period of transition. That path culminated in the Pixel 5, which abandoned high-end flagship processors in favor of a mid-range Qualcomm Snapdragon 765G chipset, a uniform-bezel design, a rear fingerprint sensor, and a high-density battery. The Pixel 5a with 5G followed a similar template with a larger form factor and water resistance.

The Pixel 6 and 6 Pro marked the biggest moment in the lineup since its inception. Introducing custom Google Tensor silicon, a horizontal camera bar design, the series briefly pushed Google back into true flagship territory. The subsequent Pixel 6a brought this design language and processor to the A-series lineup, but had the killer addition of the best Tensor chip at a time when most mid-rangers were still forgoing high-end SoCs in favor of middling performance.

Refinement continued with the Pixel 7 and 7 Pro, which upgraded to the Tensor G2, addressed thermal efficiency, and refreshed the camera bar with an aluminum finish. The 7a brought high-refresh-rate screens and wireless charging to the lower price bracket for the first time.

Expanding Form Factors and Beyond

Google’s smartphone ecosystem expanded significantly with the introduction of the Pixel Fold and the Pixel Tablet. The Fold represented Google’s entry into flexible displays with a wider outer screen, while the Pixel Tablet offered a dual-purpose home display experience via its charging speaker dock.

The Pixel 8 and 8 Pro introduced seven years of OS updates, Tensor G3 silicon, brighter Actua displays, and a flat screen design for the Pro model. The 8a brought those long-term software commitments to a lower price point and arguably blurred the lines between the A-series and the base model for the first time.

	

The Pixel 9 series expanded the lineup further, introducing a third flagship size with the Pixel 9, Pixel 9 Pro, and Pixel 9 Pro XL, alongside the refined Pixel 9 Pro Fold. The series introduced updated industrial design with flattened sides, updated Tensor G4 chips, and satellite connectivity.

Since the 9 was launched, we’ve had a couple of years of effectively the same device with minor iterations. Most of the changes have been focused solely on hardware efficiency and processing performance.

Reaching the 10-year mark, the Pixel 11 series builds upon that decade of iterations. From off-the-shelf components to custom chips that may not have quite hit the heights many have wanted, there’s never a dull moment with a Google phone, for better or worse.

Which device stands out as the best release over the last 10 years? We’ve omitted wearables in a bid to streamline the entire poll, but be sure to cast your vote in the poll below and let us know the reasons behind your choice in the comments.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Max Can’t Make a Call on AT&T? Apple Says It Will Replace It for Free
snippet: A software and carrier settings update should prevent future problems, but people who have been affected will need a replacement phone.
fullText:
Some owners of Apple’s new iPhone 18 Pro Max may be enjoying the new camera system and improved battery life. But if they’re AT&T customers, they could find the phone unable to perform its most essential task: making calls. That also includes being able to dial 911 in emergencies. The fix appears to be a pair of Apple updates rolling out on Friday – but anyone who has already been affected by the problem will need a replacement phone, according to Apple. An Apple representative says the company will replace those phones for free.

Last week, some iPhone 18 Pro Max owners on AT&T’s network reported no cellular access. MacRumors reported that AT&T sent a text message this week to iPhone 18 Pro Max owners, encouraging them to update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately. MacRumors estimates that thousands of customers have been affected.

On Friday, Apple said it’s issuing a separate carrier-settings patch to pair with the iOS 27.0.1 update. But the patch comes too late for certain owners of the new phone.

			

More from CNET

An Apple representative told CNET that the updates are intended to guard against this problem in the future and won’t fix the situation for iPhone 18 Pro Max owners who are already experiencing it. Apple will provide a new phone free of charge to those owners. Affected customers should contact Apple Support or AT&T.

In Reddit threads about the issue, some owners report that the 27.0.1 update by itself did not fix the problem, nor did upgrading to the public beta of iOS 27.2.

Only the iPhone 18 Pro Max is affected

So far, the issue seems limited to iPhone 18 Pro Max models on AT&T’s network. I reached out to contacts at T-Mobile and Verizon, and both report they’re not seeing similar reports on their networks. I haven’t experienced the issue on an iPhone 18 Pro that runs on AT&T’s network, which isn’t surprising given that this particular problem affects iPhone 18 Pro Max units, not iPhone 18 Pro phones. A CNET colleague’s iPhone 18 Pro Max on Google Fi (which uses T-Mobile’s network) is not experiencing the issue.

It’s unclear whether the lack of connectivity is related to the phone’s hardware. While the standard iPhone 18 Pro is equipped with Apple’s C2 modem, the iPhone 18 Pro Max in the US is the only model with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X80 modem, as shown in this teardown of the phone by iFixIt. Qualcomm has been Apple’s modem provider for years, but Apple has worked to move away from relying on the third party for the essential phone component. That relationship is due to expire this year.

According to a TechInsights iPhone 18 Pro Max teardown, the X80 modem is also used in the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro Max, but a new millimeter-wave antenna has been added to the 18 Pro Max. Millimeter-wave offers much faster data speeds in areas where the technology is installed, but it can have a shorter range and be reduced by obstacles. Apple’s C2 modem also includes a millimeter-wave antenna.

A representative from Qualcomm didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: The iPhone 18 Pro is selling well in China for three reasons
snippet: A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China, making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week. Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone … more…
fullText:
A new market intelligence report says that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are selling well in China, making Apple the best-selling brand in the country during the launch week.

Counterpoint Research has said there are three reasons for the popularity of Apple’s latest iPhone … 

Rising costs have seen overall sales of new smartphones in China decline 17% year on year since July, according to Counterpoint Research’s China Weekly Smartphone Sell-Out Tracker. However, the firm reports that this trend was reversed by the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro.

During the first three days of its sales (which accounted for only three days in Week 38), the iPhone 18 Pro series recorded 12% YoY growth compared with the iPhone sales. The strong initial performance helped Apple move into the No. 1 spot in sales in Week 38, with a 33% share of China’s smartphone market.

Three reasons for success

Counterpoint suggests there are three reasons underlying the popularity of the new model.

First, the delayed launch of the base iPhone 18. Because Apple has launched the two iPhone 18 Pro models well ahead of the standard model, some may have decided to upgrade to the premium version rather than wait.

Second, rising prices across all premium smartphones have led to consumers being willing to pay higher prices than would previously have been the case. Apple has absorbed some of the increased component costs, making the iPhone 18 Pro comparatively better value.

Third is what Counterpoint describes as “aggressive channel support,” generally meaning heavy advertising and promotions by retailers and carriers.

title: Pixel Recorder makes it easier to access audio files
snippet: Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device. more…
fullText:
Pixel Recorder is getting a small quality-of-life update that surfaces your audio files to other apps on your device.

Previously, accessing the actual audio file involved opening a recording and then the share menu for the “Audio or transcript file” option. This took you to the system share sheet for a manual save. 

Pixel Recorder now has an “Access recordings in other apps” setting that lets you “View your recordings in the Files app or other apps for easier access.” 

This is enabled by default, with a prompt on the homepage announcing the new feature: “Access recordings in other apps. Manage this in Settings anytime.”

	

The new “Recordings” folder on your device shows all audio that you’ve recorded or downloaded from the cloud.

Version 4.2.20260823.x of Pixel Recorder widely rolls out this capability.

It follows the last update in August that introduced the new app icon, which is not yet live (along with Weather) on the Pixel Watch. Recorder will also be available on Googlebooks going forward.

title: Spotify billionaire’s body scan startup has come to America
snippet: Farooq Abbasi, an investor in Neko Health, talked to Equity about the hot health tech company and what's next for it.
fullText:
Neko Health seems to be the hottest body scan in the world right now. 

The scan, co-founded by Spotify’s David Ek and Hjalmar Nilsonne, uses advanced technology to screen for issues in the blood, skin, and metabolism. The company was founded in Sweden, has raised nearly $1 billion total, and just landed in New York. It has a global waitlist already topping 300,000 people, the company says. 

TechCrunch sat down with Farooq Abbasi of Preface Ventures, who invested in the company. He hopes Neko Health can be the future of preventative medicine, especially in a country like the United States, where the medical system is notoriously plagued with issues. 

Abbasi contends that preventative care utilization is low in the U.S. as people have concerns about how much it costs. Currently, Neko health charges $500 for its one-hour scan, which is not covered by insurance but should qualify as an acceptable expense for those that have Health Savings Accounts. “I think preventative care and healthcare should be cheap and accessible,” Abbasi said. 

The hope is that Neko Health can tackle some of these issues, and it’s currently eyeing an expansion across the U.S. Abbasi has been scanned twice already and, perhaps, no surprise, says he loves it. “I think there should be Neko clinics everywhere,” he said. 

He says the product has grown so much since he first tried it. “In my generation one scan, it was a blood test with 15 biomarkers,” he said. “It was fifty-five this time.” 

Neko also uses advanced computer vision for its scans and Abbasi sees this as another example of how AI is improving the medical sector overall. He argues that Neko Health isn’t just another wellness fad, but something that gives people “actionable insights to make their lives better,” he said. 

Neko still has a long way to go in the U.S., especially on scaling and regulatory approval. But Abbasi is an optimist; he hopes more venture dollars will pour into the right companies and doesn’t think anything is too broken to fix.

title: Elder fraud is rising – here’s how to protect your family
snippet: Elder fraud – where seniors are deliberately targeted due to this demographic having lower rates of tech literacy – is becoming a growing problem in the US. According to Incogni’s analysis of FBI data, 72% of elder fraud cases in 2024 were enabled by victims’ personal data being exposed online, accounting for $4.2 billion in losses. more…
fullText:
Elder fraud – where seniors are deliberately targeted due to this demographic having lower rates of tech literacy – is becoming a growing problem in the US.

According to Incogni’s analysis of FBI data, 72% of elder fraud cases in 2024 were enabled by victims’ personal data being exposed online, accounting for $4.2 billion in losses.

How these scams work

Family chat groups can be a goldmine for scammers. Everyday updates ranging from doctor visits to travel plans provide personalized information scammers can use to make it much easier to convincingly impersonate family members in trouble.

Given that iMessage, WhatsApp, and most other messaging apps use end-to-end encryption, you might assume this information is completely safe, but that isn’t always true. One of the most dangerous tools employed by scammers is what’s known as SIM swaps.

With this, they’ll use whatever personal information they can find from public sources in order to convince a mobile carrier that they are the person they are targeting. They claim the phone has been lost or damaged and ask the carrier to switch the mobile number to a new SIM card they have purchased.

If the carrier is fooled, then all texts sent to the victim will instead be received by the scammer. This includes SMS-based two-factor authentication codes to reset passwords, access bank accounts, and more. It is this capability that can give the scammer access to family chat groups.

The combination of the personal data they’ve already found online with the additional details they can glean from the chats gives them everything they need to convincingly persuade their victim that they are a family member in need of urgent assistance. This includes voice notes providing the audio required to create deepfake speech that appears to be the voice of the family member.

How to protect your family

There are three main steps you can take to protect your family members against this type of attack.

First, minimize the personal data a scammer can find online. Scammers use data broker sites to obtain information like family names and phone numbers, as well as information like hobbies and travel history. There are literally hundreds of different data brokers, and getting personal data removed from all of them is a mammoth task. Fortunately, Incogni can do it for you.

Second, ensure that two-factor authentication (2FA) is switched on for all messaging apps, social media, and more. The bottom line is that any time you are offered the opportunity to use 2FA, you should accept it. If you’re offered the choice between text message and authenticator app to receive the codes, always choose the app. This is your best protection against SIM swap attacks.

Third, always contact the family member by a different method in order to verify that it really is them. If you get a text message, for example, then email them in response. If you get an email, then phone them. The more communications channels a scammer has to compromise, the lower the chance of them succeeding.

Finally, agree a secret family password which will be used to verify identity during emergency calls. If you receive a call claiming to be a family member in need of urgent assistance, always ask them for the password, even if you think you recognize their voice and they know seem to know lots of personal things. This is the final layer of protection against a scammer who has access to a family member’s phone number, email account, and more.

title: The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
snippet: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the collapse and the resurgence of the portable media player, follow Terrence O'Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers' inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. With the advent of the MP3 player in … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the collapse and the resurgence of the portable media player, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

We are spoiled for choice, musically. Most of us walk around with access to hundreds of millions of songs in our pockets. But it wasn’t until 1998 that portable digital music was even a thing. Before that we lugged booklets full of CDs on the bus or stashed a handful of cassettes in our backpacks. With the advent of the MP3 player in the 2000s we were soon able to carry massive libraries of music everywhere we went — over 1,000 albums’ worth depending on the file format and the size of your MP3 player.

The MPMan F10 is generally considered to be the first commercial MP3 player. It was roughly the size of a deck of cards and looked like an oversized pager. It launched in Asia in March of 1998, but it barely made a blip on anyone’s radar. It was the Diamond Rio PMP300 that broke through in the West a few months later, in September of 1998. It was slightly larger, and its design more closely resembles what we envision when we think of a media player (namely the iPod). But even then, it drew more attention because the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) sued Diamond Multimedia in an attempt to stop the spread of MP3s.

The F10 and the PMP300 were, unsurprisingly, primitive by today’s standards, shipping with just 32MB — yes, that’s megabytes — of storage. That tiny amount of built-in memory only allowed for around 12 songs to be stored on them. They held less audio than a CD and generally sounded worse. But it wasn’t that big of a limitation, in comparison to the nightmare that was the UI on their tiny monochrome LCDs. Plus, you could expand storage on both using SmartMedia cards if you really needed to.

Eventually, some companies addressed the storage issue by swapping flash storage, which was still relatively limited at the time, for traditional spinning-disc hard drives. The Creative Nomad Jukebox, for instance, had a 6GB drive inside. It also had a more familiar design modeled after portable CD players. But that made it bulkier than the competition; it weighed a shocking 14 ounces. Unsurprisingly, it also failed to usher MP3 players into the mainstream.

It wasn’t until the introduction of the iPod in November 2001 that the golden age of portable media players truly took off. By 2007, roughly 20 percent of Americans owned a personal media player. Other companies, including Microsoft and Creative, tried to carve out space for themselves with Zune and Zen lines, respectively. But Apple’s iPod was the dominant force in the market, accounting for over 70 percent of media player sales.

While 20 percent isn’t ubiquitous, the iPod and the digital music revolution certainly felt inescapable in the 2000s. Bands like Radiohead and Nine Inch Nails were experimenting with pay-what-you-want digital releases. Napster taught everyone the phrases “file sharing” and “peer-to-peer.” And Apple’s iconic ads combining silhouettes and white earbuds were everywhere.

The personal media player’s spotlight was relatively short-lived. While Apple didn’t fully discontinue the iPod lineup until 2022, it retired the Classic model in 2014 and cut the Nano and Shuffle in 2017, leaving the iPod Touch — essentially an iPhone without the phone — as the last iPod standing.

By 2011, the writing was on the wall as iPhone sales eclipsed iPod sales for the first time. The portable media player market shrank quickly as modern smartphones replaced flip phones and BlackBerrys, and music consumption moved away from purchasing CDs or digital downloads toward streaming. What was, at its peak, a $21.6 billion industry in 2008 had collapsed to just $613 million in 2012, according to research firm Mintel.

How it’s going

It’s difficult to get reliable numbers for the size of the digital audio player market these days. Some research firms lump all media players together, regardless of whether they’re audio or video, streaming or offline. Others that do track audio-specific players as a separate market segment can’t seem to agree. Some report that it’s a $180 million-plus industry on the rise. Others say it’s only a $1.2 million market and it’s shrinking. One thing is certain, though: Portable media players have become a very small niche.

For most of the last 10 years, dedicated portable music players were primarily the realm of audiophiles. Companies like Sony and Astell & Kern have been steadily releasing high-end audio players that can sell for well north of $3,000. Sony’s NW-A306 is the only device offered by either company that even approaches a mainstream consumer price, at $399.99.

These devices aren’t just more expensive, they’re more complicated than the iPods of yore. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are a given. They feature large touchscreens and high-end digital audio converters. They also often run Android, opening them up to streaming apps like Spotify and Qobuz. Sony has fully embraced the iPod Touch model, giving its players full access to the Google Play store.

The sky-high prices and embrace of apps has led many to reject these players. Instead, those looking for an offline listening experience free from notifications and algorithms have turned to the past. Vintage iPods still fetch hundreds of dollars on eBay. An entire cottage industry has cropped up around modding them — adding modern features like Bluetooth and USB-C, replacing the dying hard drives and batteries, or just customizing the appearance.

What happens next

As popular as the iPod was, the world’s supply of working used units will eventually run out. As they age, batteries will stop holding a charge and spinning drives will fail, and most people don’t want to open up a piece of delicate electronics or mess with a soldering iron. But the renewed interest in iPods is starting to drive up prices on other media players, and modders are now swapping new drives into Zunes and selling them for hundred of dollars on eBay.

With Google searches for “MP3 player” nearly tripling since last year and The New York Times running trend pieces about the iPod resurgence, a number of companies and startups are trying to cash in. Chinese manufacturers have flooded AliExpress, Temu, and Amazon with a ton of dirt-cheap players and shameless iPod knockoffs.

Wildly successful crowdfunding campaigns, like that of the AP30 Music Boy, show there is pent-up demand for retro portable music players. But most out there aren’t moving the needle much in terms of design or usability.

Sleevenote is one startup that’s attempting to break the mold, but its success is far from guaranteed. It’s a startup from musician Tom Vek that embraces some modern conveniences like syncing over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth headphones, but skips on any extraneous features like streaming, apps, or games. It swaps scrolling text lists of artist names for a grid of album art. It’s highly visual, and attempts to re-create the experience of paging through a CD booklet. It also has limited integration with a host of digital music storefronts like Bandcamp, Subvert, Bleep, Qobuz, Amazon Music, and more.

Vek has a promising-looking concept on its hands that actually approaches the portable media player in a fresh way. But the bulky Day One edition still has a lot of kinks to work out, including disappointing battery life. (I’ve been testing one for a couple of months now.) Plus, it’s currently sold out and the company doesn’t know when the next batch will be made available.

There’s growing anti-streaming sentiment, and the slowtech trend doesn’t seem to be going anywhere anytime soon. But no obvious heir to the iPod throne has stepped in to fill the gap in the MP3 player market.

It seems unlikely that the MP3 player will see a resurgence on the scale of vinyl or even CDs. In part because, for whatever convenience advantage an iPod might have over a limited edition LP, it lacks the collectibility factor. And that has been a major driver of the physical media resurgence, as evidenced by the fact that, while Gen Z and millennials might be buying up CDs in record numbers, half of them don’t own a CD player.

By the way

Suzanne Vega is sometimes called the “mother of the MP3.” Karlheinz Brandenburg was working on audio compression technology at the Fraunhofer Society (FHG) in Germany and turned to Vega’s “Tom’s Diner” as his benchmark due to her “warm, human voice” that would be a challenge to encode. Thousands of miles away, James Johnston also turned to “Tom’s Diner” while working on audio compression at Bell Labs. Brandenburg and Johnston’s work ultimately led to the creation of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III standard, better known as MP3.

Kane Kramer is widely credited with inventing the first digital audio player in 1979, and successfully patented it in the UK in 1985, and the US in 1987. Many of its features, including an online music store, would eventually find their way into the iPod and iTunes. And Paul McCartney was an early financial backer, but his IXI never saw a commercial release. Kramer’s patents lapsed in 1988. While Apple eventually gave him credit for his invention, it was primarily a legal maneuver to undermine a company called Burst.com that sued Apple for patent infringement. 

Read this

Brandon Shaw, host of YouTube channel Digging the Greats, ditched streaming for an iPod two years ago and documented the experience over the course of several videos.

The New York Times looked at how younger generations were embracing old-school media formats, including the iPod, in an attempt to break free of the shackles of streaming.

The Verge crew shared their fond memories of the iPod when Apple officially put it out to pasture in 2022.

This visual history of the iPod charts its evolution from clunky brick to sleek icon of modern design.

title: DoorDash now lets you order by text in Apple Messages
snippet: DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
DoorDash today launched a new way to order your next meal: via text in Apple’s Messages app, powered by AI. Here are the details.

DoorDash text ordering launches on iPhone, powered by AI agent

AI agents are here to stay, and they don’t just look like cute digital creatures. While Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have gotten a lot of attention, AI agents are popping up in ways that are less obviously “AI” too.

For example, today DoorDash launched the ability to skip the app and simply text to place your food order in Apple’s Messages app. It’s available in the US only to start, and interested users will need to first join this waitlist. And it’s all powered by an AI agent.

Here’s the rundown on how it works, via DoorDash’s announcement:

Text what you’re craving: Ask for a specific dish, request a local recommendation based on your mood, or simply reorder your go-to Friday night meal for the family.

Skip the search: DoorDash searches local spots, scans menus, and suggests a cart based on what you’re in the mood for. It even texts you photos of the food it recommends right from the restaurant’s store page on the DoorDash app. 

Truly personalized ordering: Text “order my usual” and it knows you mean your Friday night order — no need to spell out the dish, the modifiers, or the restaurant. It already knows whether you skip cilantro, always add extra sauce, or never miss dessert. The more you order, the more it learns, and if you want, it can message you proactively to ask if you want your usual coffee order based on your daily habits.

Manage group preferences with ease: Ordering for large groups is never easy, especially when everyone wants something different. It can handle mixed dietary preferences and different quantities in one order, so you’re not the one juggling everyone’s requests.

Checkout without ever opening the app: Confirm your order right inside the text thread and it manages checkout.

To get started, join DoorDash’s waitlist and you’ll be notified when text access is granted. Depending on demand, that access might arrive right away, or it may take some time.

Are you interested in using DoorDash’s AI agent to order via Apple’s Messages app? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google’s original Pixel Fold was the right idea years ahead of its time
snippet: Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time. more…
fullText:
Google’s original Pixel Fold was inherently flawed but also fundamentally way better than I expected and, thanks to recent arrivals, also way ahead of its time.

Foldables were still very much going through growing pains in 2023 when Google stepped up to the plate with its first foldable, the Pixel Fold. At the time, I called it “better than it should be, but far from perfect,” and I stand by that. Even with hindsight of three more Google foldables and the rapid improvements of the rest of the industry, the Pixel Fold managed to do a lot right at the time. It offered sturdy hardware, respectable cameras, and less compromises than most other foldables of the time.

Has it aged well? Not particularly. The glossy finish to the metal frame remains a fingerprint magnet in the worst kind of way, and the sheer heft of this phone is wild. I don’t often take issue with a heavy smartphone, but especially compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 I’ve been using the past couple of months, the original Pixel Fold is noticeably heavy in the hand. The crease down the center is huge, and it’s a thick device too. And, three years later, I can only imagine how bad Tensor G2’s heat management issues have become – that was ultimately the deal-breaker for me when I was using the device last. 

Yet, for everything it got wrong, the Pixel Fold got one thing right, the form factor.

	

In the wake of Apple’s debut in the foldable market, brands are quickly pivoting to wider form factors, and they seem to be resonating with customers. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is a smash hit, and I bet we’ll be seeing a lot more of these wide foldables over the next year. 

But the Pixel Fold did it three years ago, albeit with a lot less flash. 

Google’s foldable looks almost normal compared to a Galaxy Z Fold 8, but the core idea is the same. The wider canvas is designed for better multitasking and tablet apps, something that I pointed out in my original review. Where Samsung’s foldables were really good at using phone apps on a bigger canvas, the Pixel Fold was far more likely to trigger a proper tablet version of an app instead. 

	

Google ultimately threw that away. Why? Android apps simply weren’t ready at the time. While Android apps have always been designed around scaling to form factors, bigger and wider canvases were still in the minority, and most apps didn’t fully support them. As such, the taller and squarish design just made more sense.

Arguably, it still does, but Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 has shown that it works when you do it “right.” Two months into using it, I’m thrilled with this form factor, and a bit annoyed that Google gave up on it so quickly even though, at the time, it probably made sense. Unfortunately, that’s a bit of a trend in the Pixel’s legacy and Google’s as a whole – Inbox, Stadia, etc. It doesn’t take much to find a Google idea that was left behind too quickly.

It’s anyone’s guess when Google might revisit this design, but I hope it happens.

title: AT&T claims iOS 27.0.1 fixes iPhone 18 Pro Max cellular issues, but users disagree [U]
snippet: Update 1:50 p.m. PT: More details from Apple are available here: Apple confirms iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T cellular issues, affected devices require hardware replacement Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched, some AT&T customers have complained of various connectivity issues. fullText:
Update 1:50 p.m. PT: More details from Apple are available here: 

Apple confirms iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T cellular issues, affected devices require hardware replacement

Since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched, some AT&T customers have complained of various connectivity issues.

In a new text message to customers, AT&T says affected users should update their devices to iOS 26.0.1 to fix the issues … but early reports indicate the update doesn’t actually fix the problem.

AT&T tells iPhone 18 Pro Max users to install iOS 27.0.1 

In a thread on Reddit today, an AT&T customer says they received the following automated text message from the carrier:

Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately — Settings > General > Software Update. Please contact AT&T or Apple if you have questions.

Apple released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week. According to the release notes, the update addressed bugs related to Face ID and camera performance for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max users. The release notes made no mention of any fixes for cellular connectivity problems impacting AT&T customers.

Early reports from AT&T users suggest that iOS 27.0.1 does not fix the connectivity problems affecting iPhone 18 Pro Max. Many affected users say they updated when iOS 27.0.1 was released on Monday and are still facing the same problems.

Affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users can’t connect to AT&T’s network for calls, texts, and data. The users see “SOS” in their iPhone’s status bar. The connectivity issues aren’t impacting every iPhone 18 Pro Max user, but they do appear to be relatively widespread.

Interestingly, the problems appear to be exclusive to the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which uses a Qualcomm modem. The iPhone 18 Pro, which uses Apple’s C2 modem, is seemingly unaffected by these AT&T connectivity issues.

Are you an iPhone 18 Pro Max user facing connectivity issues with AT&T? Does iOS 27.0.1 fix the problems? Let us know down in the comments.

Update 10:50 a.m. PT: In a statement to MacRumors, AT&T emphasized that affected iPhone 18 Pro Max users should update to iOS 27.0.1. The carrier added that it’s working with Apple to solve the problems. Apple also released an AT&T carrier settings update today.

title: Meta wants your next gadget to be Muse-infused
snippet: Meta wants Muse in your TV and your toaster, so it's giving the code away for free.
fullText:
Meta’s Muse, a personal AI agent that books travel, fills out forms, and shops on a user’s behalf, has already proven popular with the masses, but a new side project could be particularly alluring to tinkerers and hackers.

On Friday, the company introduced Muse Gadgets, an open-source project that lets developers build their own hardware that connects to Muse.

Meta is providing open-source firmware (the low-level software that runs a device), and a Linux software development kit (SDK), along with a few project ideas to get users started. These include giving Muse a color e-ink display or loading it onto a stick that plugs into a TV’s HDMI port.

There don’t appear to be many limits, either. Users can set up a low-cost hobbyist computer like a Raspberry Pi or an off-the-shelf ESP32 board, and then connect Muse “to your displays, buttons, sensors, actuators, and whatever else you’ve got lying on your workbench,” Meta notes.

The company has also set up a Discord channel to support users. 

Meta has already tried the code itself, naturally. Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, said in a post on X that the company built a gadget called Muse Home Link. The USB-C-powered device lets Muse connect to a home network and talk to the smart devices on it, including speakers and smart TVs.

Meta made 5,000 of these Home Links, in fact, and is giving them away for free to Muse subscribers while supplies last, according to Friedman. Considering Friedman’s post about Home Link received nearly 30,000 views in a few hours, we’re guessing those freebies have been claimed. Friedman said Home Link would be ready to ship a few weeks.

Muse Gadgets may not have wide appeal, but it fits nicely into Meta’s all-in strategy to make Muse more than a standalone chatbot. Meta isn’t content to push Muse on everyday consumers; it’s also trying to woo small businesses and enterprises.

The company earlier this week introduced Muse for Small Business, which is free with usage limits and connects Muse to tools such as Shopify, Dropbox, and Slack. It has also launched a new business unit, Meta Enterprise Platform, to help it push its AI offerings to businesses and corporate customers.

title: What’s new in Android’s September 2026 Google System Updates [U]
snippet: The monthly “Google System Release Notes” primarily detail what’s new in Play services, Play Store, and Play system update across Android phones/tablets, Wear OS, Google/Android TV, Auto, and PC. Some features apply to end users, while others are aimed at developers. more…
fullText:
The monthly “Google System Release Notes” primarily detail what’s new in Play services, Play Store, and Play system update across Android phones/tablets, Wear OS, Google/Android TV, Auto, and PC. Some features apply to end users, while others are aimed at developers.

The following first-party apps comprise the “Google System”:

Android AICore: Search the “All apps” list in Settings and open App info for the version number

Adaptive Connectivity Services: App info

Android Developer Verifier: App info

Android Pulse: App info

Android System Intelligence: App info

Android System Key Verifier: App info

Android System SafetyCore: App info

Android System WebView: App info

Android TV Core Services

Device Health Services: App info

Google Partner Setup: App info

Google Play Protect Service: App info

Google Play services: App info

Google Play Services for AR: App info

Google Play Store: App info

Google Play system update: Settings > About phone > Android version

Private Compute Services: App info

Quick Share Extension: App info

Search Engine Selector: App info

Settings Services: App info

SIM Manager: App info

System parental controls: App info

To update, open the Settings app > tap your name at the very top for “Google services” (on Pixel) > All services tab > Privacy & security > System services.

A feature appearing in the changelog does not mean it’s widely available. Some capabilities take months to fully launch.

	

Google Play services v26.38 (2026-09-28)

Account Management

[Auto] You can now sign in to your Google Account directly within the setup flow when you get started with Gemini in your vehicle.

Developer Services

[Phone] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Maps related processes in their apps.

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Analytics & Diagnostics related processes in their apps.

Support

[Phone] You’ll now get new features for Gemini, Circle to Search, Quick Share, Find Hub, and Android Auto.

Google Play Store v53.4 (2026-09-28)

[Phone] Removed the “Users are saying” header above the review paragraph summaries in the Details Page Rating & Review section.

Android WebView v155 (2026-09-23)

Refactored the androidx.webkit Navigation and NavigationListener APIs to be thread safe.

Improvements to security and privacy and updates for bug fixes.

New developer features for Google & 3rd party app developers to support functionality related to displaying web content in their apps.

Important: Some features may be experimental and available to certain users.

Related: Google rolls out Motion Assist bubbles to Pixel, Samsung

Google Play services v26.37 (2026-09-21)

Health & Fitness

[Wear] With this update, you’ll get improvements and bug fixes for real-time metric data sent from your watch to your phone.

Safety & Emergency

[Phone] With this update, Motion assist can help mitigate motion sickness with subtle, visual shapes that move in sync with a vehicle’s motion.

[Phone] With this update, you can more easily find the Driving Do Not Disturb feature.

System Management

[Phone] Updates to system management services that improve Device Performance and Stability.

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] This update adds support for larger and more refined system emoji font downloads.

Google Play Store v53.3 (2026-09-21)

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] You can now make purchases in local currency in Argentina, Azerbaijan, Uzbekistan, and Ethiopia.

[Wear] This update includes changes to the search results page.

[Phone] You can add a pre-registered paid title to your wishlist once it’s published.

Google Play services v26.36 (2026-09-14)

Account Management

[Phone] Bug fixes for Account Management related services.

Developer Services

[Phone] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Maps related processes in their apps.

Device Connectivity

[Phone, Wear] New developer features for Google and third party app developers to support Device Connectivity related processes in their apps.

System Management

[Auto, PC, Phone, TV, Wear] Bug fixes for System Management & Diagnostics related services.

Wallet

[PC, Phone] Enable real-time cart price adjustments when a user selects or changes their payment method during checkout.

Google Play Store v53.2 (2026-09-14)

[Phone] You can now use the Contribution Hub cluster on the “You” tab to submit ratings and reviews while you track the social impact of your contributions.

Android WebView v154 (2026-09-10)

We changed WebView Finch from Application consistent to Device level consistent.

Improvements to security and privacy and updates for bug fixes.

New developer features for Google & 3rd party app developers to support functionality related to displaying web content in their apps.

Important: Some features may be experimental and available to certain users.

Android AICore

[PC, Phone] Model management enhancements, expanded device compatibility, performance optimizations, and enhancements to diagnostics.

Google Play services v26.35 (2026-09-07)

Account Management

[Phone, Wear] Improvements to Supervision.

[Phone] A new infrastructure within Kids Auth Module to manage and display regulatory compliance notices on Android.

Location & Context

[Phone] This update adds safety status information to shared locations in the location sharing API.

Wallet

[Phone] You can now use NFC to add physical transit card passes and balances to Google Wallet.

[Phone] This update introduces a new “Add a card” success screen with an improved UI.

Google Play Store v53.1 (2026-09-07)

[Phone] You can now find a short description that highlights a key feature in similar apps, in the similar apps section of the app details pages.

[Phone] You can now find on what devices an app is installed when you browse recommendations on the other devices sub-navigation.

[Phone] With a new navigation bar, you can explore more of your interests directly on Play home pages.

Related: How to check if Motion Assist has rolled out to your Android 17 phone

Android System Intelligence B.29 / C.7 (2026-09-03)

[Phone] Bug fixes and maintenance changes.

title: Gemini app starts rolling out big side panel simplification, settings redesign
snippet: The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation. more…
fullText:
The next big update to the Gemini app on Android and iOS is beginning to roll out with a focus on simplifying core navigation.

There are no major changes to the homepage, with the first differences found in the side panel. Search has moved to the top-right corner, while the chat history now offers filters: All, Ready, Needs attention, and In progress.

“Scheduled” is a new item in the list and replaces the “Scheduled actions” page. You get “Suggested” prompts like Create a news digest or Build a study quiz.

“Customize” is the big update today. The “Discover” tab surfaces skills, which are replacing Gems, and third-party connected apps. Notably, skills are activated using the ‘@’ symbol instead of a forward slash like in Gemini Spark. This page feels like a mini-app store for Gemini.

	

Meanwhile, the “Connectors” tab serves as a modernized “Connected Apps” page. Gemini is leaning into that app store parlance with the ability to “Uninstall” from the overflow menu.

Meanwhile, Gemini is getting a much-needed Settings redesign when you tap your profile avatar in the top-right corner or the gear icon. Manage account and Usage limits make up the first grouping, followed by:

Preferences: Notifications, Personal Intelligence, Avatar, Gem manager, Theme, Voice, Media, Device controls, Gemini Notebook

Data & privacy: Import memory, Contact info from your devices, Gemini Apps Activity, Your public links, Privacy Help Hub

Support: Help, Report a problem, About, Updates 

This redesign is not yet widely rolled out and only appearing on one of our Google Accounts. That said, it’s appearing on both Android and iOS.

title: Google says Chromebook updates end in 2034, ‘many’ models move to Googlebook OS
snippet: As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward. more…
fullText:
As Googlebook arrives, Google is offering a bit more information on what Chromebook owners can expect going forward.

Google has said that Chromebook updates will continue in the Googlebook era, while some models will also be eligible for upgrades. On a support page, Google provides a bit more detail.

Starting with Chromebook updates, Google says that “Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime,” with all Enterprise and Education management capabilities remaining in place as well:

We will maintain support for current Chromebook devices running ChromeOS as outlined in our Auto Update policy and the Chromebooks you have today will continue to receive updates through their supported lifetime. Chromebooks remain available for all school and enterprise deployments today.

Your active ChromeOS Enterprise Upgrade and ChromeOS Education Upgrade associated with existing devices will remain and maintain their current management capabilities.

Google adds that similar management tools will be coming to Googlebook, but they’re not available yet. Apparently they’re planned for the second half of 2027. Meanwhile, Google says that “many” existing Chromebook models will be eligible to transition from ChromeOS to Googlebook OS. More details are coming “soon.” A later note specifies that Google is referring to “newer commercial Chromebook models.”

	

Many of our newest Chromebook devices will be eligible to transition over to Googlebook OS. Details on migration paths and device eligibility will be shared soon.

We are working to deliver a comprehensive management experience for Googlebooks which will start rolling out in the second half of 2027.

Notably, Google specifies a year when ChromeOS updates will come to an end in a later note – 2034. Chromebooks with a 10-year update policy that extends past 2034 will be eligible to move to Googlebook OS.

ChromeOS devices will continue to receive regular updates and security patches through mid-2034. For qualifying devices purchased today whose 10-year support lifecycle extends beyond 2034, Google is committed to supporting your transition to Googlebook OS, with many devices offering direct migration paths.

This 2034 date was previously mentioned in a court case as the time when Google would “phase out” ChromeOS.

	

Finally, in regards to apps, Google says that it is “committed” to web developers despite an increased focus on Android apps on Googlebooks.

Googlebook pre-orders are open now, with models shipping in early October.
