title: The clever way Apple embedded Face ID beneath the iPhone 18 Pro screen
snippet: In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display. Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering … more…
fullText:
In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken one of the next steps toward its long-term vision of the iPhone as a single slab of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without having the Face ID array be visible through the display and without compromising the quality of this section of the screen required some clever engineering …

Jony Ive described his long-term vision of the iPhone design as a single slab of glass, and while he is no longer with the company, that goal has remained. Eventually, Apple wants to embed all of the technology requiring screen real estate beneath the display, including both Face ID and front-facing camera.

The iPhone 18 Pro has achieved the first of these, but it was no easy task. Face ID requires infrared light to be both emitted and received by the TrueDepth module – and IR light cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple needed to create gaps between the pixels large enough to allow the IR light to pass between them, but without any visible degradation in the display. To do so, the company’s engineers set out to design a different pixel layout with larger gaps without visibly impacting what can be displayed on those pixels. 

iFixit used a microscope to show this pixel pattern, with Apple confirming to me me that the overall pixel density over the module is reduced by half. This would potentially have created a second problem: half the pixel density might have created a visibly dimmer section of the display, so Apple increases the brightness of these pixels to compensate. There also appears to be an IR pass filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further hiding the components.

The result is remarkable. For all practical purposes, the TrueDepth camera array is impossible to see even when staring at it extremely closely. I couldn’t capture it even using macro photography with different screen colors and lighting conditions. That’s not to say it’s completely impossible to detect, as iFixit’s microscope view shows, but rather that there is absolutely no way you’ll notice it in everyday use.

Right now, that achievement reduces the size of the Dynamic Island, which in turn enables support for three live activities rather than two. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. That’s technically possible today, but the compromise in image quality is currently greater than Apple is willing to accept. Solving that issue is a matter of when rather than if.

title: Star Wars: Galactic Racer Review: A Fantastic Burnout Successor From a Galaxy Far, Far Away
snippet: Developer Fuse Games’ debut release is one of the most impressive arcade racers in recent memory.
fullText:
It pains me to say it, but Star Wars’ cultural staying power has taken a massive blow in recent years – and for pretty good reason. Most of the Disney Plus shows have flopped, and the franchise’s return to cinema, The Mandalorian and Grogu, performed worse than any other theatrical release in the series’ history. Despite my lifelong fandom, I cast my eye upon the current state of the sci-fi space opera and feel a sense of apathy.

But Star Wars video games have remained consistently impressive in recent years – the soulslike Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor duology and the turn-based Star Wars: Zero Company were engaging entries in the canon, prioritizing fun gameplay over anything else.

Developer Fuse Games has continued this string of bangers across wildly different genres with Star Wars: Galactic Racer, an arcade-y game with speedy ships, plenty of underhanded action and a refreshingly self-contained story. It’s F-Zero meets Burnout, and it’s one of my new favorite racing games.

			

More from CNET

A classic underdog sports story with Star Wars set dressing

From the outset, I was uncertain if a plotline about a Star Wars racing league would remain narratively engaging over the course of an entire game — its spiritual predecessor, the 1999 podracing classic Star Wars Episode 1: Racer, didn’t bother with one. Once I found out Star Wars: Galactic Racer takes place between Return of the Jedi and The Force Awakens, I was even more skeptical – the sequel timeline hasn’t been an era for consistently engaging stories, after all.

It was a pleasant surprise, then, to discover that Galactic Racer tells a mostly novel story about a small corner of the universe coming to terms with a new normal after the downfall of the Galactic Empire. As it turns out, there’s not much time to engage with speeder racing when entire worlds are buckling under the tyranny of space fascism, so everything has to be put together again from the ground up.

Racing promoter Darius Pax has a passion for high-speed sports, and he’s wrangling sponsors for a new league by pulling in some of the best talent from across the galaxy. That includes shady characters like ex-TIE Fighter pilot Griff Halloran and kindhearted thrillseekers like old Soren Zaks. The most talented racer is nepo baby Kestar Bool, who is using his family’s riches to fund top-tier racing machines and initiate a hostile takeover of Pax’s assets. 

Players can choose among agile skim speeders like the one shown here, bulkier landspeeders or nimble speeder bikes.Fuse Games

To stave off the imminent threat of Bool seizing the league, Pax enlists the help of main character Shade and their happy-go-lucky mechanic Hibi to win the league championship and keep the sport pure. Shade has a devil-may-care attitude and a mysterious vendetta against the egoistic antagonist, so they’re happy enough to sign on to the competition.

The setup is your classic sports underdog story where you’re looking to score petty vengeance against your sneering opponent. There’s no high-stakes galaxy-level threat – this is a story about outperforming one bad guy on the most dangerous racetracks in the universe, and it rules.

Fuse Games describes the campaign structure as “runs-based,” which essentially means it plays out like many other roguelikes, where random rewards build up your kit as you progress up a procedurally generated tournament bracket. I’m not entirely sold on the integration of this concept for an arcade racer, but I appreciate how crashing out and losing too many events essentially scraps your vehicle and causes Shade and Hibi to begin anew. Shade is supposed to be a scrappy upstart, so losing your parts and upgrades and needing to retune the whole racing kit feels like it serves a narrative purpose.

The game features returns of some classic characters, and special modes where you can race their vehicles.Fuse Games

Galactic Racer does indulge in a little bit of nostalgia: Anakin Skywalker’s podracing rival, Sebulba, appears as a washed-up legend, while the antagonistic Bool family apparently built a large chunk of its wealth running part of the empire’s slave trade. There are plenty of cameos and one-off dialogue lines that will tickle lore nerds pink.

Still, there’s more restraint in this game’s storytelling than in most Star Wars projects, and the narrative is better off for it. I think fans want to explore new corners of the galaxy rather than follow the same handful of families – I know I do – and Galactic Racer debuts plenty of fun characters that don’t connect to high-stakes galaxy-ending plotlines.

The seedy underbelly of the Star Wars universe is perhaps the space opera at its most entertaining, even if that wretched hive of scum and villainy is largely composed of comically evil mobsters and smugglers. It’s great fun to explore that side of the sci-fi world without forcibly including a legacy character like Han Solo or Boba Fett.

Fuse Games

Scrappy, speedy and strategic playstyles are equally viable

There’s a surprising amount of depth to Galactic Racer’s build system. Before you even start a run, you need to decide whether you’re flying a versatile landspeeder, risky speeder bike or graceful skim speeder – each vehicle has different acceleration speeds, turning rates and drifting capabilities.

You’ll start a campaign tournament with mostly stock equipment, but each race won provides credits and upgrades that will help you prepare for the knockout championship event. Different parts provide passive bonuses on the track, and active abilities let you expend the vehicle’s energy at key moments to score advantages in a race.

As with any roguelike, I found a build type that worked for me: I routinely invest in my speeder’s afterburners and its volatile ramjet engine, picking up parts that permit boosting in the dangerous redline zone for longer before worrying about blowing up my craft. There’s still an appreciable level of friction that forces players to make hard decisions – you’re not guaranteed to find parts or abilities you like to use, and crashing or corroding your ship during races can do damage that carries debuffs over to the next event.

More kinetic abilities that encourage brawls with other racers are probably going to be fan favorites, because Galactic Racer has a sickly satisfying takedown system ripped straight out of the old Burnout games. Brushing up against other speeders and watching the sparks fly feels intense, and slamming into an opponent will reward you with a crash cam as they go careening off the track. This type of carnage may not win every run, but building a resilient chassis or dropping bombs to cause mayhem is absolutely cathartic.

That’s not to say that I’m completely in love with every ability you can pick up in the game. The addition of an autopilot is particularly silly to me, especially since drifting around sharp turns and racing clean lines feels gratifying. Worse, while it might buy a couple of seconds to activate traps or fix malfunctioning parts, the ability could just as easily betray you by ending right before you speed directly into a wall. It just isn’t particularly well-implemented – but that’s one of the exceedingly few balancing missteps I discovered.

Lots of thought was put into the roguelike structure of Galactic Racer, and it feels like there’s a viable path for every type of racer to win – whether you enjoy running clean lines or using underhanded tactics to force opponents off the track.

Fuse Games/Screenshot by CNET

This arcade racer can go the distance

There’s plenty of content for budding racers to take on once they’ve taken Kestar Bool down a few pegs in Galactic Racer’s story mode. The game features arcade time trials, multiplayer races, podracing events and more cosmetic rewards than you can shake a rathtar tentacle at. These are genuinely challenging races that could take hours to score a gold medal on, and I started to feel like a bit of a masochist after half a dozen attempts to master the ramjet-themed arcade event.

A notable pain point is the lack of an AI quick race – it seems like a massive oversight that there’s no mode where you can hop on, pick a track and difficulty and duke it out in a single match against some bots. This is something that I hope gets rectified soon.

A few flaws notwithstanding, it’s obvious that the development team at Fuse Games has an earnest love for this storied universe, and it shows through plenty of little tidbits and extra flourishes that flesh out the gameplay experience. Runs build into their own diegetic narratives as players crash out opponents and form rivalries that last throughout multiple races.

Characters react to your skill (or lack thereof), challenging Shade to one-on-one knockout races and proposing lucrative side bets before each event. It makes sense that any headstrong individual willing to strap themselves into a speeder bike and speed through the wreckage of a downed Star Destroyer would arrogantly put their money where their mouth is, and it makes the world feel alive.

Many of those elements carry over to the multiplayer tours, where players are able to gamble among themselves with credits earned in previous races. I can foresee this potentially getting a tad toxic in a public lobby, but in my experience, it was a great way for emergent narratives to form and made the mode feel all the more meaningful.

I can’t imagine this game will make many critics’ GOTY lists, especially when so many blockbuster projects have already been released. But Star Wars: Galactic Racer is easily one of my favorite games of 2026 – and not just because its gameplay loop had me inadvertently staying up for “one more run” at 3 a.m.

Among its many virtues, the game reminded me that there’s still value in a galaxy far, far away. Over breakneck races and loving details, my apathy for the series melted away, returning a childlike spark of awe and wonder for this sci-fi universe. I doubt a game like this will dictate the future creative direction of a juggernaut franchise like Star Wars, but Galactic Racer is surely something special for anyone who wants to ride their ramjet from Crait to Tatooine.

Star Wars: Galactic Racer is set to be released for PlayStation 5, Windows and Xbox Series X and S on Tuesday.

title: Apple TV renews French drama ‘Carême’ for season two
snippet: Apple TV today announced that French-language drama “Carême” has been renewed for a second season. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple TV today announced that French-language drama “Carême” has been renewed for a second season. Here are the details.

Apple TV renews ‘Carême’

Earlier today, Apple TV announced that “Carême,” starring Benjamin Voisin, has been renewed for a second season, with filming expected to start next week in Paris.

“Carême” debuted in April last year, and ran for 8 episodes with a 7.9/10 average on IMDb. The drama is based on Ian Kelly’s “Carême: The First Celebrity Chef” book, and is currently nominated for an International Emmy Award in the Drama Series category, as well as two Hollywood Music in Media Awards (HMMA) for its original score and main title.

The 54th International Emmy Awards Gala is set to take place on November 23 in New York City, while the 17th annual HMAA will be held a few days earlier, on November 18, in Hollywood.

Here’s Apple TV on the show’s premise:

“Carême” follows the thrilling story of the world’s first celebrity chef, Antonin Carême (Voisin), who rose from humble beginnings in Paris to the height of culinary stardom in Napoleon’s Europe. While he dreams only of becoming the most famous chef in the world, his talent and ambitions attract the attention of renowned and powerful politicians who use him as a spy for France. Determined to escape poverty and fulfill his dream, Carême can choose revenge or he can have it all — women, wealth, fame — but at what cost? His love? His soul? His life?

The platform didn’t announce a release date for the second season.

iPhone Duo pre-orders start on Friday, October 16, but Apple just announced when you can get an early start on the process. Here are the details.

Apple will let you ‘Get ready’ for iPhone Duo pre-orders beginning October 12 for fastest checkout

When Apple launches a major new iPhone model, it usually offers a window of time during which you can ‘Get ready’ for the pre-order by making your selections in advance.

The company just confirmed it will do the same for iPhone Duo. Per a new update on Apple’s website, you can begin the iPhone Duo pre-order process as early as Monday, October 12.

Starting October 12, and likely running through much of the day October 15, you’ll be able to go to the Apple Store app or Apple’s online store and make your pre-order selections in advance.

This includes choosing your iPhone Duo color, storage amount, wireless carrier, payment method, and more.

	

By completing this process ahead of time, Apple says you can get through checkout faster when iPhone Duo pre-orders go live on Friday, October 16 at 8:00 a.m. ET / 5:00 a.m. PT.

If you haven’t done it before, I highly recommend the ‘Get ready’ process to anyone ordering directly from Apple. It’s a great way to minimize potential hiccups on the morning of pre-orders, which means you’ll have a better chance of launch day delivery.

title: Honor Magic 9 Pro Max goes official with 8,800 mAh battery, ARRI cameras, Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on. more…
fullText:
Honor has officially announced its latest flagship in China, with the Honor Magic 9 Pro Max packing powerful specs, upgraded cameras, the latest Snapdragon chip, and confirmed for an global launch later on.

The Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is an all-out flagship with a heavy focus on its cameras, so let’s start there.

Continuing its ARRI partnership that debuted on the Robot Phone, the Magic 9 Pro Max packs a 200MP main camera with “gimbal-level stabilization,” a 200MP telephoto camera with 3.5x optical zoom, and a 50MP ultra-wide camera. Those are arranged on the back in the style of an ARRI cinema camera, and they’re also tuned by ARRI to produce better colors both in photos and videos. Honor is also building out additional hardware including two teleconverter lenses and a “Mobile Video Kit” in partnership with SmallRig.

The front-facing camera is no slouch either, with a 55MP sensor that’s paired with a 3D depth sensing camera for face unlock.

	

The phone surrounding those cameras packs a punch too. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max is powered by the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 and starts at 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage. Honor is using its own “Imaging Chip H1” to enhance camera processing, with MagicOS 11 based on Android 17 also available out of the box (with all its Liquid Glass-y-ness). The display is a 6.8-inch 2868×1320 OLED panel with Honor’s NanoCrystal Shield on top (which is both anti-scratch and anti-reflective), 10,000 nits of peak brightness – somehow –, 1-120Hz adaptive refresh rate support, and a 4,320Hz PWM dimming rate for better eye comfort. There’s an 8,800 mAh battery inside with 100W wired charging and 80W wireless, and the whole phone has IP68, IP69, and IP69K dust/water resistance ratings. 

Honor Magic 9 Pro Max specs

6.8-inch 2868×1320 LTPO OLED display, NanoCrystal glass, 4,320Hz PWM, 10,000 nits peak brightness

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/256GB, 12/512GB, 16/512GB, 16/1TB

MagicOS 11 based on Android 17

Rear Cameras: 200MP main (f/1.57), 200MP telephoto (f/2.6, 3.5x optical zoom, up to 200x digital zoom), 50MP ultrawide with autofocus

Front Camera: 55MP + 3D depth-sensing camera

8,800 mAh battery, 100W wired charging, 80W wireless charging

IP68/IP69/IP69K

The Magic 9 Pro Max is available today in China, but Honor says global availability is coming soon. Europe, MEA (Middle East & Africa), SEA (Southeast Asia), and “other key international markets” are all confirmed at this point, but there’s no reason to expect this one in the US. 

Honor also launched the Magic 9 in China.

It has a similar design but with a smaller 6.37-inch display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, a very similar camera array, and an 8,000 mAh battery.

title: John Ternus has big plans to make Apple ‘leaner’ and release more products
snippet: New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more. more…
fullText:
New CEO John Ternus has plans to “overhaul” Apple in an attempt to make it “run faster and leaner,” according to a new report from Bloomberg. This includes introducing more products, eliminating “middle-management positions,” and much more.

John Ternus wants to reshape Apple, here’s how

First, the new Apple CEO wants to release more products faster than before, including becoming “more experimental.” One idea is to shake up Apple’s release calendar and rely less on the typical spring-and-fall cadence, instead releasing more new products throughout the year. 

Ternus also wants to “create a leaner organization with a greater focus on engineering.” This includes several cost-cutting measures and restructuring. For instance, one change is “eliminating some middle-management positions to reduce the layers separating engineers from senior executives.”

The report says Apple has dismissed “a number of engineering program managers, or EPMs,” in its hardware engineering division over the last two weeks. Bloomberg describes these roles as having been “central to Apple’s product-development process for decades,” responsible for “managing timelines and coordinating work across teams.”

“The cuts affected several program managers, including roughly half a dozen directors, one of the company’s most senior employee levels,” the report says. “Those employees were given just weeks to find other positions within Apple. Those who don’t secure new roles will be laid off later this year.”

Bloomberg says the cost-cutting measures could go much broader than that, though. Ternus has reportedly advocated for Apple to be “leaner” for years:

Ternus, 51, has advocated for a leaner organization for years. While leading hardware engineering, he told employees during an all-hands meeting that Apple should hire fewer people, ask more of its existing engineers and reduce organizational bloat. During a presentation, he showed a slide charting annual headcount growth and argued that the company should be accomplishing more with fewer employees.

Furthermore, Apple reportedly scrapped a plan over the summer to lay off 5,000 AppleCare employees, believing that AI-powered agents could handle those responsibilities.

At the same time, Ternus wants Apple to increase revenue from Apple’s services division alongside Eddy Cue and CFO Kevan Parekh. “They have discussed launching new services and extracting more revenue from existing products and offerings,” the report says.

Ultimately, one source told Bloomberg that things are “hectic” inside Apple right now:

“Everything is a lot more hands-on than it used to be,” said one person familiar with the situation. “It’s hectic right now.” That person and others said managers in product-development groups are being pushed to deliver more products, more frequently and on shorter timelines.

You can read the full report at Bloomberg. It’s a fascinating piece that I highly recommend reading in full.

title: iOS 27 brings three key new features to Find My
snippet: iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 brings new features to almost all of Apple’s apps, including Messages, Apple Music, Wallet, and more. Apple’s Find My app has its own share of changes in iOS 27. Here’s everything new.

iOS 27: What’s new for Find My?

Apple touts three changes to Find My in iOS 27:

More flexible sharing options

UI enhancements

Apple Watch updates

First, more flexible sharing options in Find My give you more control over when and for how long you share your location with others. “Share your location for a custom duration or until a set date and time,” Apple says. You can also now “pause sharing with people individually, whenever you want.”

One of the bigger changes here is that you can now hide your location from a specific person without sending them any notification or alert. The other person won’t be notified when you pause, stop, or resume sharing your location with them.

Previously, you could turn off your location in the Find My app altogether, which wouldn’t send a notification. This, however, hid your location from everyone. In iOS 27, you can disable your location for specific people. 

To manage this, you’ll see a new “Hide Location” toggle on each person’s card in the Find My app. If you pause sharing your location with someone, they will see a “No Location Found” message in their Find My app.

Design changes

As for the UI enhancements, Find My in iOS 27 has been refreshed with a new Liquid Glass interface. The app largely missed out on Liquid Glass in iOS 26, but this year it has a new tab bar design that matches Apple’s other apps.

The Find My interface now also shows more specific location information on the app’s main page. This means you don’t have to tap on each person to view exactly what street they’re on at any given moment.

There is also new iconography in the Find My app in iOS 27. The “Items” tab, for example, is now denoted by a new AirTag-style icon.

Apple Watch updates

Finally, for cellular Apple Watch users, sharing your location will automatically use your Apple Watch when you’re away from your iPhone or iPad. 

Also on Apple Watch, there’s a redesigned, unified Find My app that integrates people, items, and devices into one interface.

snippet: Good morning. fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m going crazy over the NYT’s list of the best TV shows of the 21st century, redoing all of my vibe-projects with Opus 5.5, girding my loins for another Witcher 3 play-through now that the free remaster is out, and devouring Colson Whitehead’s new novel, Cool Machine.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

October 4th marks 10 years since Google debuted the Pixel, and over the next few days we plan to dive into the brand’s storied legacy. What started with a couple of HTC-built devices has expanded into an ecosystem that includes budget and flagship smartphones, smartwatches, earbuds, tablets, and more. 

	

The Pixel has served several purposes for Google throughout its lifespan, beginning as an extension of Nexus’s “Android best practices” before morphing into something a bit more complicated and abstract. When it debuted, Google emphasized the Pixel’s camera advantages, of which there were many, along with timely annual platform updates that arrived months before other Android devices.

As time went on, the Pixel brand came to encompass more than just smartphones; the company debuted its Tensor SoC inside the Pixel 6, and expanded the line to include the Pixel Watch, Pixel Buds, and a couple of failed Pixel-branded tablets. 

Perhaps the most remarkable thing about the Pixel lineup is its longevity; under Rick Osterloh, the brand has become synonymous with deep integration into Google’s services — of late, particularly Gemini — and a steward of thoughtful software and hardware design. The company’s products have made inroads in many markets, but still represent a single-digit share in most, including the US (despite solid year-over-year growth in 2026).

It’s perhaps also worth pointing out that the Pixel lineup has persevered in spite of many challenges, from major hardware issues with the Pixel 2 and 3 series to Covid-related supply constraints in the Pixel 5 to reputation-harming modem performance in the Pixel 6. It really wasn’t until 2023’s Pixel 8 series that Google shook its image as a mediocre hardware vendor and married superlative hardware with delightful software.

Today, the Pixel lineup is both the best and most predictable it’s ever been. The Pixel 11 series is yet another iteration on a design that debuted in 2021 with the Pixel 6. The Pixel Watch has looked identical since its 2022 debut. The Pixel Buds are fine but not competitive. The Pixel Tablet appears to be dead, and there’s no sign of a Pixelbook successor on the horizon.

Ten years in, is the Pixel brand where Google wanted it to be, with its cultural influence outpacing its financial viability? Perhaps not, but it’s also not likely to disappear anytime soon, which speaks volumes about its importance, both to the company and the community that keeps it in the conversation.

✉️ Inbox

🤝 Cc: Max Weinbach

Welcome to Cc:, where I ask interesting people in the community about what’s making them happy both inside and outside the world of tech. This week, I’m speaking with Max Weinbach, who used to contribute to 9to5Google and is now a tech analyst with Creative Strategies.

Who are you?

I’m Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. You might also know me from writing about phones at XDA and 9to5Google, or from spending way too much time talking about technology on Twitter.

What do you do for work?

I research and write about consumer technology, especially phones, PCs, chips, and AI. A lot of my work now is figuring out what AI can actually do when you give it a real task, real data, and the tools to finish the job. I also consider my job to be just knowing a lot about many different technology topics. 

That has turned into building things, too. We’ve been working on Diligence Stack and practical agent benchmarks, testing how the model, the tools, and the surrounding software affect the result. I want to know whether something can produce useful work and how much fixing it needs afterward. That tells me a lot more than a score by itself.

What do you do for fun?

I build things and play games. There’s quite a bit of overlap between my hobbies and my work. I’ll get interested in some software problem and end up with another side project. I’ve been spending a lot of time on native apps and experimenting with AI agents.

Reviewing gaming hardware is also a very convenient excuse to play something I’ve been putting off. That’s how I finally got around to Alan Wake 2 and picked Spider-Man 2 back up. 

On top of that, the classics of harassing playing with my dog and going to the gym. I’ve spent a lot of time learning about health and wellness. It’s just interesting to learn about and put into practice for me!

What is your relationship like with technology these days?

I’m still excited about it, but I care a lot about the experience of actually using something. A great spec sheet only gets you so far if the laptop is annoying, the software gets in your way, or the AI needs more supervision than the task was worth.

Some of my favorite products are the ones that are almost boring because they get the basics right. A comfortable laptop that runs the things I need, lasts a long time, and doesn’t have some weird deal-breaking issue is genuinely exciting to me. I’m also interested in how much easier it’s becoming to build the software I want to use.

What are three apps you can’t live without and why?

ChatGPT. I love ChatGPT as a product. It’s one of those apps that just let me kinda delegate whatever I want, and it will simply do it. It’s good for research, good for building one-off apps here and there, and just a great platform to help with anything I can think of. It doesn’t replace any actual work for me, but makes that work much easier and quicker. 

Whoop. Technically, an app and a product, but the product powers the app so I’m going with it. It’s one of my favorite ways to track health and wellness because it’s the first that has basically nailed the feeling of recovery and strain on a daily basis. In the morning I actually try to guess what the number will be based on what I feel, and I get it pretty close every morning. 

X/Twitter. X is one of my favorite ways to actually consume media and news, share my thoughts, keep up with friends. Yes, I know this is such a normal choice and nothing unique here, but I don’t know, I really like the app. My life would be very different without it.

What is a gadget that you love right now?

Plaud’s Note Pro MagSafe thing. It’s fantastic, and makes my life significantly easier all around when it comes to notes. I tend to have a good memory when it comes to meetings, so I tend to not take notes. That only gets you so far when it comes to specific details, and I find actually writing notes distracting. This thing solves it for me: take a recording, transcribe, and generate key notes while I can listen. Yes, voice memos exist on every phone and watch but I like this a lot more.

How does AI fit into your life right now?

It’s a big part of how I build and research things. I use agents for coding, testing ideas, and working through problems, then look at what they actually produce. The useful question for me is how close they get to a result I can use.

One recent example is having agents write and optimize Metal kernels for a local model, testing changes on the hardware as they go. I still choose between cloud and local models based on the job. Having the option to use both is valuable. 

I also have a ton of little ideas of how things should work, apps I want, little fun animations or widgets or whatever I can think of for my different products or phones or connecting to Siri and I can just make it by dictating into a magic box and an hour later it’s installed on my products.

What is a recent TV show you loved?

Lanterns, I think it’s just a fun good show that, while it’s not done yet, is just fun. It’s a superhero show that’s not a superhero show entirely. It’s simply a great story told extremely well with characters I like.

What is a recent game you loved?

Marvel’s Spider-Man 2. I bought a PS5 to play it and then never finished it, so reviewing the MSI Claw gave me a good excuse to start again. It looks fantastic, and the movement and combat work really well on a controller. I ended up getting into the game rather than constantly thinking about the hardware. When the testing was done, I kept playing.

What is something offline you do every day that brings you joy?

Spending time with Malibu, my Goldendoodle. It’s a good reason to put the computer down for a bit. Otherwise, I enjoy being online. It’s a good way to connect with the world and what interests me. I know a lot of people want to disconnect because the world is stressful, but that’s reality and I like it. I’d rather absorb it all and just make using technology, or being online, a normal thing rather than seeing it as this overarching bad thing that is ruining lives.

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

This year’s MTV Music Awards were pretty bad, but there was one standout performance that deserves mention. GENER8ION’s intense and beautifully choreographed song features Yung Lean standing in a sea of synchronized waving young men, and it’s a sight to behold.

Google’s updated Arts & Culture app is out — remember the one that went viral in 2018 for its selfie-matching feature? — and while it’s got some great stuff, it also got me to explore the little-known Labs section. In it I found this very cool AI-powered collaboration with SFMOMA on Henri Matisse, whose work is explained in dynamic richness through narration and augmented imagery.

It’s hard to believe that the hype around OpenClaw happened this year given all the changes and improvements to agentic AI since. Developer and AI enthusiast Simon Willison, who popularized the “pelican riding a bicycle” benchmark, has a thorough roundup on his blog of all the major announcements of 2026 so far.

🗑️ Trash

Samsung sells a lot of refrigerators. But as reported by Ars Technica (via Star News Korea), a failed firmware update caused some Korean owners’ fridges to “suddenly [lose] power and stop functioning.”

The unfortunate situation occurred right before the Korean holiday of Chuseok, so fridges were likely stocked full of perishables. Samsung said that it immediately halted the firmware update and was “taking emergency measures” on behalf of affected customers.

This is why we can’t have nice things… like dumb fridges that don’t require software updates.

title: Google Pixel 2 XL set the stage for a decade of ups and downs
snippet: Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel. more…
fullText:
Google Pixel’s 10-year anniversary has me taking a look back at a bunch of the milestones throughout this lineup’s history and, when picking up the Pixel 2 XL, hindsight really kicked in as to how this phone was very much a sign of the tumultuous roller coaster that would become Google Pixel.

The original Google Pixel hit the ground running and really did a great job pitching itself. A stellar camera was the main selling point, but Google’s thoughtful software, well-designed hardware, and ecosystem as a whole filled in the bigger picture to deliver a product that, outside of minor gripes, was about as “perfect” as you could ask for from an initial debut in a product category.

Fast-forward to a year later and, oof.

The Pixel 2 and Pixel 2 XL both arrived with some welcome upgrades across the board, but it was also abundantly clear that Google made some serious missteps. The smaller Pixel 2 was a tame revision in basically every way and, outside of the mega-thick bezels, was still a perfectly fine phone.

	

Pixel 2 XL, though, had some glaring flaws.

While I can look back fondly now on many aspects of the Pixel 2 XL, it’s wild in hindsight that a company at Google’s scale, even nearly a decade ago, made such a massive blunder. The Pixel 2 XL’s overall hardware stuck the landing. The updated dual-tone design still has that iconic “Panda” look and the colorful accent button that lived on through prior generations, but the glaring flaw on this device was the display. 

The LG-made panel was horribly inconsistent. In the best-case scenario, you’d get a panel with not-great viewing angles, slightly off colors, and burn-in issues. Worst case, a panel with a blue tint, black smears, and/or a grainy look. I still remember feeling like it was playing the lottery with buying this device and exchanging it to get a “good” one. Google tweaked this over time with software as well as by upping the warranty coverage, but it was still a huge problem with an otherwise great design.

And, in hindsight, that was kind of a signal of what was to come for Pixel as a whole.

	

The Pixel 2 XL tried something new and ultimately fell short, leading to a big correction the following year. Pixel 3 had a stunning display by comparison, and even to this day, Google has invested heavily in giving its phones some of the best displays you can find. The same pattern has been found throughout the lineup. New swings lead to new problems, with Google ultimately scrambling to make the best of it through software updates and making corrections later on. A similarly big problem came with 2020’s Pixel 6 series, with the modem in the first Tensor chip being truly terrible, but Google working to make the best of it in later software updates, only to iterate on the modem with each new generation to the point where, today, Tensor’s modem is roughly on par with anyone else in the ways that matter most.

Google Pixel remains a series that delivers ups and downs through each new generation, but it’s also clearer that the company has finally settled into something that works in 2026. Where the Pixel 2 XL was still in an era where Google would pivot on a whim, the Pixel 11 series comes from a place of stability, predictability, and at least mild success.

title: Vivo X Fold 6 skips the wide form factor, but will launch globally with strong cameras
snippet: Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises. more…
fullText:
Vivo’s new X Fold 6 doesn’t join in on the wide foldable trend, but it has some pretty wild camera promises.

The Vivo X Fold 6 packs a punch with an 8.02-inch inner display, a 6.51-inch outer display, and is running on a MediaTek Dimensity 9500 Super Edition chip. That’s with 12GB or 16GB of RAM and 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of storage.

The cameras are perhaps the biggest standout here, though, as foldables usually have to make some serious compromises in that department. 

The main camera is a 200MP Samsung HPB Large Sensor backed up by a 50MP 3x periscope shooter and a 50MP ultrawide. Everything uses ZEISS imaging and Vivo has a teleconverter add-on to extend the range of the camera. Vivo also says to expect a more responsive shutter and improvements to portrait mode and subject tracking.

	

Rounding out the package is a 6,900 mAh battery, IP58/59 dust and water resistance, and Android 17-based OriginOS 7 out of the box. 

Vivo has confirmed the X Fold 6 will see a global debut though, as always, don’t expect a US release.

title: Motorola’s wide Galaxy Z Fold 8 competitor might be very tiny and called ‘Razr Flex’
snippet: According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs. more…
fullText:
According to a new leak, Motorola’s upcoming entry in the wide, book-style foldable space may be called “Razr Flex” and pack some very familiar specs.

Specs for Motorola’s wide foldable were shared by Android Headlines alongside a possible name for the device – “Razr Flex.” That’s apparently the name being used internally around the device, so it’s unclear if that would be used as a consumer-facing name. The codename is “Parker,” the report claims.

Much more interesting are the details around the side of this foldable, which shares the same general form factor as Samsung’s smash hit Galaxy Z Fold 8, just in a much smaller footprint. Apparently, the outer display is just 4.97-inches in size – the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is 5.5-inches – while the inner display is less than 7-inches across. Very tiny by modern phone standards, even in this new form factor.

The leaked specs include:

	

4.97-inch outer display (1736×1140)

6.92-inch inner display (2364×1728)

110x149x5.8mm unfolded | 110x76x12.6mm folded

215g

Snapdragon 8 Gen 5

12GB RAM

256GB of storage

5,000 mAh battery with Qi2 (magnets unclear)

IP48/49

50MP main/50MP ultrawide rear cameras, 32MP selfie cameras

PANTONE Coriander, PANTONE Dark Botanical Garden

It’s important to stress just how much smaller this is compared to other wide foldables. iPhone Duo is thicker and heavier than Samsung’s phone, but has roughly the same screen sizes. The closest comparison is the Xiaomi 18 Fold, which has a 5.38-inch outer display, but even that still has a 7.58-inch inner panel. 

The specs are otherwise pretty familiar to the full-size Razr Fold that launched earlier this year.

Concept renders were also shared, but they’re explicitly not based on, well, anything except sketches and Motorola’s general design language – take them not just with a grain of salt, but maybe a whole container.

The “Razr Flex” is said to be launching this year with a “mid-December” debut mentioned.

title: Pixel Buds app update lets Gemini control audio and settings
snippet: With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update. more…
fullText:
With the Pixel 11 launch, Google promised a big Pixel Buds update in September. We’re now starting to see Gemini audio controls with the latest Pixel Buds companion app update.

After updating to version 1.0.981607934 of the Pixel Buds app, we’re seeing @Pixel Buds in Gemini as the latest Connected App. You can control “settings like EQ preset, ANC mode, conversation detection, and touch controls.”

Hey Google, turn up the bass

Hey Google, turn on noise cancellation

This brings up the Gemini overlay, with a “Connecting to Pixel Buds” message appearing along with verbal confirmation.

On devices without the app update, those commands just open the system Bluetooth settings page.

	

We’re seeing Pixel Buds 1.0.981607934 widely rolled out via the Play Store today.

The three other features Google previewed presumably require a firmware update. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 will get Dynamic ANC that adjusts to “compensate when subtle shifts in the seal happen,” like if the buds move in your ear. There’s also Pixel Watch sleep sync that pauses music, disables touch controls, and silences notifications on the Pixel Buds. Finally, you will be able to trigger Live translate by tapping your Pixel Buds.

title: Here’s When You Can See October’s Meteor Showers, Views of All 8 Planets and More
snippet: Skygazers can look forward to some spectacular sights this month, including one last good view of the Milky Way.
fullText:
As autumn paints the leaves, the universe is putting on its own seasonal spectacular. October features an action-packed lineup of meteor showers and celestial showcases. 

All eight planets are visible at some point in October

Mercury is visible just before sunset for several days in October.Stellarium

Every planet in the solar system is easily seen at some point this month, with Mercury being the most difficult. That’s not unusual, thanks to its proximity to the sun. Here’s a quick rundown on the best times to view each planet in October. 

Mercury: Mercury is in elongation (the furthest it can get from the sun) on Oct. 12, making that day and the two or so days before and after the best possible time to view Mercury. 

			

More from CNET

Venus: Venus spends most of the month being right next to the sun, making it virtually impossible to see. However, by the end of the month, it begins to separate from the sun, making it visible just after sunset. The best view is on Oct. 31, and the view is only set to get better going into November.

Mars: Mars will be visible in the night sky every night in October. It rises from the eastern horizon right around 2 a.m. and stays there until the sun comes up.

Jupiter: Jupiter and Mars are going to be pretty close together all month, so most of the same rules apply, except that Jupiter rises about two hours later than Mars on most nights in October. 

Saturn: Saturn is living its best life in October. It’s visible almost right at sunset ET and stays visible in the night sky until sunrise.

Neptune: Neptune is also visible every day in October and follows a very similar path to Saturn. It rises in the east, streaks across the sky, and sets in the west right around sunrise. They’re actually pretty close together in the night sky every night during the month, so if you can find Saturn, Neptune isn’t far off, but you’ll definitely need magnification to see it. 

Uranus: Uranus is visible the entire month and follows a very similar path through the sky as Saturn and Neptune, but its trek happens later at night. It rises on the eastern horizon about 2 hours after Saturn and follows it across the sky, but never really catches up, ending up in the high western sky when sunrise comes. 

Oct. 3-4: Saturn is at opposition

Saturn rises from the eastern horizon and treks across the sky overnight.Stellarium

Skygazers hoping to get the best possible view of Saturn can do so in the first week of October. The planet is at opposition — the point at which it’s closest to the Earth — meaning it’s as big and bright in the night sky as it’s going to get for the next year. This is prime time to pull out the telescope or high-powered binoculars and get a look at Saturn, along with its fabulous rings.

The planet reaches opposition at around 8 a.m. ET on Oct. 4. The best time to view is the night before, Oct. 3, or the evening after, Oct. 4. For both nights, Saturn rises out of the eastern horizon just before sunset and streaks up into the southern sky as the night goes on. The moon may cause some light pollution, but the planet is bright enough that it shouldn’t be hard to spot with the naked eye.

Oct. 5: The moon and Mars hang out

The moon and Mars are getting cozy on Oct. 5. Stellarium

The various objects in the sky are always having a dance party, at least from the perspective of viewing them here on Earth. Mars and the moon are due for a dance on the evening of Oct. 5. In the days leading up to it, Mars appears further up in the night sky but drifts closer to the moon. After Oct. 5, the moon will move rapidly away from Mars. The two will be almost right on top of one another, so if you can find the moon, Mars should be nearby. 

Oct. 6: The moon covers Jupiter entirely

The moon will pass in front of Jupiter, hiding it from view. Stellarium

Just one day later, the moon is meeting up with another dance partner, Jupiter. The moon will completely cover Jupiter, hiding it from view for much of the night, a phenomenon known as a lunar occultation. This is a pretty rare event. Per The Old Farmer’s Almanac, New York City saw a Jupiter occultation in 2004. The prior one visible to New Yorkers was in 1889. 

This one is pretty easy to see. The moon and Jupiter will be right on top of one another all night, but depending on where you live, you’ll see Jupiter dip behind the moon at some point and pop back out again. The times vary wildly depending on where you are, so we recommend checking out The Old Farmer’s Almanac, which has a table of times this will happen in major cities. 

Oct. 7: Draconids Meteor Shower

The Draconids meteor shower is in the Draco constellation near Vega. Stellarium

The Draconids meteor shower is a minor meteor shower that occurs every year around the first week of October. It officially starts on Oct. 6 and runs until Oct. 10, making it one of the shortest meteor showers of the season. It peaks on the evening of Oct. 7 and continues into the middle of the night. It’s fed by the 21P/Giacobini-Zinner comet, which is part of the Jupiter family of comets. 

Draconids meteors appear to originate from the Draco constellation. It sits high in the western sky in the northern hemisphere this time of year, with a slight lean to the north. If you’re using a sky map app, all you need to do is find Vega, and you’re already in the right neighborhood to catch Draconids. 

The peak is a little tame, at around 10 meteors per hour most years, but it has a history of surprising astronomers. In 1933 and 1946, Draconids spat out thousands of meteors an hour in what were two of the most intense meteor showers of the 20th century. On the plus side, the moon is below the horizon for this meteor shower, so you won’t need to worry about light pollution from the moon. 

Oct. 10: The last good chance to see the Milky Way

The Milky Way captured with the Tiny1 camera.

TinyMOS

The very best time to view the Milky Way is at a new moon in the warm months of the year, from May to August. This is when the Milky Way is high in the sky all night, giving night owls great views and plenty of time to photograph it. The problem is that it’s best viewed on nights with a new moon between midnight and 4 a.m. local time, which can be a bit late for some folks. 

September and October are great for this because the Milky Way is at its highest point between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. local time, giving the early birds a chance to snap some sweet photographs of the Milky Way. After October, the Milky Way is too low on the horizon to allow really good pictures of it until the following May. So, if you have a camera and are some place that’s dark, the new moon on Oct. 10 is probably your last chance to capture a striking photo before next spring. 

Oct. 21: Orionids meteor shower

The Orionids meteor shower will be low to the horizon in the east when its peak occurs. 

Orionids is the better-known of the two October meteor showers. This one officially starts on Oct. 2 and runs until Nov. 7. It’s possible to spot a meteor from Orionids any night during the month, but the shower reaches its peak on the evening of Oct. 21. Meteors for this shower come from the 1P/Halley comet, which also feeds the Eta Aquariids meteor shower that happens every year in May. 

This is a slightly more active meteor shower than the Draconids, and you can expect about 10 to 20 meteors per hour. The moon is set to be about 76% full that night, so you can probably expect to see fewer meteors thanks to lunar light pollution. The Orion constellation, where the meteor shower will appear to originate, doesn’t pop up over the eastern horizon until after midnight, so make sure to pack some coffee if you’re staying up late for this one. If you can find the stars Betelgeuse, Capella and Rigel, then you should be able to find Orion easily. They’re in the same general area. 

The Orionids meteor shower is best known for its bright, fast-moving meteors, which leave long trails that can last for over a minute and sometimes result in fireballs. Their brightness will be a boon, with the three-quarters-full moon in the sky hindering viewing. 

Oct. 26: The Hunter Moon

A full moon rises behind the Washington Monument. NASA/Bill Ingalls

October’s full moon falls close to Halloween this year, perfect for spooky views. According to The Old Farmer’s Almanac, October’s full moon reaches its peak on Oct. 26 at 12:12 a.m. ET. It’ll also be over 90% full for a couple of days before and after, giving you a solid five days to check it out. 

October’s full moon isn’t quite a supermoon. A full moon is only classified as a supermoon when the moon is in perigee and full at roughly the same time, and October’s full moon misses the mark by a couple of days. October’s full moon is the last normal full moon of the year. November and December close out 2026 with supermoons before January opens with the final supermoon of this cycle. 

Oct. 27: The moon eclipses the Pleiades

The moon will eclipse the Pleiades before either rises in the sky, but most people will still get to see part of it.Stellarium

Pleiades is one of the best star clusters to view in the night sky. They’re known as the Seven Sisters, and in terms of clusters of stars, it’s one of the easiest to see. The exception is on Oct. 27, when the moon will cross in front of them, blocking them almost entirely from view. When this happens depends on where you’re located. 

The moon begins passing in front of them before sunset in eastern time, and moves out of the way around midnight. Those on the East Coast will start the night in the middle of this little eclipse, while those on the West Coast will glimpse it at the very end. Finding it should be simple enough since the moon is the easiest thing to see in the night sky.

All month: Constellations and asterisms

The sky is continuing its rearrangement from summer into autumn, and there are tons of constellations to gaze at over the course of the month. Many of September’s constellations appear again, including both Dippers, Aquarius, Pegasus, Pisces and many others. October plays host to a few new ones in the night sky cycle, including Taurus, Cetus, Auriga and Orion, which will appear low on the horizon as they begin their months-long ascent into the sky for the winter. 

There are some smaller asterisms to observe as well, including the Coffin of Delphinus, the Circlet of Pisces and the Northern Cross. We recommend using a sky map to find them all, as there are quite a lot. That’s good news, because even if you don’t go out during one of the big events in October, you’ll still have plenty of objects to look for in the night sky.

title: The Googlebook marketing push starts with Henry Cavill and his mustache
snippet: Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill. more…
fullText:
Ahead of next month’s launch, Google is beginning the marketing push for Googlebooks with Henry Cavill.

The company announced today that it partnered with actor and tech enthusiast Henry Cavill to “help showcase the potential of this next-generation laptop.” Google is specifically referring to “unique software experiences like Continue on phone syncing, Rambler speech-to-text, Antigravity and so much more.”

Cavill, who is a big PC gamer, uses an Android phone. He previously used Pixel phones, with the last appearing to be the Pixel 5, while he was most recently spotted with a Galaxy S25 Ultra.

Google is very much leaning into that: “We recently met with Henry to discuss his own creative ambitions and the conversation quickly turned to the need for a laptop that could keep up with him and work seamlessly with his Android phone.”

	

The premise of this marketing campaign is that Henry Cavill will use a Googlebook to “build a video game.” He’s seen using the HP Googlebook 14 today.

“When Google reached out to me and explained what they are doing with Googlebook, and all of its new, integrated tools, it had me intrigued. So, I asked for the opportunity to have a play with it ahead of release. After being hands on and spending some time with their team, I believe this has the potential to be the start of something rather special. Time and technology are marching forward at a breakneck pace, this, and all that Google are trying to do with it, has the whispers of the next generation.”

—Henry Cavill

This passion project will get underway in November, with @Android on Instagram providing updates, while there’s now a dedicated page: googlebook.google/henry-cavill.

More broadly, Google heavily advertising Googlebooks will be key to its success and this is definitely a start. Hopefully, this will be followed by traditional online and TV campaigns.

title: Reminders just got more powerful, here’s what’s new in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 adds new features to Apple Notes, Messages, Wallet, and more, and it has a few improvements for the Reminders app too. Here’s everything new for Reminders in iOS 27.

#1: Describe your reminder

Reminders has offered some level of natural language support for new reminders for a while. But in iOS 27, Apple Intelligence upgrades the feature.

When creating a new reminder, type everything out in natural language and when you type certain info, like a due date, the keyboard row will suggest adding that date to the reminder.

Some basic version of this was available before, but Apple Intelligence makes it more accurate and provides more options than before. Per Apple:

Describe a New Reminder: Use your own words to describe a reminder and Apple Intelligence will help create it for you.

This ‘Describe’ functionality now extends to the reminder detail screen too, letting you jot down your reminder and have it automatically adopt all of the relevant metadata you mention. 

Every time you add or edit reminders inside a list, iOS 27 upgrades the experience with more tools conveniently accessible than before.

In iOS 26, when creating or editing a task you would see five options above the keyboard row: Date, Location, Tag, Flag, and Camera.

In iOS 27, Reminders moves all metadata options into a new box that surrounds your active reminder. And it’s far more robust, with the new UI letting you modify the following:

Date

Time

Urgent

Repeat

Location

Tag

Flag

Camera

You can still tap the ‘i’ icon to view the full set of metadata options, but with iOS 27 you shouldn’t have to do that nearly as often.

#3: Grocery list improvements

Apple says that Reminders’ grocery list auto-sorting feature has been made better in two ways:

it now “sorts grocery list items more accurately”

and grocery list sorting expands to multiple languages

Essentially, due to the more powerful Foundation Models in iOS 27, this feature that’s been around a while is going to work better than ever.

More info on Reminders’ grocery list feature is available here.

title: Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are $399 with better hardware, ANC, and audio upgrades
snippet: Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output. more…
fullText:
Nothing is today introducing its new Headphone (1) Pro over-ear headphones which deliver hardware improvements, better ANC, and deeper control over how you can tune the final output.

Following up on last year’s Nothing Headphone (1), the new Pro model brings upgrades across the board. That includes the physical hardware, which is a tiny bit lighter at 327g, while also getting softer ear cups, a wider headband, and thicker padding throughout. The design is also updated with a cleaner look and subtler accents, as well as glass in place of the previous plastic portions.

The biggest upgrades here are the ones that power the audio, though.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro gets a triple-driver design that provides not only better audio quality, but far more control and flexibility throughout the tuning. In the Nothing X app you get a more advanced custom EQ interface with the option to independently adjust the main drivers and the third “precision driver.” You can get into the weeds of every little detail of the audio here, and it’s far more advanced even compared to the rest of Nothing’s audio gear.

	

Nothing built out the audio experience here with the help of Metropolis Studios, and Headphone (1) Pro also offers a physical switch to let you quickly jump to a “Flat” EQ for a completely neutral sound profile. There are also several presets for Spatial Audio that simulate listening locations such as “Live House,” “Concert Hall,” and more, with head tracking optional.

Active Noise Cancellation is also boosted here, hitting 46 dB, up from the 42 dB on Headphone (1). Nothing says this is through a 10-mic system and a stronger sound seal from the new earcups. 

Like on Headphone (1), Pro supports lossless audio over USB-C while supporting Hi-Res wireless playback as well. You also still get the same plethora of physical controls across the side including the paddle and wheel. 

I’ve been using Nothing Headphone (1) Pro for a few days and, while it’s too early to make a full verdict, there are meaningful improvements throughout, including the much more comfortable hardware. The sheer number of options around tuning the sound quality borders on overwhelming, so I’m still figuring out exactly how I like to listen.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro will be available starting tomorrow, September 29, at Nothing’s website, Amazon, and Best Buy.

title: ‘HomePad’ coming: Will Apple hold an October special event?
snippet: With Apple reportedly planning to unveil new products on October 13, here’s when the company could announce an event, based on the timing of its previous October announcements. more…
fullText:
With Apple reportedly planning to unveil new products on October 13, here’s when the company could announce an event, based on the timing of its previous October announcements.

Will Apple hold an October event?

While Apple’s September event history tends to follow a very predictable pattern, the company’s October event history is much less precise, both in terms of when the events are held and how far in advance they are announced.

Since 2010, Apple has held an October event just 10 times, with the most recent one being the Halloween-themed “Scary Fast” event on the evening of October 30, 2023.

Here’s how far in advance Apple has announced each of its October events since 2010:

That said, Bloomberg recently reported that Apple plans to unveil its long-rumored smart home hub, a new generation of the HomePod mini, and a new Siri AI-powered Apple TV 4K on Tuesday, October 13, though it did not specify whether the company will hold an event to announce the products.

If that turns out to be the case, Apple could potentially announce the event as early as next Monday, October 5, but likely no later than Wednesday, October 7.

It’s worth noting that Apple is also expected to announce an OLED iPad mini, new iMacs, and several new MacBook Pros, including touchscreen models, in 2026. So it remains to be seen whether some of those products would be unveiled at the same event, at a separate event, or through press releases.

Looking back, Apple announced new Macs through press releases over three consecutive days in October 2024, while in October 2025, it unveiled the M5 chip alongside new iPad Pro, MacBook Pro, and Apple Vision Pro models without holding an event.

By contrast, Apple has only held a November event once, in 2020, when its “One More Thing” event introduced the first Macs powered by the M1 Apple silicon chip.

Of course, 2020 was an unusual year for Apple’s event schedule, with the company also holding separate events in September and October after a rare late-June WWDC, as the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted its usual timeline.

Which new products do you think Apple will announce at the rumored October event? Let us know in the comments.

title: What to Expect From This Week’s Microsoft Windows and Surface Event
snippet: The Surface Laptop Ultra with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip could take center stage.
fullText:
Microsoft is gearing up to drop even more news for Windows and Surface laptops. The tech titan is hosting a Windows and Surface event on Wednesday in San Francisco, its first laptop-centric event in two years. This is everything we’re expecting to see — and no, sorry, Windows 12 is not on the list.

The event will be a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” according to Microsoft. That makes sense as Microsoft has been all-in on AI by incorporating Copilot everywhere and partnering with chip makers like Qualcomm to bring enough firepower to its devices to handle the computational load of generative and agentic AI tasks. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and the head of Windows and Devices, Pavan Davuluri, are slated to speak.

This event could be when Microsoft actually drops the Surface Laptop Ultra, a 15-inch high-end variant first announced this spring at Computex. The Ultra is powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip, so Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s slated appearance at the event is another sign toward the Ultra. 

			

More from CNET

We already got two new Surface laptops this month, previewed at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit. At the Hawaii event, Microsoft upgraded its Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface 13-inch laptops, running on Snapdragon Elite X2 chips, and introduced a new Surface mouse to go along with them. The new laptops have better cameras and “embody the PC-phone marriage Qualcomm promised years ago,” CNET’s David Lumb reports.

A big question will be prices. Computer hardware companies have raised their prices across the board, from Apple to Asus and Acer, over the last year to keep up with rising manufacturing costs. AI is at least partially to blame, with advanced chips in hot demand for data centers as well as laptops and phones. Other costs, like price increases in Windows licenses during the manufacturing process, may also be contributing to higher price tags. The result, sometimes called RAMageddon, is that it’s more expensive to buy new devices.

Microsoft’s Windows and Surface event begins at 10 a.m. PT / 1 p.m. ET on Wednesday. It is being held in San Francisco and will be livestreamed on YouTube. CNET will be on the ground to bring you all the latest Microsoft news.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.
